The Bridge known as Doctors Bridge carrying Greenway Road over the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal. The Bridge known as Waterloo Bridge carrying Waterloo Road over the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal. The Bridge carrying Greenway Road over the London and North-Western Railway. The Bridge carrying Heath Road over the said Railway. Sandy Lane. The Bridge known as Victoria Bridge carrying Victoria Road over the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal at the entrance to the Big Pool. The Bridge called Bates Bridge which carries Sea Lane over the Duke of Bridgewater's Canal. The footbridge which crosses the Duke of Bridge- water's Canal at the top of Ellesmere Street into the Manchester Ship Canal Works, known as the " Sprinch Yard." The footbridge which crosses the Duke of Bridge- water's Canal from Halton Road (near to the bottom of Stonehills Lane) to Canal Street. The footbridge which carries the footpath from Balfour Street across the London and North-Western Railway to Picow Street. ' Westfield Road (otherwise Cock and Hen Lane). The continuation of Percival Lane to its junction with Westfield Road (otherwise Cock and Hen Lane) by the road which runs in a south-westerly direction from the said continuation under the bridge, carrying _ the Dock Branch of the London and North-Western Railway, The Towpath of the River Weaver Canal. The Manchester Shin Canal. (b) RAILWAYS—The Dock Branch Railway Line of the London and North-Western Railway Company in the Urban District of Runcorn. The Dock Branch Railway Line of the Manchester Sbip Canal Company in the Urban District of Runcorn,and the extension of that line in a southerly direction to joie the siding or tramway of the Com- pany. (C) TRAMWAYS.-110 private tramway of the Runcorn and Helsby Red Sandstone Company. 5. TO authorise the Company to take, collect and recover rents rates and charges for the supply of, electricity for lighting power or other purposes, and the use of any machines, lamps, meters, fittings or apparatus connected therewith, and to prescribe and limit the price to be charged therefor.

_ 6. TO confer upon the Company all or some of the powers of the Electric Lighting Acts, 1882 and 1888, and any enactments incorporated therewith, and to alter vary or extinguish all rights and privileges which would or might interfere with any of the objects of the Order, and to confer all other rights and privileges necessary for carrying such objects into effect. 7. TO incorporate with the Order such of the pro- visions contained in the Schedule to the Electric Lighting (Clauses) Act, 1899, and in any Act amending or extend- ing the same as are applicable to cases in which the Undertakers are not the local authority, and to apply such provisions to the undertaking to be authorised by the order subject to such variations and exceptions as may be contained therein. 8. TO make special provisions with respect to the rights and obligations of the Company to afford a supply of electricity to premises having a separate supply, and the terms and conditions on which such bupply will be afforded, and if and so far as is necessary to modify or exempt the Company from the obligations in reference thereto imposed upon undertakers by the Electric Lighting Act, 1882, and the Acts amending or extending the same. 9. TO provide that the Company may refuse to supply electrical energy to any persons whose payments for the supply of such energy may be in arrear, and bo require that the consumers of electrical energy shall give notice to the Company, before quitting any premises supplied with such energy by the Company, and to provide for the liabilities of such consumers when the requisite notice is not given. 10. TO empower the Company within a limited period after the commencement of the Order and with the consent of the Board of Trade, to transfer the undertaking authorised by the Order to a Company to be named in the Order on such terms and conditions as may be approved by the Board of Trade. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the draft of the Order will be deposited at the offices of the Board of Trade on or before the 21st day of December next and printed copies of the draft Order when deposited and of the Order when made may be obtained (at the price of one shilling for each copy), at the Counting House at the Works of the Company at Weston Point Runcorn and at the offices of the under-mentioned Solicitors and Parliamentary Agents. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN that a map shewing the boundaries of thearen of supply and the streets in which it is proposed that electric lines shall be laid down within a specified time and a copy of the advertisement as published in the London Gazette will be deposited on or before the 30th day of November, 1909, for public inspection with the Clerk of the Peace for the County of Chester at his office at Chester, at the office of the Clerk to the Runcorn Urban District Council at Runcorn, and at the office of tbe Clerk of the Runcorn Rural District Council at Runcorn and at the office of the Board of Trade. Whitehall, London.

AND- NOTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN that every local or other authority, company or person desirous of bringing before the Board of Trade any objection respecting the application must do so by letter addressed to the Board of Trade marked on the outside of the cover enclosing it "Electric Lighting Acts" on or before the 15th day of January 1910 and a cony of such objection must also be forwarded to the udder-mentioned Solicitors or Parliamentary Agents. (Conferring further Powers on the Corporation of Warrington; New Bridge to replace present War- rington Bridge; ' Construction of New Bridges over River Mersey; River Walls; Widening and Improve- ment of Streets and Roads; Purchase of Garven House Property; Purchase of Lands by Compulsion or Agreement; Extension of Public Baths and Technical School; Sale of Howley Recreation Ground; Power to deal with proceeds of Sale ; Extension of Town Hall; Further Provisions as to the Gas, Water and Electricity Undertakings of the Corporation; Free Wiring; Supply of Electricity in bulk; Motor Omnibuses; Licensing of Drovers, ; Ice-Cream Provisions: Advertising Vehicles; Common Lodging-Houses; New Streets and Build- ings; Sewers and Drains; Infectious Disease and Sanitary Provisions; Subscriptions; Borrowing Powers; Rates ; Police Provisions; Incorporation, Amendment, and Repeal of Acts). -NOTICE is hereby given that application is intended to be made to Parliament in the ensuing Session, by the Mayor, Aldermen and Burgesses .of the county borough of Warrington (in this Notice called "the Corporation ") for leave to bring in a Bill for all or some of the following purposes (namely) :- 1. To empower the Corporation to make and main- tain, wholly in the county borough of Warrington, and the County Palatine of Lancaster, the following of -works or some of them, or some part or parts thereof (that is to say) : Work No. I,—A Bridge to replace the present Warrington Bridge crossing the River Mersey between Bridge Street and Knutsford Road and occupying as -nearly as may be the site of the existing bridge. Work No. 2.—A training wall on the northern bank of the River Mersey commencing at a noint 70 yards measured in a south-westerly direction from the south-east corner of Bridge Foot House and extending in a north-easterly, direction for a distance of 120 yards or thereabouts and terminating at the westerly end of the Packet stage. Work No. 3.—A training wall on the southern bank of the River Mersey commencing at a point 33 yards or thereabouts measured in a north-westerly direction from the south-west corner of the Bridge Inn and extending in a north-easterly direction for a distance of 75 yards or thereabouts and terminating at a point 47 yards or thereabouts measured in a north-westerly direction from the south-west corner of Water Street. Work No. 4.—A widening of Knutsford Road com- menting on the southern hank of the River Mersey at the south-east end of Work No. 1 and ektending in a south-easterly direction for a distance of 103 yards or thereabouts and terminating on the east side of the premises now occupied by Mr. John Lunt. Work No. 5.—A widening of the western side of the southern approach of Warrington Bridge from a point on the southern bank of the River Mersey at the termination of Work No. 1 and extending in a southerly direct ;MI for a distance of 50 yards or therenhonts to Wilderspool Causeway. Work No. C.—A widening of Chester Road on the south-east side from its Junction with River Road to its junction with Stag Bridge. Work No. 7.—A bridge crossing.'"the River Mersey at Howley commencing en the western bank at a point. 87 rrds or thereabouts measured in a southerly fiirer ti on from the south corner of the warehouse of the Bridgwater undertaking of the Manchester Ship Canal Company and terminating on the eastern bank at a point 70 yards or thereabouts drawn in an easterly direction from the point of commencement. Work No. B.—An approach road on the western side of the said bridge and commencing by a junction with the said bridge at its commencement and terminating by a junction with Parr Street. at a point 90 yards er thereabouts, measured in a westerly direction from the point of commencement of this work. Work No. 9.—An apnrosch road on the western side of the said bridge commencing by a junction with the said bridge at its commencement and terminating by a junction with. Navigation Street and Egerton Street, at a point 134 yards or there- abouts measured in a northerly direction from the commencement of this work. Work No. 10.—An approach road on the eastern. side of the said bridge. commencing by ajnnetion with the said bridge at its termination and terminat- ing by a junction with Knutsford Road, at the entre:lee to Victoria Park, Work No. 11.—A river wall alone the south side of the River Mersey and a widening of the north side of Knutsford Road commencing at a point 120 yards measured in a westerly direction from the entrance to Victoria Park, and extending in a westerly direc- tion for a distance of 210 yards and terminating at a point 57 yards or thereabouts measured in a north- easterly direction, from the centre of the north end of Grove Street. The whole of the above works will be situate in the

21. To provide that enactments relating to hackney carriages and other public vehicles shall apply to vehicles conveying passengers to and from railway stations within the Borough. 22. To empower the Corporation to lay out, improve, furnish and equip for the purposes of publio recreation and enjoyment the lands known as Victoria Park and to authorize the Corp&ation to purchase part of St. Elphin's Park arid to lay out and improve the same. 23. To make further provision for improving the water snpply of the Corporation. 24. To make further provision with regard to the manufacture and supply of gas and particularly to pro- vide for the increase of discounts on gas accounts and the use of anti-fluctuators'for gas engines, the giving of notices of removal and discontinuance of supply and the method of dealing with erroneous registration by gas meters, to require any person who has a private installation of gas for power or other purposes to pay a minimum charge for gas supplied by the Corporation and to impose other terms and conditions in connection with such supply, to prescribe a minimum charge for gas laid on to premises having a supply of electricity, and to regulate the construction and repair of pipes and apparatus between the mains of the Corporation and the meters on the premises of consumers. 25. ro amend the provisions of the Warrington Cor- poration Gas Act, 1877, as to charges for gas in and beyond the borough, and in particular to provide for a lower minimum additional charge or for an increased discount to consumers outside the borough. 26. To amend section 107 of the Warrington Corpora- tion Act, 1899, and to empower the Corporation to make byelaws with respvit to the nature materials, 'work- manship and strength. and the mode of connection, disconnection, alteration and repair of gaspipes, meters, taps, fittings and apparatus, and with respect to the giving of notice to the Corporation by persons -requir- ing a supply of gas or intending to construct or alter their gas-fittings, or other apparatus. 27. To authorize the Corporation to supply, fix, repair, and remove motors and electrical fittings of all kinds and all materials and work necessary in connec- tion therewith, and to take such remuneration and make such terms and conditions as they may think fit in relation thereto, and to provide that the same shall not be liable to distress for reet or to execution.

28. To require any person who has a separate supply of electricity from any installatian other than that of the Corporation to pay a minimum charge for any supply be may require from tbe Corporation, and to enable the Corporation to impose other terms and conditions in connection with such supply.

'29. To require electric lighting COniumers to give notice to the Corporation before removing from any premises supplied with electric current by the Corpora- tion, to provide that the Corporation may refuse to supply electric energy to persons owing money to the Corporation, and to authorize the Corporation to allow discounts or rebates on electric lighting and power accounts. 30. To enable the Corporation to enter into and fulfil agreements for the supply of electric energy in bulk or otherwise to the local authorities, companies or persons outside the district, and particularly to empower the Corporation to supply energy to any consumer whose premises are within 200 yards (or such other distance as the Bill may prescribe) of any electric main or cable of the Corporation, and to empower the Corporation to supply electric energy for traction Purposes to be used either within or beyond the borough, and to authorize the purchase of electric energy in bulk by the Corporation. 31. To empower the Corporation to lay mains, pipes, wires and other apparatus for electric supply in streets and other places not dedicated to public use. 32. To empower the Corporation to provide and run' motor omnibuses either within or outside the borough and to take fares and charges for conveyance therein, and in connection therewith to acquire and provide land, buildings, plant, apparatus and other things, and to make bye-laws and regulations for regulating the travelling in and use of such omnibuses and for prevent. inc nuisances and injury. 33. To confer further powers upon the Corporation in reference to the laying out of new streets, the erec- tion of new buildings, and the construction of sewers. 34. To authorize the removal of dilapidated build- ings, to prescribe the area of habitable rooms, to prevent water flowing on footpths, and soil and sand from being washed into streets. 35. To amend section 70 of the Warrington Corpora- tion Act, 1899, and to make provision with respect to the removal or alteration of any door, shutter. trap, platform, sign or other projection, apparatus, or thing against or in front of any building and causing or likely to cause danger or obstruction to the use of any street. • _ _

36. To require that all communications wit la sewers of the Corporation he made by the Corporation at the expense of the owner or occupier of the premises con- cerned, to amend and extend the provisions of section 11) of the Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 1890, to provide that watercoursesmay not be covered up except in accordance with an approved plan. 37. To make further provision for improving the aanitary condition of the Borough and particularly to impose penalties for the improper construction or rertair of water closets or drains, to enforce the pro- vision of sanitary dustbins, and to authorize the Corporation to provide street orderly bins, to require a certificate to be given in the case of a person dying of infectious disease, and to prohibit the blowing or inflation of carcases, and to make provision with regard to the manufacture and sale of ice creams and other similar commodities and the inspection of premises in connection therewith, and the use of vehicles and stands by ice-cream dealers." _ _

County Borough of Warrington. 2. To enable the Corporation in connection with the above-mentioned works to construct all necessary and proper foundations, embankments, training walls, arches, girders, piers, supports, anchorages. piles, plat- forms, jettys,landing stases, wharves, sluices, engines, dynamos, weighing-machines, sheds, offices, approaches, buildings, lifts, stairs, apparatus, machinery, appliances, and works connected therewith. 3. To provide for the carrying of tramways Inning and pipes and electrical conductors, wires and apparatus on or along the intended bridges, and to authorise agreements with companies and persons in respect thereof. 4. To empower the Corporation to niece piers and supports for the intended bridges in and upon streets and roads, end in the foreshore or bed of the River Mer.ey, and in other respects to alter or interfere with the bed, banks or foreshore of the said river. 5. To make such provisions as may have been or may be agreed upon, or as may be thought proper by Parlia- ment to he prescribed or authorized by the Bill for the protection of any Commissiorers or other body having jurisdiction over any part of the River Mersey, or for the protection and benefit of landowners and other bodies and persona whose property, rights and interests will or maybe affected by the intended works, and to authorize, confirm or give effect to any agree- ments or arrangements which may he entered into between the Corporation and such landowners, bodies or persons. or some or any of them. and to empower the Corporation to execute any works necessary for the purpose. C. To authorize the Corporation to remove, scour, take, and carry away all rock, beds of gravel and sand and other impediments, and execute all other works necessary or convenient for making or maintaining and I repairing the intended works and approaches thereto. I'. To empower the Corporation to deviate laterally and vertically from the lines and levels of the intended bridges, street works, river walls and other works shown on the deposited plans hereinafter mentioned to the extent to be shown on the said plans, or to he defined in the intended Act, and in either case beyond the limits of lateral and vertical deviation prescribed by the Reilways Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845. 8. To authorize the Corporation, for the purposes .of the intended Act, to break up, cross, alter the level of -and otherwise alter, widen, narrow, divert, stop up and interfere with (either temporarily or permanently) streets, roads, highways, footpaths. rivers, streams, navigations, watercourses. sewers, drains, pavements, mains, pines, tramways, telegraphs, telephones, electric wires and conductors, and apparatus, to raise, sink or alter step: areas, cellars, windows, spouts and pipes, and to tinder-pin or otherwise strengthen (either tempo- rarily or permanently) houses or other premises. 1. To make special provisions as to the accommoda- tion of persons of the labouring class displaced by the execution of any of the works authorized by the Bill. 10. To empower the Corporation to purchase or acquire by compulsion or agreement or to take on lease lands, houses and buildings, and rights or easements therein. 11. To make special provisions with respect' to the compenvation to be paid in respect to the taking of lands or the execution of works under the potvers of the 13111, end with respect to the method of ascertainment of such compensation, the payment of costs, the delivery of claims, and other matters of procedure connected therewith, and to provide that the benefits accruing to any person from any street improvement or other work shall be set off against the purchase price or compensa- tion payable by the Corporation. 12. To exempt the Corporation from the operation of section 92 of the Lands Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845. so as to enable them to purchase compulsorily part only of certain properties. 13. To make provision for the correction of errors in the plans. sections and books of reference to he deposited in connection with the Bill as hereinafter mentioned. 14. To empower the Corporation to' bold lease and dispose of any lands acquired or to be acquired for the purposes of the Bill and not reqnired for those purposes. 15. To authorise the Corporation to appropriate and use for the purposes for which they were hcquired, or for any purposes specified in the Bill, certain lands and properties now held by the Corporation, and to empower the Corporation to borrow moneys for the purchase of lands and properties. 16. To prohibit the anchoring or mooring of vessels under or near the intended bridges or either of them,and to authorize the Corporation to make, place, and main- tain beacons, lights, buoys, mooring-posts, work's, and conveniences under or near to or in connection with the bridges, and to authorise and enforce bye-laws and regulations in regard to the navigation of the said river in the neighbourhood of the intended. bridges or either of them. 17. To sanction and confirm the purchase by the Corporation of No. 78, Sankey Street and the lands adjacent thereto, and to empower the Corporation to ,utilize the same for the extension of the public baths, or for such other purposes as the Corporation may deem expedient. 18. To authorize the Corporation on lands already acquired or to be acquired by them to alter, extend, improve or enlarge the existing Town Hall buildings and public baths and technical school. 19. To empower the Corporation to sell, lease, or dispose of the lands known as the Howley Recreation Ground, in the borough, and to make provision for the application of the proceeds of such sale. 20. To authorize the Corporation to grant licences to drovers, slaugbtermen and others, and to prohibit under penalty unlicensed persons from holding them- selves out as holding licences, and to empower the Corporation to make provision for the licensing of ;

38. TO make further provision for the regulation and control of common lodging-houses, and to empower the Corporation to close or obtain orders for the closing of common lodging-houses infected with infectious diFelse.

39. To enable the Corporation to pay compensation to persons who may for the purpose of stopping the spread of infectious disease cease their employment, and to prescribe and enforce penalties on persons with- holding information from the Medical Officer of Health and to make other provisions for preventing the spread of infections disease. _ .

40. To prohibit and prevent street cries and other noises, and to prohibit any person having the care of more than one cart when passing through the streets. 41. To make such provision as the Corporation may consider necessary or the Bill may prescribe for the protection gf their gas and water mains against electro- lytic action or interference by the laying of telegraphic or telephonic cables' "wires or other apparatus. 42. To require that dairies and milkshops within the Borough shall be registered and to make such provision in reference thereto as may he considered desirable. 43. To make provision for the regulation of the trade of hairdressers, tarbers and fried fish dealers, and to amend the provisions of the Public Health Acts with respect to any such trades. 44. To authorise the Corporation to deal with persons found in unlawful possession of stolen goods tbe owners of which cannot be found and to make further provisions in reference thereto. 45. To enable the Corporation to borrow moneys for the construction of the intended bridges. street works and other works, and for the widening of Market Gate and Buttermarket Street, and for any of the pur- poses of the Bill or or the water undertaking of the Corporation upon the security of any of the revenues and properties of the Corporation or the borough fund and borough rate or improvement fund and improve- ment rate, and to provide for (the repayment of such moneys and the suspension of the sinking fund or instal- ments of principal with other usual provisions in con- nection therewith, and also to authorize the borrowing of money to repay expenditure incurred in connection with the widening of Bridge Street and in connection with the water undertaking of the Corporation, and for other purposes to beTspecified in the Bill. 46. To enable the Corporation to collect all rates upon one basis of assessment and to consolidate all the rates levied in the Borough, and to provide for the same being collected upon one demand note and to alter the existing mode of assessing the rates levied in the Borough. 47. To enable the Corporation to use one form of morteage for all purposes, and to secure all loans indifferently upon the properties or revenhes of the Corporation, to use sinking funds instead of borrowing, and to make further provisions with regard to the borrowing powers of the Corporation. 48. To enable the Corporation to subscribe towards hospitals, infirmaries, nursing institutions, charities and other banevolent objects not exceeding such sums as may be prescribed by the Bill, and to pay other expenses reasonably incurred in the administration of local affair.

49. To provide for the payment of the expenses of carrying into effect the purposes of the Bill, and to permit the application of any funds, revenues, and rates of the Corporation for that object. 50, To make farther provision with regard to the evidence of appointments of officers of the Corporation, the confirmation of bye-laws, the recovery of demands and penalties, the right of appeal and other matters of procedure, the authentication and service of notices, the application of penalties, the indemnification of persons acting under the powers of the Bill, the saving for indictments and that justices shall not be dis- qualified. 51. To provide that in executing works in default of an owner or occupier the Corporation shall _not be liable save in case of negligence. 52. The Bill will, so far as it may be deemed nc3essary or expedient, vary and extend or repeal, alter, and consolidate, and amend all or any of the provisions of the Warrington Improvement and Market Act, 1854, the Warrington Corporation Gas Act, 1877. and the Warrington Corporation Act, 1899, and all other Acts or Orders relating to the Corporation, and will or may incorporate in extenso or by reference and with or without alteration the provisions or some of the provisions of the Lands Clauses Acts, the Railways Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845, the Harbours, Docks, and Piers Clauses Act, 1847, the Electric Lighting Acts of 1882 and 1888. and any Act amending the same respectively, and the Bill will vary or extinguish all rights and privileges which would interfere with any of its objects and confer other rights and privileges. ADMINISTRATIVE COUNTY -OF CHESTER (excepting the Municipal Boroughs situate therein. NTOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Cheshire -LI County Council, at a Meeting held at Chester Castle, on Thursday, the 11th day of November, 1909, made the following BYE-LAWS, viz.: DEFACING BUILDINGS. WALLS, FOOT PAVEMENTS, &c. __ _

1. No person shall, except With the consent of the owner or occupier or person having the charge thereof, or unless authorised so to do by law, deface by writing or other marks any building, wall, pillar, window, lamp- post, or otber post in or abutting on a street or public place, nor shall any person affix any posting bill, advertisement, or other paper upon the foot pavement in any street or pnblio place, or deface by writing or other marks any such foot pavement. INTERPRETATIONS.

2. "Street "-means and includes a highway, any public bridge, and any road, lane, footpath, square, quay, court, alley, or passage, whether a highway or not, to which the public have access. Public place," includes any common, park, pleasure ground, or roadside waste, to which the public have access.

div.head: MAYOR'S SUNDAY.
div.p: MAYOR'S SUNDAY.
Rev. G. C. Briggs on Civic Duty.

On Sunday morning the newly elected Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) and the members of the Corpora- tion observed the time honoured custom of inaugurating the civic year by attending divine service at the Parish Church. The weather conditions were entirely favour- able, the keen, frosty air being quite exhilarating, and there was a large muster for the procession which left the Town Hall shortly after ten o'clock, beaded by the Territorial Band. Next came members of the Territorial Force, under the command of Colonel J. D. Fairclough; the Service Company, led by Captains Picton and R. Delo. Roberts; the Church Lads' Brigade in charge of Captains Brooks, Sankey Reid and Hepherd, and Lieutenants Bracecamp and Bunch; the Boy Scouts, under the direction of Mr. John B. Starkey, Mr. Prince and Mr. Bairstow ; the Warrington Fire Brigade, in charge of Superintendent Turner; a detachment of police; under the command of Chief Inspector Williamaon ; and the boys of the Blue Coat School, under the care of Mr. E. Rose. Immediately preceding the Mayor walked the mace and sword bearer, (Sergearit Bell and P.C. Leonard). The Mayor, who wore his robes and chain of office, was accompanied by his chaplain (Rev. G. C. Briggs). Mr. A. H. Crosfleld M.P., and the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) Amongst others taking part in the procession were the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), Alderman Bennett, Burton, and Tinnion ; Councillors Fulton- Smith, Wilkinson, Locker, Steel, Jenkins, Ashcroft, Roberts, Skelland, Sankey, Birtles, Wilson, Singleton, Howard. Rogers, Hawthorn, Bellian, Toole, and Halli- well • Messrs. J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), J. Moore Murray (director of education), R. B. Roberts (assistant director of educa- tion), T. H. Spinks (assistant town clerk) F. G. Ruddock (borough analyst), A. M. Kerr (deputy borough sur- veyor), E. Place (market inspector), G. F. F. White (magistrates' clerk), M. Nicholls (chief constable), W. S. Howard (cashier' gas department), R. Young (Cemetery registrar), W. T. Flood (sanitary inspector), J. Houghton (borough treasurer's department) ; R. T. Fairclough, W. Richardson, G. Pilling, A. J. Jolley, J. W. Hayward, E. Woods and W. T. Williams (local magistrates), Dr. Bennett, Messrs. E. England (elective auditor), W. B. Forshaw, H. B. Houghton, H. Ferguson, H. J. Willett, W. Dilworth,. J. A: Rushworth, W. H. L. Gorse, A. Jolley, W. Dennett, T. Sangster' W. Payton, J. Partington, C. Plinston, E. Plinston, F. H. Aukland, A. Wright, J. Bailey, T. Mason and others. On arriving at the church gates the procession was met by the churchwardens (Councillor Craik and Mr. S. Taylor). At the entrance to the church tle clergy and choir were-in waiting and preceded the Mayor and Corporation up the centre aisle. The clergy taking part in the service were the Revs. Canon Willis, Canon, Morley Stevenson, T. A. J. Ridpath and A. J. Bratt, while the preacher was the Rev, G. C. Briggs, the Mayor's chaplain. The hymns "All people that on earth do dwell" and "Stand up, stand up for Jesus" were sung and the choir gave an effective interpretation of Myles Foster's well-known anthem "0 for a closer walk with God," the soloist being Mr. J. H. Draper. Mr. F. M. Darby, Mus. Bac., was at the organ.

The Rev. G. C. BRIGGS based his sermon on the words" We are members one of another." (Ephesians iv., 25) and emphasised the lesson of brotherhood and unity. After alluding to the need for men who were animated with the highest motives to serve on public authorities and to the part which every citizen could play in helping to form a healthy public opinion, the preacher said the civic duty of Christians was to make the life of the town represent the Christian ideal. It was to abstain from mere thoughtless criticism : it was o live godly, righteously, soberly and honestly; to protest against smoke, dirt and ugliness ; to boldly rebuke vice ; to show some practical sympathy with the poor. In such ways each one of them might help to create a public opinion more potent for righteousness than any ruler, however powerful. We could at least try to cultivate in ourselves a truer sense of human brotherhood, by showing the poor a special considera- tion and sympathy and respect, and by helping them to see that at any rate, no fault of ours should debar them from just wages, from a decent house to live in, from some chance of living a really human life. Then again, they might very briefly, and warily, apply the words of the text to their political life. We were living in stirring, and what seemed likely to prove stormy times. We mast go back at any rate a quarter of a century, possibly very much longer, to find a time when parties were more violently opposed to each other than they were to-day. The situation was not a , pleasant one. The newspapers, of both political parties, were full of speeches and articles, most of them con- • taining misrepresentations, ridicule of opponents and imputations against them. It was said that the great principle they were considering that day was not lost sight of, that the most bitter political enemies were often the best of private friends. That might or might not be true, but he (the preacher) entirely agreed with the statement that the interests of their land were too great to be used as a shuttlecock. And it was certainly high time that much of the bitterness, hatred and malice should be put away. As a spectator, who stood outside the arena of party politics, he might, perhaps, be allowed to express the hope that in the great struggle which was inevitably, and shortly, coming to pass, neither one side nor the other would altogether lose sight of the principle that they were "members one of another." Finally, let them take the words and apply them to their religious life. "We, being many, are one body in Christ." So St. Paul had been able to say. They could not say the words with equal truth to-day ; their divisions were only too patent. Nor was anything to be gained by affecting that there were no grounds of difference ; no serious differences, for example, between the Church of England and other Christian bodies. They were there and they could not hide them ; the mischief of them was tremendous. And that they should waste their strength in criticizing and disparag- ing one another was surely one of the saddest spectacles which the angels saw and the very saddest spectacle which met the eyes of Him whose prayer it was that they should all be one. By all means let them cling firmly to their own convictions, their own principl es but do let them try to show more charity and toleration and strive for more co-operation on those practical questions upon which there could be no disagreement whatsoever. After all, the battle of Christianity was the battle of good against evil. All Christians, if they were true to their profession, sLould be fighting for the good. The powers of evil were so great and so persist- ent that it was the maddest folly to divide forces which would be a hundred times more effectual than they actually were. It did seem that on such practical questions as betting. and drunkenness i and immorality and crime they ought to show a more united front than they did at present. The service. concluded with the National Anthem after which the procession was re-formed and returned ' to the Town Ball.

div.head: AT TIIE BLUE COAT SCHOOL.
div.p: AT TIIE BLUE COAT SCHOOL.

The Mayor is justly proud of the fact that he is an "Old Blue," and to. show his affection for the institu- tion in which be spent his early days, his Worship again attended the evening service there on Sunday. He was accompanied by the Mayoress and the Misses Forshaw, and Mr. and Mrs. Neil, while among others present were :—Aldermen Smethurst, John Evans and Burton; Councillor Fulton-Smith and Mrs. Fulton-Smith, Councillois Sankey and Craik, Mr. A. T. Hallaway (deputy Town Clerk), Mr. T. E. Burgess (a former usher of the school), Mr. Short (secretary of the Brotherl3 Society), and Mr. and Mrs. Edward Rose, headmaster and mistress of the institution. As usual the children conducted the whole of the service, and they entered the chapel singing as a processional "I was glad when they said unto me." The first boy in the pulpit was Ernest Smith and his place was afterwards taken by Percy Roughley. Then the 'hymn, "Heavenly Father, send thy blessing" followed. After the opening prayers T. A. Kendrick recited the 14th chapter of Hosea, and Clara Sorton recited the gospel for the day. Then followed the hymn "Children of the Heavenly King," and the Catechism on the means of grace, the questions being asked by Ernest Smith. The anthem was How amiable are thy tabernacles " (T. Mee Pattison). The Nunc Dimmittis was sung to a setting by Watson, Then the hymn usually sung at the gatherings of Old Blues, "Lord dismiss us with Thy blessing" was sung and a bright and encouraging service concluded.

div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
THE LATCHFORD CLUB.

Latchford scored a brilliant vidtory over Bankfield at Liverpool last week by 7-2. Ths home team were first to score but Latchford quickly equalized, and as a result of splendid passing among the halves and for- wards, five more goals were pct on before half-time. Bankfield pressed very strongly in the second half but being met by a sound defence, only scored once. Latch- ford also scored another. Travis and Hackney each found the net three times and Booth once.

Bankfleld "A "were defeated by the Second Eleven at Latchford 9-4 in a very enjoyable game. The home forwards displayed more dash than of late,and showered the ball into goal more frequently. The wing halves also showed better form. The goals were scored by Starkey (3),Eccles (2),Allanson (2), Isaac (I),Conway (1). The First Eleven against Liverpool University at Liverpool to-day. is:—W. div.head: THE' HEADMASTER, MR. J. A. YONGE, M.A. ELDEST SON OF THE REV. JOHN YONGE OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE' HEADMASTER, MR. J. A. YONGE, M.A. ELDEST SON OF THE REV. JOHN YONGE OF WARRINGTON.

had a chat with the oldest living " Silcoates boy." I refer to Dr. Guinness Rogers. He was sent to the school when it was first opened in 1831. The-veteran preacher's reminiscences were very vivid and very fragrant. It appears that the boys ivere often invited to spend their week-ends with friends in Leeds. Dr. Rogers distinctly recalls being the guest more than once of the famous hymn writer Mr. George Rawson. He was one of the founders of Silcoates, and one of the pillars of Congregationalism in the West Riding. We honour his memory all the more when we know that he combined the grace of Christian hospitality with the genius for religious poetry.

In those early days the school fees amounted to £l5 per annum, and the holidays consisted of six weeks in midsummer. There was no break ,at Easter or at Christmas. The boys enjoyed the privilege of over ten months' continuous work, unspoiled by vacations, an idyllic state of affairs, at least from the parental standpoint.

When I read that " The Nonconformist Catechism was taught weekly 1,!. then I know where Guinness Rogers learnt the fundamental principles of Noncon- formity. The battles of religious freedom, in which he has been so brilliant a protagonist were won in the class rooms at Silcoates.

Within five years of its foundation the school num- bered sixty boys, all ministers' sons; but evidently the financial strain became severe, and the question was seriously entertained ' as to whether the school could be . carried on. Most , of our denominational enterprizes have to pass through these periodical crises. The trustees decided to hold on, calling on the laymen's sons to reduce the deficit on the ministers' —a most laudable transaction. This policy has been

And then in 1904 there occurred an overwheln3il disaster. At least, so it appeared at the time. The builu- ings were burtit down by fire. Mr. Yonge was awaY on holiday; he came back to see the school in ruins' What was to be done? For long months the questi°r! was debated with varying issues. But in that thne crisis there were some valiant spirits that never lost hope or courage. Men like Alderman Baines of We 4 Hartlepool, and like the Haworths, Of Manchester, came to the rescue with noble generosity, and were it not for their action it is very probable that Sikoates would to-day be existing only as a pleasant memorY; Congregationalism owes them a great debt. Out or the ashes of the old building there has risen up a nos' and noble Silcoates, equipped with every mode''' appliance, and enabled to accomplish far better Ivori than was possible under the old regime. When look upon the library, and the music room, the laboratory, the work shop, and the gymnasium, • the playing fields and the class rooms, I envy the boys whose lines have fallen in such pleasant places. Th 7. new Silcoates can accommodate over one hundreet boys, and I believe that the full limit has ahead'', been reached. It is true to say that the school nev'er stood higher than it does to-day in public esteem.

It is a school a which, as a denomination we are - justly proud. The headmaster is a man who h4s,-1"4,1 in - a very exceptional degree the confidence 911' affection of his constituency. Throughout the last five't „ critical years he has borne himself with magnificell, courage. His personality has always been a poxverfai asset in the success of Silcoates, and we congratulat _ him on the work that has already been achieved, all on the greater work which he is destined t 0 - taccomplish.
Y. T.

Merthyr Tydvil found themselves in sorry plight at Warrington on Saturday, and were defeated by no less than 56 points to nil. Two of their players missed a railway connection,and with the help of a reserve a team of 12 was made up instead of the usual 13. Warrington were at, full strength, and the way they toyed with the opposition afforded great amusement to a crowd of 4,000. rho weather was One and dry and the game pleasantly contested. Teams : Warrington—Tilley, back ; Fish, Dickinson, Taylor, and Bradshaw, three-quarter backs; Lloyd and Jenkins, half backs; Thomas, Shugars, O'Malley, Boardman and Belton, forwards.
Merthyr—G. %V. Reed, back; Ponty Thomas, Edwards, Charles and James, three-quarter backs; Lewis and F. Jones, half backs; Norris, Bevan, Hughes, Jenkins and Jones, forwards.

Referee, Mr. E. 11. Smirk, Wigan. Touch judges, Messrs. E. Robinson, Runcorn, and E. Williams,Widnes. Warrington started attr ck from the moment the ball was id mation and the game was barely a minute old before Fish took a pass from Lloyd, and scored at the corner. Belton next put on the finishing touch to a for- ward rush. Warrington still forced matters,and a brilliant individual effort by Dickenson led up to a third try. Fine combination gave the Welshmen further troubles, and Fish raced in and kicked the goal. The visitors showed poor defence when the home forwards swept down on the Merthyr lines, ShOgars scoring the try,
YORKSHIRE CUP SEMI-FINAL REPLAYED TIE. WAKEFIELD TRINITY v. BATLEY.

At Wakefield, on Wednesday, in dull weather, between 5,000 and 6,000 people being present. In the first half Ward scored a try for Batley, and Wattle Davies kicked a goal. Then Newbold scored a try for Wakefield. In the second half Debney and Will Davies scored tries for Batley, who thoroughly deserved their victory. Result: Batley 1 goal 3 tries (11 points), Wakefield 'try (3 points).

and Fish goaling, a performance Fish repeated when Bradshaw raced in from half-way. Turning round, the Warringtonians were always on the aggressive, and Dickenson soon opened Warrington's account, whilst a minute later Fish landed a penalty goal from near half-way. Fish next scored a sensational try from half-way, running through the opposition with ease. The visitors continued to be outclassed and out- paced, and Tilley scored after charging a kick. Tries followed by Bradshaw, Taylor, Shugars, Fish and Lloyd, and goals were placed by Fish (two) and 'Thomas. Result :—Warrington, seven goals and 14 tries (56 points) ; Merthyr, nil.

div.head: WIDNES GIVE OLDHAM A FRIGHT.
div.p: WIDNES GIVE OLDHAM A FRIGHT.

At Widnes, before 2,000 spectators. Both teams were at full stiength. In the opening stages Oldbam had the best of matters, but Widnes defended splendidly. Ableza.k made some brilliant movements, but the backs seemeil unable to handle the ball. O'Gara dribbled in r‘, than half length of the field, and just as a Widnes w is about to drop on the ball Smith made it dead. row r•ls the interval Widnes plAyed up well, and had as much of the game ftS their opponents. At 1.0 f-ti me there was no score.

Oi commencing the second half Widnes attacked very strongly, and for fully ten minutes Oldham were oeinied on the line. The visitors worked their way to he home quarters, and McLean got over at the corner. Ferguson failed at the goal kick. O'Gara made a brilliant opening for Widnes, and just as he had a clear field he stumbled. Close on time Avery forced his way over the line at the corner. Ferguson failed at goal. Result—Oldham 2 tries (6 points), Widnes nil. Teams and officials :

Widnes—Jones, back; Dainteth, Reid, Lambert, and Ince, three-quarter backs; Lally and O'Gara, half backs; G. Aspey, S. Aspey, Colgrave, Johnson, NicCarthy, and Rigby, forwards. Oldham—Wood, back; McLean, Dean, Llewellyn, and Smith, three-quarter backs; Anlevirk and White, half backs; Ferguson, Avery, Wright, Owens, Jardine, and Helm, forwards.
Referee, T. H. King, Salford; touch judges, F. Turner, Warrington, and T. Foulkes, St. Helens. ,

SURPRISING DEFEAT FOR HUDDERSFIELD. At Huddersfield,on Wednesday,before 3,000 spectators, Biadford got a surprise victory. Huddersfield played several reserves. In the first half, which was character- ised by scrappy play. Haley and Dunbavin scored tries for Bradford, and Kitchen for Huddersfield. Play did not improve in the second portion of the game, and Orchard made the score level with an unconverted try. Dunbavin then ran the length of the field and scored for Bradford, who ran out winners. Result : Bradford: liradford 3 tries, Huddersfield 2 tries.

div.head: Lancashire Cup.—Semi-final.
div.p: Lancashire Cup.—Semi-final.
RUNCORN BEATEN AT LELOr ff.

Runcorn failed to qualify for the Lancashire Cup final on Saturday, then they were beaten at Leigh, before a crowd of 9,000. The home supporter 4 were surprised to find Leigh turn out minus Da % i.e and fsherwood and Neville and Whittqler played instead. Battersby turned out for the first time since his set ere injury ot a month ago. Runcorn warted ai.ainst the wind a few minutes late. Marsh made a hard at tempt to get in but failed. Then Runcorn were penalized for off-side play and Battersby landed an easy goal. The " Linnets " made a big effort, and in solipe loose play at the Leigh end Moran gave to Flanagan, who was forced out of play. Runcorn pressed and Sam Johnfon mulled, with the result that. Pactbury dabled ()Fur the line and registered a try, Britterwor.h goaled. Bolewski ran brilliantly, but missed a pass with which he might have scored. Richardson, who was playing finely for Runcorn at full Lack, char( d his lines grandly. Even- tuslly, Sam Johnson dashed brilliantly through the visitors, and, though often attacked, he kept going. When near the line he passed to Whittaker, who tricked his oppouents and scored an excellent try behind the posts. Battersby placing a goal. Leigh now led by two points. The home team's success encouraged them greatly, and they again made tracks for the Runcorn goal. Richardson kicked away to Sam Johnson, alto dropped a magnificent goal from his team from outside the quarter line. Another goal was dropped by Battersby, after a brilliant run. Runcorn got the ball from the scrimmages, but their backs seemed too slow. Half-time t—Leigh, four goals one try (11 points); In the second half the wind favoured Runcorn. Leigh who were going "great guns," missed a glorious chance, Gallop failing to pass ughes. Runcorn now had a turn, and Hughes, after defeating his opponents, passed to Butterworth. This player bad a clear course for the line, but Neville- overtook him and the ball rolled clear. The united efforts of Hughes and Butter- worth almost ended in a score for their team, Neville overhauling the latter near the line. Next Kennedy scored. Butterworth failed at goal. The small differ- ence of three points made the play very keen. Result: —Leigh, four goals one try (11 points); Runcorn, one goal two tries (eight points).

div.head: WARRINGTON " A's " NARROW VICTORY.
div.p: WARRINGTON " A's " NARROW VICTORY.

Warrington "A " found themselves fully extended on Saturday at Runcorn and it was only in the closing stages of a very hard game that they gained the verdict. There was a fair gate despite the big crowd which accompanied the Runcorn first team to Leigh. Runcorn pressed for some little time, but found a grand defence opposed to them. Then Warrington had a turn on the attack and might have made more headway but for off- side tactics. Talbot tried a shot at goal from a mark, but failed to lower the citadel. Abel and Steel were both conspicuous, but neither team had scored when half-time arrived. Early in the second half Massey had a shot at goal for the "Greens," but ha proved to be as unsuccessful as the rest. The visiting backs com- bined prettily and pressed, only to find Talbot in capital form. In the closing ten minutes Warrington worked the ball up the field and a neat passing bout ended in a try to Cartwright. No goal was kicked. A. hard-fought game ended in a victory for the" Wire- pullers." Result :—Warrington "A," one try; Runcorn A," nil.

Pearson and Knowles team visited Earlestown on Saturday when they carried everything before them. The match was one-sided from the beginning, the following scoring for the ironworkers :—Hannan,3 tries 1 goal ; Ashton, 1 try; Crawford, 1 ; Waywell, 1 try; J. Harrop, 3 tries. div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
WARRINGTON ALDIONS V. WIDNES WESLEY GUILD.

Warrington Albions engaged in their first match for the " Observer " Cup on Saturday, when they played Widnes Wesley Guild. The Albions were fully repre- sented, but the Wesley Guild only had a reserve team as the First were playing in a league match. Some time after the kick-off Ritchie,for the home team,got hold of the ball and centred, but Whitfield was unsuccessful. Atherton, for the visiting team, made a good attempt., but his efforts were in vain, and the ball just grazed the top bar. There was some stiff work, and then the home team forwards secured the ball after a delightful display of combination. Whitfield passed it to Cheaters, who switching round punched the ball for all he was worth, but he made a wrong estimate of his position, and the ball went wide. Play centred in neutral territory for some time until Hunter made an attempt to secure a goal for the home team, but Harrison, the custodian, prevented him. Then the visitors pulled themselves together, and were about to get a goal when they were thrown off-side by Short. It was thought that no goal would be registered on either side in the first half, but Ritchie made a rush and sent in a fine centre. T. Whit- field headed the ball and secured a goal for the Albions half a minute before the interval. In the second half the Albions had the game to themselves, five more goals being added, whilst the visitors had to go away without one. The following were the scorers: —Chesters, Thomas, T. Whitfield, the latter doing the hat trick. Result :—Warrington Albions, 6 goals ; Widnes Wesley Guild, nil.

div.head: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
div.p: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
Dr B. BENNISON.
ILLUSTRATED BY JACK DODWORTH.

The contention set up by many arewd people that the footballer was not a workman in the every-day accepted sense of the terns has always appealed to me as being utterly wrong, and the players were bound to succeed in their attempt at being so defined. How far the,decision of the Court of Appeal will afrxt the game it is, of course, impossible to say, but the law as inter- Preted muet be of serious concern to the little clubs.. To my thinking, the .Football Associa- tion—themselves p. limited liability company— not for the purpose's of profit-making, I readily agree, but for the sake of self-protection—have been entirely wrong in the point of view they have taken with regard to the definition of a player. It does not sound nice to say that a footballer is a workman, but the conduct of the -game is such that one has never had any other alternative.

Great Centre-Forwards. Woolwich Arsenal have been to Scotland, and have landed two yOung players of whom high hopes are entertained. It would seeni that the Arsenal's draw against Sheffield Wednesday at Przxs r4l\coß:r ThE 1• -- 4 inLK AI:3OU TEFFR I KtocK

Ovrlerton means that the Plumstead team are improving, and that the presence of new blood among the forwards will bring about a most de- sirable change. It is really wonderful sometimes what a tretriendous difference a new man will make. Take Preston North End as an ex- ample. Here we have them, after floundering about in a most helpless way for the greater part of the season, beating Newcastle United by four goals to none. Was there ever anything more remarkable? I have not seen McLean play since he came to Deepdale from the Celtic, where he was understudy to the great Quinn, but I am told he has, with the help of the stodgy Bannister, who has spent most of his football days with the Manchester clubs, wrought an improvement in the play of Preston forwards as if by magic. When a club gets a 'good centre-forward they have a treasure. Centre-forwards of high merit can be counted on one hand; we do not seem able to develop them nowadays; we base long despaired of. seeing such leaders as Johnny Campbell (who was at the head of the Sunderland team when they came near being invincible, and who, in, my opinion, was one of the greatest centres who ever toed a ball); Johnny Goodall, Southworth (whose career was all too short); G. 0. Smith, and Robert McColl, when he was in his prime and Queen's Park were a great team. The best centre-forward in all countries is James Quinn, of Celtic; it would be hard to say who is best of the English centres. Ido not think we have a great artist, though, as a dan- gerous player, as distinct from a clever and subtle footballer. Freeman, of Everton, will take a lot of beating. - An international Defence. Everton found Blackburn Rovets too much for them. I am not surprised Hirt the idea of Playing Ashcroft, Crompton, and Cowell for England has found much favour. There is no better or more reliable trio in the country. It is a moot point whether Silas Hardy is a bet- ter goalkeeper than Ashcroft, though it would be hard lines if Hardy had to give way to the Rovers' man merely because he is part of the best club defence in the country. But hero we have three men playing together who as a combina- tion are by themselves, and they must be seri- ously considered whett International honours come to be distributed. At any rate, Crempton and Cowell seem certain for the back position. Those who know Clayton will agree at once that a more desirable football centre, from every point of view, cannot be imagined. How Manchesi Red have managed to build lip

a reputation there I don't know. Visitors to this most salubrious spot have long complained bitterly about the ground and atmospheric con- ditions, and it will come as pleasant news to hear that the Cupholders will have a new ground ready at Old Trafford, close to the head- quarters of the Lancashire County Cricket Club, by Christmas. I hear it said that certain of the Manchester United supporters do not like the idea of a removal; if this be so, then they are very hard to please. I am sure that the United will be more comfortable in their new home; Old Trafford is Arcadian after chemical Clay- ton. Chelsea had a most unpleasant experience, as others have had before them, a week ago at Clayton. They were asked to play on a ground that resembled a sea of mud rather than some- thing upon which a football match was to be decided. And, being without Hilsdon, Fairgray, Brawn, and Windridge. no wonder they lost. By the way, Manchester United are credited with being anxious to obtain the services of a Scotsman named Hodge. And so are many other clubs, notably Reading. Unreliable Fulham. While there is not a very great change in the First League, so far as it affects the strongek teams, London people are happy in the know- ledge that Tottenham managed to pull through against LiV'erpool. But in the Second Division teams like Manchester City and Fulham, not to

mention %Vest- Bromwich Albion, are somewhat fearful of the future. Leiccker Fosi-:e have come on with a bound; they are, playing a particularly good .• game; but, really, after their clefcat by ,Glinsborough Trinity, one 'cannot place any reliance in Fulham at all. They are positively among the worst fighters in a given test I know. Glossop continue to do manfully.

'Crystal Palace and West Ham United am, bracketed first for the leading position of the Southern League; but what of Swindon Townl Surely a team that can come to Park Royal and defeat the Rangers by three goals must be con. sidcred to be well in the running for the charm nionshin? There its no 'mistaking the finality el wincton's football, one ot toe ortg,ntest reaturee of which is the play of Harold Fleming. I won. d-sr what sonse,of the big clubs would give for a player like Fleming—l wonder!

As soon as I had ascertained that Ulm could boast the loftiest spite of any church in Christendom I silently made up my mind to climb it. But this was quite impossible on(ihe day of my arrival and my only chance was ere we left for Munich on the Thursday morning. I slept most soundly, rose betimes, packed up my bags, each swelling visibly as the long tour proceeded, had my customary rolls and coffee, and, at ten o'clock, set out to ease my soul and satisfy my aspirations. I had just an hour to do it in. I The total height of tower and spire is 528 feet. The ' steps are firm and spacious, and the •climber is at every point most adequately guarded. But there are 758 steps in all, aid I am not used to going up so many. Moreover, I was tired before I started, and ray time was short. I went up rapidly. But I was glad to pause at each of the three stages into which the tower and spire are very sensibly divided, and, more than once, at intermediate points, I paused to rest awhile, my heart, on each occasion, thumping like a piston and my forehead bathed in perspiration. At one point of the journey, just as I was at the bell chamber, I beard a solemn iron tongue boom ten. But the authoritive stopping places were, first of all, the spacious platforms of the square tower, at a height of 70 metres, and after climbing 328 steps; then, after climbing 168 steps more, at the platform of , the cctagon,height 102 metres; and then I gct into the spire itself, and, panting up the beautiful cylindrical staircase, and climbing 208 steps further still, I paused, at last, triumphantly on the top gallery, at a height of 143 metres, or 176 yards. This is the highest point to which the most ambitious climber can ascend at any church in any country, and it is eighteen metres below the topmost portion of the spire. When I mention that the stairs in the Cologne cathedral only lead to the foot of the helmet, arid cease at a height of 96 metres, some con- ception will be gained of the enormous height to which The visitor may climb. And at every stage of the journey there is some new wonder in the solid masonry to notice, some additional evidence of the daring skill of those who carried out triumphantly this noble work. I ought to have had a magnificent view of the valleys of the filer and the Danube, but a heavy mist lay over all the town, and I had to peer out patiently for several minutes ere I caught,at last, a fleeting vision of the larger stream; but, as it was, I found it difficult to find the Rathaus, and my view was almcst limited to the coloured tiles of the Cathedral rcof and to my pigmy fellow-mortals in the Munster Platz so far below. I was naturally fain to linger till the air grew clearer and the vision widened. But it was not to be. The fingers of my watch sped on with maddening rapidity. It had taken me just forty minutes to reach the top, and I had only fifteen left to get to the Station, and I practically galloped down acain. But my ambition was achieved, and the inward sense of satisfact: on which this fact afforded bade my fluttering heart be still. I had previously scrambled up the spire of Antwerp, and gazed down upon that quaint old city from a height of 123 metres. I had climbed the loftier spire at beautiful Rouen, 149 metres. I had twice been up the spire of our own Parish Church, once on the ladders and once in a skip. But Ulm excelled them all, and was, as I have said, the loftiest spire in all tho world, and I got to my hotel in time to get my bags and catch the train, hot, tired and panting, but quite satisfied. But it is too big a task to tackle in a hurry, and it would be easier to go up in a skip. We left at 10-58, and lunch was thoughtfully provided in the train. Immediately outside the town, we crossed the Danube, which is navigable from this point, and, entering Bavaria, glided smoothly through the pleasant precints of New Ulm. Near Nersingen, the traveller may see the town and abbey of Elchingen, the heights of which were occupied by the Austrians under Laudon, only to be stormed by the indomitable Ney. At Gunsburg, the Danube is augmented by the waters of the Gunz, and, passing a range of wooded hills on the right we reached Neu-Offiogen, and bade good-bye —or shall I say" Auf wiedersehen ?"—to the great river, on whose bosom I was soon to float to Wien. And now we cross the Zusam, and then the Wertach, and arrive at Augsburg, at the junction of the Wertach and the Lech, and one of the most important towns in Southern Germany, with 94,500 inhabitants. Its ample water power is utilized by numerous canals which traverse it, and has given rise to various industries, weaving, cotton spinning, and machine making. In the middle ages, Augsburg was a free imperial city and the great centre between the traffic between the North of Europe, Italy and the Levant. It reached its prime in the fifieenth and sixteenth centuries. Three of its fair children, one of them Agnes Bernauer, the beautiful daughter of a barber, married princes. Another citizen, Bartholomew Weiser, fitted out a squadron to conquer Venezuela, whilst the Fugger family once poor weavers, rose to be the wealthiest merchants in the city, or perhaps in Europe, and were the Rotbschilds of their age, assisting to replenish the depleted coffers of the Emperors Maximilian and Charles the Fifth. At Augsburg, too, Charles held his famous Diets,at one of which the Protestant princes presented the famous Augsburg Confession. Hans Holbein flourished here about 1500, and, of course, the history of the place goes back to the time of the Romans. But we bad not time to more than glance at these particulars, as we stopped at the Station, and to try and catch a fleeting vision of the great Cathedral, and to picture the old Rathaus,with its golden hall, its great Museum, and its Royal Picture Gallery; the, Fuggerhaus, the Fugger Bath Rooms, and, of course, the usual array of churches, which, Badaeker assured us, were amongst the features of the place And now we cross the Lech, and traverse a sad, sterile plain, and. later on, the Amper, the discharge of the Ammersee, and then the Dachauer Moos, and, after that, the Wilms, which drains the Lake of Starnberg ; and then the houses thicken, and the signs of a great city crowd upon us, and, after a pleasant twc hours run, the train pulls up at Munich. And what shall I say of Munich or of Munchen, to cell it by its proper name, the beautiful capital of Bavaria, with its population of over half a million, the largest city in the German Empire save two, tho home of Art and Music and of Lager Beer? First of all, it was not in the least what I had pictured it. I had thought of a German Antwerp, but I found a smaller Paris. I expected quaintness and antiquity. I found much modern splendour. But Munich is, in fact, extremely old. It was founded by Henry the Lion in the middle of the twelfth centnry. But it is to Louis the First that Munich mainly owes its modern air of stately grandeur, for be built the Glyptothek (or hall of sculptures) and the Old and New Pinakotheks (or picture galleries), and raised the city to the foremost rank as a school of German art. The second Louis carried on the work by the building and embellishment of royal palaces. The reign of the Prince Regent Leopold (since 1866), has seen a later outburst of architectural magnificence, mainly marked by a "harmonious adaptation of the new structures to the existing conditions such an has probably never been excelled in any city." I have not space to more than hint at its reputation as a great art centre, and we had not time to even peep inside its world-famed galleries; but we had not left the station for a minute ere we had begun to realize the grace and beauty of the town itsglf. Our Hotel, the Bayerischer Hof, stood in a broad. spacious street that was filled with trees and statues. My room was sumptuous in the extreme. And when, at 2.15, Professor Berlepsch Valendas and a little company of influential Mrinchenites invited us to enter the long line of carriages which were waiting for us in the golden sunshine, and we set out quietly to carry out the programme which had been so skilfully arranged for our delight, and printed carefully for our instruction n both German and English, we were almost breath- ess with admiration. Through Maffei Street, and by the lovely Theatiner Church, with its two tall towers and its delightful dome; along the Residenz Platz, and by the Feldherrnhalle (or the Hall of the Generals), with its marble lions and its statues of the Bavarian heroes, Tilly and Wrede ; by the splendid Royal Residence, and the Court Garden, and round St. Ann's Church to the famous Maxmilian's Strasse, past Max Joseph's Platz, the Royal and Residence Theatre, Through the arch of the old Town Hall. and the Marien Platz, and by the Virgin's Column to the new Town hail; on through great streets of modern Munich houses; past the Academy of Science, St. Augustine's Brewery, and the Magazines of Ober-Bollinger, and by the lovely Foun- tain of Nornes to the Court of Justice, where we made fleeting stay—it was one continuous kaleidoscope of

grace and beauty! Then by the Propylees and the Slyptothek, down Schiller Street, past one of the great Hospitals,and one of the great public Rush Baths to the Exhibibition Halls. And here we paused to drink a welcome cup of tea "offered by the Municipality of Munich in the Theatre Restaurant, opposite the Exhibition Halls." These included a great edifice devoted to the leading local industry, the brewing of lager beer, a palace set apart to illustrate the wonders dJapan, and a charming ileatre (of which more anon); but we were here fk r a specific purpose,and the little time we had to spare was devoted to the very striking exhibition of Town Enlargement plans, and plans for Workmen's Houses and Cottages,and models and photographs of the chief municipal undertakings,all of which were skilfully displayed in yet another, spacious building. Too soon the Trumpet's signal' announced " Departure Time," but we had many other things to see. And now we rode ingloriously behind the great Bavarian "Glory Hall," instead of by the front of it, and on along a mighty open meadow filled with glittering booths and shows and Brobdingnagian beer halls—a sort of English Fair,five times as large as any I have ever seen—its organizers gathered here in readiness for the October Feat which was to open on the following Sunday, and which, as Autumn comes, from year to year attracts the Miinchenites and all the peasant people of Bavaria. But we had not any time to peep at Hagenbeck's immense menagerie, or any of the other popular attractions which bad been so lavishly provided, and rode on swiftly to inspect two great cheap "Dwellings Blocks" erected by the Munich kssociation for Housing Betterment, of which Professor Berlepsch Valendas was one of the moving spirits. Very hand- some was the building which we entered, with its leafy quadrangle, its flower•filled windows, its clean, airy, light, commodious apartments ; and very sweet it was to see the flower-faced children singing and dancing in the sunshine round their pleasant teacher. Every room we entered was as clean as a palace, and in all of them the humble household gods were wor- shipped with continuous care. And then the inexorable "Trumpet" sounded, and we tore ourselves away from those clean German housewives and their charm- ing babies (the husbands were, of course, at work, with some exceptions), and drove on through the Munich "slums "—which did not look like slums at all; and, passing by a handsome church, we came, at last to a great river, flowing swiftly through a broad and shallow valley ; and, as we crossed one of the many noble bridges, mostly new, which spanned its foaming, emerald waters, Campbell's rousing words rang like another trumpet through my brain, and I murmured to my German comrade, wondering if he would apprehend : "On Linden, when the sun was low, All bloodless lay the untredden snow, And dark as winter was the flow Of leer, rolling rapidly !" He answered instantly, with an assenting smile, and both of us agreed how apt the poet's words had been For the Iser rolled rapidly," a green and glittering glory of sweet waters, foaming onwards thrcugh the lovely city to the lovelier sea, and I fazed upon them with a joy which had not been exceeded when I saw, for the first time, the waters of the Rhine. Then, riding out into the country, we visited another series of block dwellings, now in process of erection, and, riling further still came to a pleasant group of "One Family Houses," the type we see at Garden City, Hampstead, Bournville, and Port Sunlight. For, much as we lave got to learn from Germany, our model housing system is admittedly much superior to theirs, and practically all the German pioneers of this great movement seem to envy us, in this respect, at any rate, and to realize that the Block System, at its best, is not desirable ; whilst, at Ulm and Munich, as we saw, they were successfully endeavonting to follow our example.

We bad not any time to dine to-night, for the Municipal Council of Munich bad offered to Ladies •and Gentlemen of the Town Planning Party places in the New Artist's Theatre, which is known throughout Europe by its excellent representations and its quite new scene arrangements.' And so we dressed, and hastened to the Theatre, which stood within the Exhibition Grounds, and missed the Overture, and found ourselves inside the magic doors in time to hear the opening words of Shakespeare's beautiful " Mid- summer Night's Dream," (" A Summer-Night's Dream by W. Shakespeare," as it was quaintly termed upon our Programme for the day. And a dream indeed it was, of lovely scenery, of fairy-like illusion, of consummate acting, of bewitching music, in a great, square, noble panelled room, with not a gallery to spoil its fair proportions; with every seat arranged to give to every occupant an absolu.ely unimpeded view. And, humbled as many of us had been at all the evidences we had come across of Ger- many's superiority, our national pride was socthed and flattered by this wonderful presentation of this noble play " by W. Shakespeare." A lengthy interval occurred about the middle of the performance,in which we sauntered to and fro about the Exhibition gardens; and, when the play was ended, we walked right through them to the tram upon the further side,and rode back to our Hotel ; and thence, in company with several kindred souls, I found my way to the great Tiofbratthaus, the largest beer house in this city of gigantic beer houses its spacious upper hall, which can occommodate 2,060 persons at a time, adorned with frescoes by Ferdinand Wagner. When we entered, almost every table in the place was filled, but we found a vacant place at last, among a jolly company of Manchenites,and fraternized with these as though they had been friends and brothers (as indeed they were, and ate their German ham, and cheese,and smoked their German cigarettes, and drank from their great lidded mugs of lager beer, whilst music filled the mighty ball, and through the cloud of smoke the hum of pleasant talk resounded cheerfully. And then we saw that all the elders of ourparty had been somehow irresistibly attracted hither too,and, at a group of tables in the farthest corner of the room, we all joined forces, and drank to our good German comrades and our noble selves in that brown beverage which " cheers " but does not seem:to really " inebriate " (I j never saw a drunken man on all the ourney),and adds, apparently, to German happiness without inflicting on the lucky populace the degradation which so often comes from drinking our strong English beer. (To be continued).
