div.head: CYCLING IN THE SOUTH.
div.p: CYCLING IN THE SOUTH.
Emulation for the Warrington Club.

There can surely be no more delightful district in which to cycle than the South of England. Just below the Thames the North Downs begin to rise and stretch away to the middle of Kent, Surrey and Hampskre, then there is a fairly level area when the South Downs begin to rise and stretch practically to the English Channel. The scenery in the Southern Counties is thus very diversified, and certainly no-one could com- plain of monotony on the roads. There are of course level roads to be found, but they are few and far between as the, country generally is of a switchback character.

The roads in Kent, owing to the very numerous motor cars on them, and consequently the distress which they have caused to the villagers along them, have now been mostly treated with tar with a view to keeping down the dust. This affords a delightful surface for cyclists, especially in its carly days, but when the roads begin to wear and the motorists have knocked holes in them a yard or two wide the-condi- tions are not so pleasant. After rain these tarred roads soon dry, but at night they are not so agreeable as an ordinary road. On dark nigh's it is scarcely possible to see one's way and there is a very peculiar sensation in free-wheeling under such conditions, as more often than not people are to be found walking in the middle of the road, and it is only by keeping the sharpest look-out, and by having the brightest light that one can avoid running them down. Kent is also remarkable for its hop and market garden, and in the spring there is nothing so delightful as cycling by large orchards in which the apple trees are in bloom. In Surrey the roads are mostly macadam, and are consequently .of a white surface which contributes more to the comfort of cyclists who have to travel in The dark. The roads generally are very fine, and the county is quite remarkable for the number of its commons, heaths, and open spaces. In Hampshire the roads ate chiefly tf a flinty character and often badly cut up by the motor traffic to Bournemouth and other South Coast towns in that direction. In this county is to be found the beautiful New Forest, which, though not so large as formerly, is now quite large enough for one to get lost in. I have travelled for days across this Forest and scarcely met a single person. I often smile when I read of the doings of the Warrington Cycling Club who manage to accomplish a four mile run during an afternoon. It is my fortune to belong to a club that thinks nothing of doing from 30 to 40 miles in the course of a run. It is a mixed club consisting of ladies and,gentlemen, and I have known one of these ladies to do 75 miles in a day's run. I should like to take some of your readers with me on the roads down South; they would find plenty of "cellar work," and on the other hand they would enjoy long spells of free-wheeling. There is a run out of Croydon which starts on the level, but at the third mile it begins to rise from 200 ft. 'above the sea level to the ninth mile when it reaches over 8001 t. It is possible to cycle all the way up except about half a mile, and then after riding on the top of the Downs for a few miles there is a well-known and steep descent. This descent, however, is quite ride- able for three parts of the way down, but then it becomes very steep and it is advisable to walk. Just at this part in the summer months a mot r car came to grief because its brakes gave out on the long descent, and its occupants were badly injured by being thrown Into the roadside which consists of high banks. At the bottom of this descent there is a delightfulfree- wheel into Limpsfield, one of the beauty spots of the district, from which one can obtain wide panoramas of the Weald of Kent. It then goes on to Oxted, another pretty place, over a switchback road in which the speed acquired on the descent carries cne almost to the top of the next hill, and so on into Godstone, a charming little village which was once a favourite of the late Queen Victoria. From this place it is po-sible to go further South into East Grimstead, or to go West into fiedhill on the London-Brighton-road. The way into nedhill is, however, somewhat remarkable as it soon begins to rise, and in one part the road appears almost to go straight up, and at its worst part a village is pitched. It is, however, possible to cycle the full length on the low gear, and once on the top one can free-wheel almost into Recihill. Quite recently this little town was the scere of a dreadful cycle accident. A lady moto list from Norwood was approaching the town when she unfor- tunately collided with a catt coming out of a cross- road, and the shaft of the cart penetrated her chest and killed her. The return to London is almost a continuous free- wheel for about twelve miles.

Then there is the beautiful Thames Valley, and this is well worth a visit from those who appreciate river- side scenery. The villages and riverside resorts! are simply delightful, and one experiences a great desire to settle down amongst such lovely sylvan scenes. This tour of course takes one into Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, and even Oxfordshire, and in returning through some of the up-river resorts it is possible to get along the renowned Bath-road which runs Londonwards through quite a number of historic places which have now become towns of considerable magnitude. It-is quite a common thing for the southern cyclists to journey on their cycles in their summer holidays to seaside resorts.

I remember on one cccasion travelling to Stone- henge on Salisbury Plain to view the striking druidical remains, coming across two cyclists from Staffordshire, who were making their way from Weymouth to the Black Country. I accompanied them for a long distance over the wry billy road that leads to Stonehenge ; and when I stepped off for lunch in Amesbury they went forward. I was just setting out for the Monuments when my newly-lound friends were returning, arid they told me it would take me half-an-hour to reach the Remains, but I should come back in ten minutes. I found they were quite right ; the road was uphill all the way, and on returning one came back at a terrific pace.

I remember on on; occasion when cycling from Southampton to London, some 79 miles, I came across the famous " Hog's Back" between Farnham and Guildford. I understood that it was impossible to cycle up this eminence, but to my surprise I was able to pedal all the way to the top. The views, how- ever, on both sides of the " Hog's Back " were so delightrul and embraced such extensive panoramas of the country that one was forced to proceed very slowly. On reaching the top there was an exhilarat- ing free-wheel several miles in length into the old yet pleasant County Town of Guildford. On yet another occasion I recall a journey from Portsmouth to London, which follows a road which winds in and out of the striking South Downs, and leads eventually to Ilindhead in Surrey. A friend told me that I should be delighted with this trip, but I reached the top of the Hindhead without having seen anything to attract attention, and I was wishing I had my friend with me so that I might relieve my disappointed feelings, However, at the top there was a magnificent view from what is called the " Punch- bowl," and the very long descent from this point into Guildford was a series of vistas which repaid all the exertions that had been required to ride up the Headland.

The London cyclists are remarkable for the pace at which they travel. Ido not know whether in your district the "Borchers" are given to taking people on; that is to say, drawing them on with a view to getting up a speed contest. It seems a very common habit down here, and once or twice I have:been "taken on" with them. A few weeks ago I went to a favourite place on the Sevenoaks road. It is over a year since I was there previously, and as the summer was waning I thought 1 would pay it a visit. I got to Farn- borough when a young man thought he would "take me on." He went down the hill at Farnborough at a rattling pace, and at the bottom I put on my top gear and passed him. This seemed to nettle him, and in a while he passed me. I let him go, and for quite a long distance be worked as hard as he could to keep in front, every now and again turning round to see if I were following, and to suggest that "I am one too many for you, old man." I knew that presently there was a long grind uphill, and as I am fairly good at this sort- of work I let him continue. I could see that he was wearing himself out on the level, and when I got to the commencement of the three mile rise, I passed him easily and saw no more of him. I just reached my destination when there was a terrific downfall of rain,and I fancy this young man's warm con- dition would be considerably cooled thereby, as there is no shelter for three miles abort of the place I reached. On another occasion a young man in an overcoat, and with a basket on his back carrier, tried the game on with me on the Brighton-road. I enjoyed a good run along the Croydon tramway to Purley on my top gear, and I suppose it was my pace that caused this young man to attempt to pass. I ran up some of the rises on my top gear, and of course, left this speed merchant behind, but he was not satisfied as for several miles I went on, and when I eased off a bit I found be had been following close at my heels, and be then passed. I know I "warmed his jacket "for him because I was feeling somewhat cold with the chilly wind, especially as J

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH LIBERALISM. MR. A. J. KING, M P., ON THE POLITICAL CRISIS. The Peerage and the Beerage. There was a large and enthusiastic gathering at a Liberal meeting held in the Hall Cafe, Stockton Heath, On Monday evening and a cordial welcome was extended to Mr. A. J. King, the popular member for the division, who delivered an interesting address in support of the Budget. Mr. A. A. Hawarth, M.P. for South Manchester, also spoke and his exposition of the land clauses was listened to with great att-ntion. Mr. J. Longland presided and there were also piesent on the platform :—Mr. A. J. King, M.P. and Mrs. King, Mr. A. A. Howarth, M.P., Mr. W. H. Sherburn and Mr. Will Ford (Liberal agent). " THE IRRESPONSIBLE HOUSE."
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH LIBERALISM. MR. A. J. KING, M P., ON THE POLITICAL CRISIS. The Peerage and the Beerage. There was a large and enthusiastic gathering at a Liberal meeting held in the Hall Cafe, Stockton Heath, On Monday evening and a cordial welcome was extended to Mr. A. J. King, the popular member for the division, who delivered an interesting address in support of the Budget. Mr. A. A. Hawarth, M.P. for South Man- chester, also spoke and his exposition of the land clauses was listened to with great att-ntion. Mr. J. Longland presided and there were also piesent on the platform :—Mr. A. J. King, M.P. and Mrs. King, Mr. A. A. Howarth, M.P., Mr. W. H. Sherburn and Mr. Will Ford (Liberal agent). " THE IRRESPONSIBLE HOUSE."

The Chairman said their Conservat ve friends wore holding a Budget protest meetieg last week, so it did not look as if the Budget were dead. One of the Con- rervative newspapers told them some time ago that Lord ltocebery had smashed the Budget, but in that event there would have been no need to proter.4 against it. The Budget was by no means dead. (Applause.) It had passed the House of Commons for good or for ill, and it had now to go to the other House—that non- representative assembly of gentlemen who sat and voted for themselves.. They wore not responsible to anybody; nobody could turn them out if they did not like what they had done. Lord Salisbury raid some years ago that there was no finality about taxation, and that if the nation did not approve of a Budget they could soon see that it was altered, but the Lords had no power to say what the nature of taxation should be, or how it should be applied. (Applause.) We had come to the parting of the ways, for the Lords now said that they had that power, and that they were going to exercise it. if they did so and we accepted their dictum and allowed them to arrange Budgets and veto taxation, the time would soon come when they would not only be vetoing but levying taxation, and they would not be responsible to the country for it. If the Lords' demand were con- ceded, Liberals might, as Mr. Birrell raid, give up at once, because the House of Lords was a permanent Tory body, and whatever Liberal meesure were brought in would, as they had been during the past session and previous ones, be spoiled and rendered inoperative.

div.head: MR. KING AND THE CRISIS.
div.p: MR. KING AND THE CRISIS.

Mr. A. J. King, M.P., said he was pleased to have the opportunity at the witsent very critical period in the history of the country of meeting some of the electors who lived at that end of the division. He was sorry that owing to the exigencies of Parliamentary dutiea he was not able to get amongst them as often as he should like, but since they did him the honour of electing him as their representative in the House of Commons he felt that the first claim upon his time was to serve their interests at Westminster. (Applame.) Everyone said—though he was not quite sure that everyone really believed it—that wo were on the eve of a general election. When they came to think about it, that was a very extraordinary state of things. It was only about four years since the whole country, after a great amount of turmoil, trouble and expense, erected representatives to a new Parliament. It sent to the House of Commons a Parliament which contained a majority for their esteemed, honoured and revered leader, Sir Henry Carapbell-Bsnnerman—a greater majority than had been known in the times of any of us. That majority was still there. They had

div.head: UNITED CABINET AND A UNITED PARTY
div.p: A UNITED CABINET AND A UNITED PARTY

and the work which the people sent them to do was not complete. In the ordinary course of things the Government ought to have another two years liefore them to carry out the measure which the electors sent them there to inaugurate. How was it that there came this talk of a general election ? They had only to go back to the last Parliament to see an instance of how a Conservative Government which had completely lost touch with the electors, as was indicated by by-election after by-election, which had lost the confidence of the country, clung to office till the very last year that was possible. Wherein lay the difference? It lay in the fact that we hadat Westminster not only a House of the people's representatives, but another Chamber of hereditary Peers who represented no-one but themeel res. That Chamber was also a

div.head: PERM ANENT CONSERVATIVE BODY
div.p: PERM ANENT CONSERVATIVE BODY

which did nothing when a Conservative- Government was in office but which no sooner had a Liberal Government been returned, than it set to work to mangle all their measures and endeavour to force a general election as soon as possible. There was another great difference between the House of Commons and the House cf Lords, especially with regard to the present Ilcuse of Commons. There never was a House of Commons where every kind of interest was so well represented as in the present House of Commons. It did not matter what subject came up for discussion whether it were finance, trade, agriculture, social reform, housing or education, there were men there who were experts and who were able to speak from every point of view—from tho point of view of the workingman, the employer, the landowner the tenant farmer or tin agricultural laLourer—every class was represented. In the Upper House there were practically three interests represented. There was, of course, the great .la.nded interest, for the Peers owned many millions cf acres. Th.) liquor interest was represented—there was the beerage as well as the peerage—(laughter)—and great wealth was also represented. There were no representatives in that Hou.so of any other interest and therefore the divergencies between the two Houses were likely to be great. No-one yet knew what the House of Lords were going to do, but they threatened us that for the first time ha the history of this country for 250 years, they were going to take a hand in saying what taxes should Le levied and what supplies should be voted to his Majesty for the carrying on of the work of the country. And yet they were the Constitutional party! They talked about the Budget as revolution, but he ventured to say that if the Lords carried out their threat it would be they who would be the

AUTHORS OF THE REVOLUTION, and he ventured also to say that it would not be they who would control the course of that revolution once it had started. (Applause.) The Budget was remark- able for three reasons—not only for the fact that the Government were asking the taxpayers to pay a largely increased sum next year, but for the purposes to shich that extra money was to be devoted, and for the prin- ciples by which the Government meant to raise it. At first sight it might seem strange for a Liberal Govern- ment, a party which had always preached the watchwords of peace, retrenchment. and. reform, to he asking for largely increased taxation. This Government had, at any rate, given them peace. He did not think a single life had been lest since this Government came into power through any war in which they had been engaged. They had also given us reform, and they would have given much more, had it not been for the influence of the Upper Chamber. Having referred to tho remission of taxes on sugar, tea and coal and to the great reduction of the national debt which the Government by thrifty finance had accomplished, and contrast- ed it with the Tory Government's policy of increasing debt a.nd taxation, Mr. King asked : What had the Liberal Government to show for the increased expenditure which they were now asking for? He claimed that they could show already a practical revision of the conditions of life of some of the most unhappy people of our country. To mention only one thing which this Government had done and which the late 'government dangled before the electors at election times but never fulfilled, they had passed the

OLD-AGE PENSIONS ACT (applause)—and to-day some 600,000 or 700,000 old people, worthy, industrious, sober and hardworking people, who had lived strenuous days who had probably brought up families, and who had maintained them- selves in independence without any recourse to poor relief, were enabled to spend their declining years free from the fear which had hitherto been before them of having to end their days in the Workhouse. That was something to have done. (Applause). Then there were. some 200,000 other people, who perhaps had been equally thrifty and industrious but who through some misfortune, sickness or accident, had been driven, in order to keep body and soul together, to apply for some kind of relief from the Guardians. They had hitherto been disqualified for the pension, but that disqualification ceased automatically at the end of next year, and one of the principal objects for which the extra money was required was to provide pensions for that large class of equally worthy people. (Applause). That was only a beginning. It always seemed to him that the real purpose for which the country sent the Government to power was that they should deal with home affairs, that they shouid pay some attention to the 43 million people who inhabited these islands, aud do something to make life for many of them a little less intolerable than it bad been. There were many terrible problems still to be faced. The whole

POOR LAW wanted taking in band and revising. We wanted to make a greater difference between the treatment of the deserving poor and the treatment of the tramp and idle vagabond who never had worked and did not intend to. We wanted to provide for the deserving unemployed, to make some provision for those hard-working people who broke down and lost their power as broad winners before they reached the age of seventy, and for the widows and children who were deprived of the bread- winner through accident or fatal illness. Mr. Winston Churchill was hard at work preparing schemes of State-

div.head: LABOUR EXCHANGES BILL,
div.p: LABOUR EXCHANGES BILL,

under which there would be set up in every great centre of industry and in the smaller towns also, but cn a smaller scale, labour exchanges, and he believed one of the great results of that scheme would be largely to empty the casual wards in the Workhouses. The Con- servatives said the exchanges would not find work; perhaps not, but they would let the man who was out of work know where work was to be found and what was perhaps even more important, where it was not to be found. (applause). ithother important measure was the Trades Boards Bill. In some of the large cities especially in London, there were what were known as

SWEATED INDUSTRIES, industries which wore badly paid, where the work was often done by women who worked every hour of daylight for a miserable pittance which hardly kept body and soul together. Under the provisions of the Bill in certain selected trades where those cokiditions were most prevalent, there would be appointed joint Boards of employers and employees with a neutral chairman, which would in future fix a minimum wage below which no-one would be allowed to work in those industries. (Applause.) It was mainly for such purposes as he bad enumerated, that the extra money was demanded. There was one other object and one which, to him at any rate, did not commend itself so warmly. There had lately been something in the nature of a scare, and the nations of Europe were rivalling each other in the building of those expensive machines called

div.head: DREADNOUGHTS.
div.p: DREADNOUGHTS.

For that scare he was afraid this country was largely responsible, because the late Government at a time when our navy was, as it is to-day, infinitely stronger than any combination of fleets which could possibly be brought ageinst us, built the first of the new type of ship, and they not only built it but they boasted and swaggered about it, and advertised it all over the world as the only type of ship which in future would be of any use. The result, if their information were correct, was practically to scrap all the existing warships, and consequently there had arisen the demand to re-build our fleet on the Dreadnought lines, and other nations were followiug suit, There was a great scare a little while ago about Germany—a most unfounded scare in his opinion. Germany was a groat and friendly nation with whom wo had NO POSSIBLE CAUSE OF QUARRF,L, and he for one was glad that Manchester had had the pleasure of a visit from his Excellency the German Ambassador, a man with whose charming personality everybody who CIIII3 into contact with him was delighted, and who expressed. and received back in return from the citizens of Manchester, the utmost friendliness and regard towards this country. Still, there were people who lived on scares. There were Jingoes on both sides of the German Ocean and there was a Press in both countries which seemed to feed and live upon stirring up ill-feeling and misunderstandings between friendly countries. Unfortunately there was also a class of men, great financier; probably,who owned loyalty to no flag except as a commercial asset, who liked to fish in troahled waters, and whose business it was to stir up ill-feeling. He was glad to believe that the scare had largely died away, and he was certain there was no ground for it. That scare was largely taken-up and fomented by the Gavernrnent's opponents in order tosbrieg discredit upon the Liberal party. The cry "We want eight and we won't wait" bad subsided &nee, they had been asked to foot the bill. (Laughter.) Whatever people might think about Dreadnought- building, it did not lie with the Opposition to con- demn the Budget in se fir as money was required to build Dreadnoughts, because they had been crying ali along thtt the Government had not been spending enough on tho Navy. Neither did it lie with them to complain about the money that went to old age pensions because if anyone ventured to hint that the Tories were nut as devotedly attached to old age pensions as the Liberals were,or that by any possibility they might not see their nay to continue them, they were called frigid and calculating liars. (Laughter.) Therefore he said the Tories were committed practically to ever) penny which the Budget proposed to raise end to spend. There- fore the only question remaining was. If this money were required—and all parties now admitted that it was —how was it going to he raised? He believed the Conservatives were busy collecting information for the use of the House of Lords as to what would be the result of an appeal to the country. With this object forms of inquiry had been sent out to the various local committees, end one recently came back filled in as follows :—" People down here don't understand Budget end they are very much in favour of tariff reform." (Laughter.) That was a very good example of cause and effect. (Laughter.) They did not understand the Budget and therefore they were in favour of tariff reform—they probably did not understand that either. He (Mr. King) believed that if the people of this country understood the. Budget and tariff reform, they would hemn favour of the Budget and they

WOULD NOT LOOK AT TARIFF REFORM. (Applause.) Mr. Lloyd-George had laid down certain principles in raising the money. In the first place he said "I will impose no tax which shall make life in the cottage of the poor any harder, any more expensive or difficult than it is to-day." (Applause.) In the second place he said "I will distribute my burden over all classes. Everyone shall contribute something but I will put the greatest burden where it can most easily be borne. The people who have the largest incomes and who, therefore, deserve the most benefit from the administration and expenditure of money by the State shall contribute most to the continuation of those services." Further he said "Any tax which I take from the workingman shall be a tax not upon his necessities, food, clothing or rent, or upon the shoes of his children, but a tax upon such things which, if they are not luxurious, he can, at any rate, very well do without, if necessary." Therefore the only taxes the workingrnan would feel were the increased taxes on tobacco and whisky. As against those taxes, which all classes would pay, the men with large possessions were going to pay their share through the increased death duties and income tax, and especially the super-tax on people who were unfortunate enough to have more than £5,000 a year. The reason why two special kinds of property had been selected for special taxation was the same in each case. Each of them had a value attributable to it because it was in the nature of a monopoly; he referred to the licence duties and the land taxes. He was told that if the House of Lords threw out the Budget it would be because they _ .

DARE NOT STAND UP AGAINST THE -DRINK TRADE. What a spectacle for a free country ! Here wo had a 1-louse of Commons, directly elected by the people and representing every interest, and they were to be con- trolled by a House of hereditary Peers which in turn was to be controlled by the drink trade. Surely it was coming to pass as Lord Rosehery said many years ago, that if the country did not control "the trade," the trade " would control the country. (Applause.) Deal- ing with the liceace duties, Mr. King explained that the Government's proposals meant that part of the extra value which had been created by the State in con- ferring the monopoly should go into the coffers of the State. At the present time the

INCIDENCE OF TIIE LICENCE DUTIES was very unfairly distributed amongst the licensed premises of different values. The small public-house in tbe country, often serving a very useful purpose, the only place where the men of the village could meet together and talk over local affairs,a house rated at about £2O a year.paid £lO a year or half its ratable value,for its licence. In London and other big cities they saw great, flaming gin palaces, which served no useful purpose, which did nothing but serve drink to people who were better without it, which were at the root of three- fourths of our crime and 90 per cent. of our lunacy, which cost the taxpayers and ratepayers of the country thousands of pounds every year in maintaining criminals, lunatics, and very largely in maintaining people in the Workhouses, These great places, turning over an enor- mous trade, rated perhaps at £9OO to £l,OOO a year, did not, like the country house, pay half their ratable value. Tee most they ever paid was £6O a year. Therefore a house rated at £6OO, instead of paying 50 per cent paid only 10 per cent. Under the Budget those houses would be levelled up and the big gin palaces would have to pay more in proportion to their value. Having stated that he would leave Mr. Howarth to refer to the land taxes, Mr. King -dealt with the contention that the Budget would drive capital out of the country and cause unomployment. That to his min-d was A PREPOSTEROUS PROPOSITION. They said that by taxity, a rich man the Government would add to the ranks a the unemployed. Assuming that the money had to be got from someone, he wanted to ask them whether they would cause more unemploy- ment by taking say £lO,OOO a year income tax from one wealthy man or by taking it in single pounds from 10,000 poor men earning .21 or 30s. per week ? A man would have to be pretty well-to-do to pay £lO,OOO income tax. (Laughter.) To meet the taxation he would not economise on food, clothing or the necessites of life; he would have to save it out of his luxuries. He might perhaps omit buying a diamond necklace for his wife. Well,that did not give much employment to British labour, because a very small quantity of diamonds would go a long way in hundreds of pounds. (Laughter.) ft was said that the wealthy man would discharge a game-keeper, a footman, a coachman, or a gardener, and that they would join the ranks of the unemployed. They never suggested that he would dismiss his cook. (Laughter.) He (Mr. King) did not think he would dismiss any of them, but that he would save the money in other ways. With regard to the men earning £1 or 30s. a week, they had no surplus funds which they spent on luxuries and out of which they could pay the taxes. Every penny they got as a rule went in buying necessi- ties for themselves and their families. If the Govern- ment took .21 a year from each of those men, they would have that much less to spend with the small trades- man : consequently the tradesman would have fewer orders to give to the manufacturer; the manufacturer would have less work to do, and then they would get the real cause of unemployment. Mr. King showed how the money taken in taxes actually helped to create employment, as the old age pensioners spent their ss. per week on necessities for the household. Referring to the contention that capital was being destroyed and driven out of the country, Mr. King quoted the state- ment of Mr. Tritton, on of the leadiug baukera of

London, that the capital savings of the country amounted to £250,000,000 a year, whereas the total amount taken in death duties was only about £20,000,000 a year, so that there was a little bit of saving left when the

DEATH DUTIES were paid. It was further stated that if they made the income and super-taxes so large there would very soon be no capital left to tax ; they were exhausting the fund. Mr. Lloyd-George gave some figures in the House of Lords the other day showing what were the actual facts. Taking the three years 1897-8-9 the total amount of money which paid death duty was £813,000,000. For tbe three years 1906-7-8 the amount was .£942,000 ,000, so that fund was not showing any signs of extinction. (Laughter). Mr. Pretyman, himself a large landowner, said the average amount of each estate which paid duty was getting less. Mr. Lloyd-George replied that that was quite true. The average amount of an estate which paid death duty fl the first period w.is £4,100, IN hereas in the second • period it was £3,900. That was to say, the average size of the fortune which paid death duties was less, . but the number of estates which came under review was very much increased. Whereas in the first period .. only 71,000 people left estates which paid death duties, in the latter period 8:,009 people left such estates. lie thought the meeting would agree with him that the pr.wisions of the Budget were fair, moderate and sound end the land taxes were a very moderate instalment of a reform which hal been too long delayed, Iho

ONLY ALTERNATIVE put forward was tariff reform, or, as it was called, broadening the basis of taxation—" in other words added Mr. King "shifting the t 'mien from their own backs on to yours." If he knew the eleLtors of the division, as he thought he did know them, they would not trouble very much at that. As Mr. Snowden told Mr. Balfour in the House of Commons. " Don't you go talking to the workingmen about making the foreigner pay. It is an insult to their intellect. It Is very bad electioneering." (Applause.) 'limy were told there would very soon be a genoral election. He did not know what was going to take place in that division. He supposed they would have a Liberal candidate— (laughter) ;he had not been asked set. (Laughter.) He came out last time with no axe to grind and no personal ends to serve—in fact. he stood at considerable inconvenience and he had found that inconvenience oven greater than he expected. Ile might be inclined to retire, but if he were asked to stand, he was not going to run away at this crisis in our history. (Loud applause). Whatever his inclinations might lead him to do, he thought the present crisis was a, time when every man who cared anything for Liberal principles or even for liberty was bound to put every other feeling on one sideand come out end do his best to maintain those great principles which our forefathers won for us and which we were bound to preserve for posterity. (Loud applause.) MR. HAWORTH ON THE LAND QUEST N. Mr. A. A. Haworth, M.P., spoke very highly of the services of Mr. King as member for the constituency. Mr. King had spoken in the House on more than one topic. He was specially commended for one speech by the late Prime Minister, Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman —(applause)—and when he spoke more recently on the Budget those who heard him said what an excellent, business-like and clear speech it was. Alluding to the Budget, Mr. Haworth said the proper way tc, look upon all the taxes T 1 as to consider not so much what they took from a man as what he had left after paying the taxes. (Applause). The death duties were not a tax on capital but a tax on deferred income. According to the Tories, tbey must not tax the rich man or the poor man; they must not tax the worker aril they must not tax the daad man. Then uho were they going to tax? What unimaginative people they were! They were not going to tax anybody; they were going to tax the foreigner. (Laughter). That was the most delichtfel idea possible. (Laughter). Referring to the licence duties, Mr. Haworth said they were an old tax increased—not only at the dictates of the Liberal party, for that Unionist weekly "The Spectator" had for years been advocat- ing getting more revenue out of licences. As to the land taxes, for some years past Corporations up and down the country had advocated the taxation of laid values. Corporations were not always Liberal, and those Corporations where there was a strong Conserva- tive majority had joined hands and came up with n great deputation some years ago in favour of the principle of the taxation of land values being introduced. Now the Tories said, !Allen the Government did what they had long been asking Governments to do, that it was wrong. They were really very hard to please. (Laughter). They said it was not quite all wrong; the only alteration they wanted was that all the money from land taxes should go to the municipalities and not to the State. Under the Budget, half the proceeds of the land taxes would go to the municipalities in relief of rates. The other half would go to the Imperial Exchequer, and he thought that was fair. The rates had done a great deal to increase the value of land but without the security of our army and navy and good so vernment,t he expenditure of the rates would not be sufficient to ere its the prosperity of the various towns of the country which had been made owing to the imperial security and to the railways bringing people and merchandise to the towns. Speaking of

UNEARNED INCREMENT, - Mr. Haworth instanced an east coast town which not much more than twenty years ago was a fishing village but which, thanks to the enterprise and expenditure of the local authorities, hadlecome a prosperous watering place. Consequently land which was formerly worthless had attained a high value and the owner, who bad been paying practically nothing to the rates, had reaped a profit of thousands of pounds. If the present Budget had been iu force, the Chancellor of the Exchequer would have demanded a share of that unearned increment for the community. He put it to any honest man or woman, if they would face the question like that—and there were scores of similar instances—were the land taxes robbery and confisca- tion ? People did not know the English language when they applied such words to those proposals. The wonder was that we had been foolish and blind enough to abut our eyes to that great source of inoo:ne which might have accrued to the community in return for the value which they alone had created. They.had adopted the unearned increment, tax in other countries, in Germany they went back twenty years in calculating the increment. Mr. Haworth showed that the land proposals had ample justification even in the Tory "handbook to speakers " which was issued before tne last election, and which stated that nothing could be more fatuous than to meet the aspirations for better housing conditions and relief from the burden of rent with a frank non-possumus or cry of robbery. The speaker also defended the undeveloped land tax, which would be an inducement to owners to put. their land in i the market instead of holding it up, n the hope that by making I eople live in *incommodious dwellings and suffer inconvenience in business, they would geta higher price. The Government wanted to encourage agricul- ture, and it was only when land had acquired some value which was greater than that for purely agricultural purposes, that the taxes could touch it. Dealing with the alternative of tariff reform, Mr. Haworth said Ger- many waa Protectionist, and if it were possible to make the foreigner pay we ought to be paying for Germany's navy. Were we? They were about £211,000.000 behind, so our account must be a bit overdue. (Laughter.) Mr. Haworth contended that the fact th it the price of whisky bad advanced since the introduction of the Budget, showed that the consumer and not the producer, who was equivalent to the foreigner, always paid the tax. As to unemployment, he did not under- stand how any intelligent man who knew the state of unemployment in Germany, France and the other Protected countries of Europe where the figures for skilled labour showed that every decade they had been worse off in the matter of employment than we had been under Free Trade, could believe that tariff reform would be the groat remedy for unemploy- ment. By increasing the price of articles and lessening the demand tariff reform would not increase but reduce employment. He could hardly believe that the Lords would be so foolish as to throw out the Budget, but if they did it meant they were claiming the right to have control over the public purse and to say they would have a dissolution when they liked. If the country allowed them to maintain that preposterous claim they could do that every year, and the electors might just as well stay at home at election times for the Lords and not they would be the rulers of the Government. The people must say they would be masters of the public) purse and not the Lords. (Applause.) SPEECH BY MRS. KING. Mrs. KING delivered a short address in which she said there never was a time when women ought to take more interest in politics than at the present day. It was a ' time that closely concerned the welfare of women and children, for if they lost Free Trade there was not the slightest doubt that everything they needed in the home would be dearer. The bogey of Socialism Nrea now being drawn across the path and Mr. Balfour his Birmingham speech said they must either go uphill to tariff reform or downhill to Socialism. Had thel less Socialism in Germany under Protection? TheY bad a great deal more and as a result of Or° years of very highly increased duties they hall greatly increased the percentage of Socialists. The recent returns from Saxony showed that where they had one Socialist before, they had now twentY; five. To one Socialist organ in this country they ha: six or seven in Germany, so it did not look as if tail' reform had extinguished Socialism there. She did not think it would extinguish it here, but that Socialise' would spread infinitely more if we got tariff reforah They were told that under Protection wages would rise: but they would be wise if they had a bargain to tbau effect with their employers before voting for i,tcj (Laughter and applause.) She did not think there wow be higher wages but they would have to pay more for everything they used, so she would advise them if thel would win at the coming election, to stick to Free Trade. (Applause). Mr. P. A. Harris moved a vote of thanks to the speakers. Mr. W. 11. Sherburn seconded and said that orerY time their Member came before them they wore prouder of him than beforelle believed the main reason for th?_ keen opposition to the Budget was the objection %rill"' the land-holders had to a valuation of the land be•ing made. It was not the little tax, but what was coming besides. Very little time was allowed to elapse befo_re a new house was valued for rating purposes and should not the land be publicly valued and till! accordingly? If they did not support the Budget the Y could no longer claim to care for liberty, (Applausel.i. The vote was heartily passed and a similar cowl'4 Ment to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: MR. BALFOUR AS A CONSTITUTION
div.p: MR. BALFOUR AS A CONSTITUTION
BREI,KER.

Mr. Balfour on Wednesday night com- mitted himself to the doctrine that the House of Lords not only technically but practically has as much right to reject a Finance Bill as any other Bill; that is, that they have the right once a year, by refusing to vote the supplies necessary for carrying on the Government, to force a dis- solution. Indeed, Mr. Balfour in so many words, claimed for the House of Lords this right to destroy Governments. He swept aside the "antiquarian laws as to the precise historic position of the House of Lords in connection with money bills," and took his stand on what he called the "modern constitutional theory of the object of a Second Chamber." That object, he said, was "to see that the Government of this country is a popular Government." This constitutional theory, to quote Mr. Balfour's own words, is "one which you will not find in the text-boks of Constitutional lawyers, which has been embodied in no resolution I know of either of the House of Lords or of the House of Commons."

div.head: CONVERT TO CONVENIENCE.
div.p: A CONVERT TO CONVENIENCE.

WHAT MR. BALFOUR SAID IN 1907. "We all know that the power of the House of Lords . . . is still further limited by the fact that it cannot touch those Money Bills, which if it could deal with no doubt it would bring the whole executive machinery of the country to a standstill."-- Mr. BALFOUR, June, 1907.

div.head: CHALLENGE TAKEN UP.
div.p: CHALLENGE TAKEN UP.
MR. HALDANE AND THE ISSUE FOR
THE COUNTRY.

"We accept the challenge. No quarter is asked, and none will be given." In .these words Mr. Haldane, the "moderate man" (as he called himself), replied on Thursday- to Mr. Balfour's treat against the Constitu- tion. Since our Constitution has become what it is to-day no step more violent or revolutionary than the one which negatived our efforts in the Budget has been taken, nor any step which asserts for the Lords an equal right to control the financial policy of the country. The Cabinet was absolutely united upon the Budget. The action of the Peers would raise the question whether a Second Chamber could be tolerated in such a form that while a Unionist party was in power there was virtually a single Chamber, and when the other party was in its bills were mauled, itS powers controlled, and its activities hampered by a majority not only enormous, but unsympathetic and hostile to Liberalism. With this issue the electors would have to consider the question of Free Trade, and the attempt of the Peers to control equally with the Commons the financial policy of the country. Duties on food, Mr. Haldane declared, led direct to Socialism.

div.head: Voice of the Workers.
div.p: The Voice of the Workers.

THE CRY GOES UP—" HOW LONG ?" Mr. Shackleton assured a representative of the "Westminster Gazette" that the resolu- tion in favour of the abolition of the House of Lords would be received with delight by the vast majority of the organized workers of the country. "I have been round to many meetings," he said, "all over the North and South of England, and whatever may be said to the contrary in London, it remains true that everywhere conclusive proofs have been given that the Finance Bill is enthusiastically popular, and that the action of the House of Lords is strongly resented. A cry is going up on all hands, and it is gathering force every hour, that the people's representatives must rule; and in that cry the voice of the workers whom we represent can very dis- tinctly be heard. A curtailment of the powers of the Lords is imperatively neces- sary, and we sincerely hope the Prime Minister will give us the lead we are asking, him for."

div.head: Voting for the Lords is Treason to the People.
div.p: Voting for the Lords is Treason to the People.
Sir John Brunner speaking at a Liberal demonstration at Middlewich declared that

Lord Lansdowne's motion was a very cleverly concocted phrase to cover the impudent defiance of the Lords. The situa- tion was grave, and every man who voted in favour of the Lords was a traitor to his fellows. No man, woman, or child was deprived of food, clothing, and shelter by the Budget, and he (Sir John) was ashamed every time he voted to tax the poor. Let them not waste any sympathy on the rich men who wanted Dreadnoughts, and objected to pay, who would not by the Budget be deprived of a single luxury.

div.head: th k,f. • '4.t. • I I
div.p: th k,f. • '4.t. • I I
An Object Lesson in Tariff Reform;
GERMANY'S NEW TAXES.

and excise duty on .paper. It was generally known that the Premier, Lord Palmerston, was against the repeal. Gladstone tells us that Palmer- ston spoke three quarters of an hour in the Cabinet against the Paper Duty Bill. The majority however sided with Gladstone, and it was passed in the Commons by a bare majority of nine and sent up to the Lords. The Lords emboldened by the small majority and by the knowledge of a divided Cabinet threw chit the Bill. Glads,Wne said in reply to Palmerston that this proceed- ing of the House of Lords amounted to the, establishment of a revis- ing power over the House of Commons in its most vital function, long declared exclusively its own, and to a divided responsibility in fixing the revenue and charge of the country for the year. In these proceedings, he stated, nothing would induce him to acquiesce. Gladstone taunted the Conservatives with the silent abetting of" a gigantic innovation on the Con- stitution." Resolutions were passed in the Commons practically telling the House of Lgrds they had invaded the rights of the Commons, and that in future they must be careful to mind their own business. He saw the importance of the issue more clearly than his chief and stated that the fiscal consideration (that was the rejection of the particular proposal) was nothing compared with the vital importance of maintaining the

exclusive rights of the House of Commons in matters of supply, and said "I for one am not willing that . the House of Commons should hold on suffrance in the nineteenth century, what it won in the seventeenth and confirmed and enlarged in the eighteenth." . In spite of the opposition of Lord Palmerston and of a divided Cabinet, Gladstone carried his point, and the Commons sent it again to the Lords but by a majority of only fifteen (296 for 281 against). This was the practical affirmation of the resolution of the House of Commons, that it possessed in its own hands the power to remit and propose taxes, and that the right to frame bills of supply in its own way was one that the Commons must keep inviolate. Sequel: The Lords meekly passed the Bill and without an election. •

How different the crisis of to-day. Instead of a disloyal chief our Chan- cellor of the Exchequer and our party has one who is loyal to the core. Instead of a divided Cabinet there has never been one so united and so enthusiastic for the financial proposals. Instead of a majority of nine or fifteen, there is a majority of 230. Surely this shows how the pretensions of the House of Lords to control the legislation of the country and to assume the preroga- tive of forcing an election whenever it thinks fit, have grown during the last fifty years. It will be for the electors of Warrington to give their opinion as to whether this unconstitutional and dangerous power of an assembly which is responsible to nobody, is to be allowed to grow, or is it to be effectually controlled once and for all?

In Warrington we have a clear issue. " Crosfield and the Commons or Pier- point and the Peers." Victory for the Peers means Protection with all the evils that follow in its train. It means victory for those Dukes whq would put a gag in the mouth of every Labour Member and keep it there for ever. Victory for the Commons means the maintenance of Free Trade upon which so much depends, and more, it means to clear out of the way the great obstruction which stands in the way of every kind of social progress.
GLADSTONE AND THE LORDS

It may be interesting at the present crisis to recall the last time the Lords threw out a Finance Bill. It was in 1860 when Mr. Gladstone, then Chan- cellor of the Exchequer,carried through the Bill for the abolition of the import

div.head: SIR W. J. CROSSLEY, BART., M.P. A CHOICE BETWEEN
div.p: SIR W. J. CROSSLEY, BART., M.P. A CHOICE BETWEEN
PATRONAGE AND LIBERTY.

Mr. Balfour in asrecent speech in the House of Commons said that if he were settling taxation he would adopt all our taxes except those on Liquor and Land and in substitution would intro- duce Tariff Reform. I therefore look upon the corning election as intended to decide the questions as to whether Tariff Reform shall take the place of extra liquor taxation and leave land free, and whether the House of Lords shall continue to obstruct Liberal policy. • Let the people now once for all decide whether they choose to be represented and taxed by the Lords or the Commons. A choice between patronage and liberty! Surely this issue is important. Tariff Reform would require at least two or. three years' notice and would not help the present situation.

div.head: MR. A. J. KING, M.P.
div.p: MR. A. J. KING, M.P.
WHY SHOULD THERE BE AN ELECTION?

lam not sure that the election will come so soon as many people believe. I hope the Government will exhaust every resource to assert the claim of the Commons to control finance, and bring the Lords "to heel " before appealing to the country.

With regard to the issue when the election does come I think that is to be found in the mere fact that there is any talk of an election. Why should there be an election? You have a united Cabinet supported by an unbroken majority in the House of Commons. Such are not the circum- stances which we are accustomed to associate with an appeal to the coun- try, with only four years of Parliament elapsed and plenty of work still to do. _

If we are -forced into an election it will be because the House of Lords is for the first time for many years assert- ing its claim not only to interfere in finance, but also to make and unmake Governments.
If the electors of the country take this "lying down " they will be surrendering the very foundations of liberty and might as well spare. them- selves the trouble of recording their votes in future.

div.head: MR. W. LONG.
div.p: MR. W. LONG.
WILL THE LORDS "FACE THE MUSIC ? "

In reply to your inquiry, I am still dubious as to the Lords facing an indignant country by inviting a revolu- tion in which they must come out losers. For forty to fifty years I have seen them opposed bitterly to every Liberal reform, and fear they are too astute to deliver themselves and their privileges into the hands of the enemy in this manner.
I am a whole-hearted supporter of the Budget, believing it to be about the finest I have ever seen , and fraught with lasting benefits to the best interests of our people.
MR. F. MONKS.
THE BUDGET AND FREE TRADE.

My opinion is that the Lords are making a huge mistake and confound- ing the issue, which is neither Tariff Reform nor Free Trade, but just the simple question whether they shall be allowed to decide any matter of the country's finances. The Liberal Party by making Free Trade a sort of Fetish, will find that the country will not be content to see its big industries destroyed by unfair foreign competition. I am a Free Trader heart and soul, but I am not a one-sided one, that is disposed to admit the foreigner just when it suits him,and for him to refuse our goods admission on a free basis. It may suit the com- mercial classes to buy and sell, but it does not suit the manufacturer to buy in a dear market and sell in the cheapest
against foreign Protection.—Yours truly,
F. AloNKs.

P.S.—There will be many like myself who will support the Budget as against the Lords, but will vote for Tariff Reform until the Liberal Party will consent to thoroughly examine the bearing of our one-sided Free Trade upon our industries.

div.head: MR. CHURCHILL'S MESSAGE TO LANCASHIRE.
div.p: MR. CHURCHILL'S MESSAGE TO LANCASHIRE.
Lords and Finance.—A " Monstrous Usurpation."

Mr. Winston Churchill has promised to address a series of meetings in Lancashire and Cheshire, early in December, with the object of rallying the progressive forces for their great constitutional struggle with the House of Lords. Great efforts are being put forth to induce Mr. Churchill
TO VISIT WARRINGTON
in the course of his tour.

Mr. Churchill gives a striking message to Lancashire in his letter to the Chairman of the Lancashire and Cheshire Liberal Federa— ation, dated November 16th. He says: " Now that Lord Lansdowne has instructed the Lords to destroy the Budget, I will certainly come to Lancashire and aid you in your fight for the rights and liberties of the British people. I have long felt that in :the conflict that is upon us the influence of Lancashire may well prove decisive. Who- ever is going to gain by protective tariffs, it cannot be the Lancashire operative or employer; whoever is eager to pay an ever- increasing toll to the land monopolist in the future, it cannot be the hard-working folk of Manchester, Liverpool, Preston, South- port, Oldham, Burnley, or Bolton, for they at least have paid their share over and over again already. Whoever is going to set up the House of Lords in plenary authority over the House of Commons, it surely cannot be the grandsons of the men who carried the great Reform Bill.

div.head: TARIFFS BAD FOR LANCASHIRE.
div.p: TARIFFS BAD FOR LANCASHIRE.

"Any system of tariffs" says Mr. Churchill, "is certain to injure the trade of Lancashire at many points. A tariff will, by excluding imports, necessarily reduce the export trade. The trade of Lancashire is mainly an export trade. A, tax on bread. and a tax on meat—and both of these gre. intended and announced—is a cruel assault upon the immense population crowded together in the Palatinate upon a soil which could not support a twentieth of their number.
There is no county in England where the enterprise and labour of the population have paid and are paying such

ENORMOUS TRIBUTES TO THE LANDOWNER.. In a hundred years the hills and dales of Lancashire have been transferred from a broad expanse of moorland to an almost continuous cluster of cities, towns, and town- ships, woven with railways, tramways, and canals, into the most marvellous concentra- tion of skilled labour, applied science, and massed capital ever yet organised for the service of man. At every state in this tremendous process the land monopolist has exacted his heavy unearned toll, which hag squeezed the labourer, handicapped trade, and hobbled progress. We are not proposing to take back what the ground landlord has obtained. We should have "spoken sooner " ; but for the future a share at least of communal values should be secured to then workers and the ratepayers who create them. THE REJECTION OF THE BUDGET

would be a double invasion by the House of Lords, both of the royal prerogative and the Commons privilege. They are trying to conceal this monstrous usurpation by the plea that all they seek is the true will of the people. Certainly, in the pass to which things have now come, the electors must decide. But let the people of Lancashire realise the full scope of the constitutional questions which are raised, and the full consequences of their decision. If the House of Lords establish at a general election their right to control the finance of the kingdom, they will have made themselves the.predominant power in the State. Not only will they be able to mutilate any legis- lation that they 'do not like but every year by destroying the annual Budget and stopping the King's revenue, they will be able to force a dissolution of Parliament upon the Crown. No Government in future, therefore, will be able to remain in power unless it makes itself agreeable each year, and from year to year, to a majority of the House of Lords.
Protection, conscription, coercion, SCHEMES OF WAR AND CONQUEsT

all these policies would pass on their way- unchallenged by the new dictatorship. "Stick to office through thick and thin," would be the motto as it was through all the ten bad years of Balfour rule. But a Liberal or progressive Government would be made to have a

div.head: GENERAL ELECTION EVERY YEAR
div.p: GENERAL ELECTION EVERY YEAR

that the Tory caucus thought they could better their party position. Such would be the practical and certain result of admitting at a general election the right of the House of Lords to reject Budgets and dissolve Parliaments, and such results would be absolutely fatal to the democratic character of British institutions. Let Lancashire and the nation decide.

div.head: – MR. E. WYNNE JONES.
div.p: - MR. E. WYNNE JONES.
" CROSFIELD AND THE
COMMONS."

The die has been cast. The Lords have made up their minds to force a revolution. It's now our business to see that they do not control it. We shall soon be plunged into the most momentous political fight that has taken place within the memory of any man living. Liberal and Labour progressives of all shades of opinion must now realise that it is their duty to fall into line, for we have to fight a common enemy. The one hope of the enemy is disunion between Liberals and Labourites. On the great issUe that is now facing us, there should be no dis- union, but complete harmony and unbroken enthusiasm. The one domi- nant issue in this fight will be the House of Lords. The extinction of the veto of the Peers is absolutely necessary ; before any progress can be made; all other matters must be subordinate to this one issue. We must bring to an end the tyranny of the Peers. The question we have to face is either the extinction of Peers' veto or the loss of four liberty, the common right of Britishers to govern themselves through their own chosen representatives. Thus our heritage of liberty and justice is at stake. It is useless to talk of liberty, democracy,of self-government, so long as the Peers' veto remains. We have now sufficient proof that all they

Local Parliament. The debate on the Bill to reform the poor law intrcr duced by Mr. J. McDermid (president of the Board of Trade), last week at the Parliamentary Debating Society, was concluded last Tuesday evening in the Conservative Assembly Room. An interesting dis- cussion ensued. While the Conservative members warmly supported the measure the Opposition main- tained that the poor law system should be swept awaY altogether and that the Bill was inadequate as it did not touch the causes of pauperism. On a division being taken 20 voted for the Bill and 17 against. Next week a Bill " to consolidate the Empire for the purpose of Imperial Defence "will be introduced by Mr. Sam Lloyd, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. One of • the leading proposals is the formation of territorial forces in the Lmted Kingdom and Colonies. service in them to be obligatory on all able-bodied citizens, and the training of the forces to be.on lines to those laid down by the National S.ervice • League.

div.p: ii

LOl-4 LANSDOWNE has taken the plunge, or, as the "Man- chester Guardian" suggests, he has been pushed over the brink and into the whirlpool by the unruly mob behind. We have no doubt at all that he is now shivering miserably. The man who invites revolution involving personal and political annihilation cannot be happy. But it is not with His Lordship's frame of mind that we are seriously concerned. His action in regard to the Finance Bill seems almost certain to precipitate a general election involving the most momentous issues within living memory. The Lords have decided—they may, of course, funk when the pinch comes—to, throw •out the Budget and defy. both Commons and people. They have thrown the gage of battle into the teeth of a foe hungry for the fray. For years the people of England have been growing more and more restive under the arrogant exercise of the veto by the hereditary Chamber. They have—to. use a Lancashire phrase—been "biding their time." That time has come. The Lords had only to lay their hands on the financial pro- posals of the Government to release the floodgates of national wrath. And at last they have dared! What will be the outcome? We have no uncertainty of conviction on the point. The Lords must either back down ignominously, or be engulfed by a passionate uprising of the people. There is no middle way. Democracy shall rule, and will rule, come what may of the arrogant and purse proud ,peers.
THE CRISIS.

We can easily understand why some persons call Lord LANSDOWNE'S motion " astute." They think it is astute because it is evasive. The resolution is based on the new military principle that in modern war it is seldom or , never safe to make a frontal attack. Lord LANSDOWNE seeks to gain a victory by a ruse. He understands quite well that the rejection of the Finance Bill would •be .a- revolu- tion in Parliamentary procedure, and that it would provoke a revolution in the country. He is clear-minded enough to perceive that a general election following on the rejection of the Budget could not be beneficial to his party in any respect, and that its ultimate result must be a vast curtailment of the powers of his order. He therefore avoids the frontal attack. He proposes, instead to change the character of the British Constitu tion at a stroke. Instead of moving the rejection of the Budget, in plain terms, he is to move that we incor- porate into our Parliamentery system a mode of procedure which is said to work well in Switzerland, but which has nothing to do with ourselves. He claims for the House of Lords the right to send the House of Commons to the country, a right which has never pre- viously been asserted, which is abso- lutely without historical support, and (however suave Lord LANSDOWNE'S manner may be) is a rude violation of the methods of past centuries. We deny the astuteness of LORD LANSDOWNE in this case, because his motive is so obviously simple, so trans- parent. He presumes, in the first place that as the Liberal Party in the House of Commons is at present in so vastly preponderating a majority its enemies must necessarily stand to win some- thing or other in a General Election. But he will run no risks. The chance that the Conservative Party would , gain any ground in an election follow- mg on the rejection of the Budget is known by the Conservative leaders and the Conservative agents to be of the very slightest. Why not turn a 'corner? Why not resort to tactics? Why not pretend that the Lords are acting in the interests of the people? Why not, in short, avoid running one's head up against a brick wall? That seems very clever no doubt at the first glance. But has it really any single characteristic of cleverness? Nothing can be more certain than that the House of Com- mons will not take its orders to dis- solve from the House of Lords. The Government is prepared for a dissolu- tion, and the Liberal party is eager for a dissolution under conditions which mean that the House of Lords claims the supreme authority over thefinance of the nation. But neither the Govern- ment nor the House of Commons will Tecognise the resolution of Lord LANS- DOWNE, however many peers may be behind it. •Itis an attempt at a most impudent usurpation. It is an intoler- able assertion of powers that do not .exist, and never have had an existence. At the same time, it is an exhibition of weakness tricked out in the attributes of might.

Warrington has THE REV. A. M. blushed to find itself MITCHELL'S notorious once again. DIATRIBE. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell has pointed the finger of scorn at us to some purpose, and neighbouring communities are shocked at our depravity and sin. As a self-respecting town we do not admit we are as black as we are painted by this heavy-handed clergyman. There are bright places within our borders as well as foul slums, and there is a spirit of righteousness in our midst which can lift its head above the mire and the murk. Mr. Mitchell knows us not well or he would love us better. The resentment of our civic dignitaries at the clerical diatribe is understandable, but they overlook the fact that there is some substance as well as ftoth in the bombshell from Burton wood. We have slums which are plague-spots and which have sprouted ' evilly for generations in defiance of corporate condemnation. We have a death-rate in these • areas which would do full credit to the " white man's grave "in distant Africa. And lest we forget these things the Vicar of Burton- wood reminds us. A dispassionate view of the situation might lead to the conclusion that the best way to refute the rankling charges would be the drastic elimination of those evils which cannot be gainsaid. Where pin-pricks have failed the bludgeon may awaken even a lethargic municipality.

The most devoted ADVANCE admirers of Warring- WARRINGTON! ton will admit that there is plenty of room for municipal improvements, and some important schemes are foreshadowed in the Bill to be promoted by the Corporation in the next session of Parliament. Full details of the powers applied for are published in another part of this issue. The leading pro- posal and the one which is generally regarded as the most urgent is the erection of a new bridge to replace the present Warring- ton Bridge. It will be some satisfaction to the townspeople whose patience has been sorely tried that this long-delayed enter- prise at last appears to be within measurable distance of accomplishment. The Corpora- tion has, of course, already decided to build a ferro-concrete bridge, seventy or eighty feet in width, and the twenty tenders received have been forwarded to Mr. J. G. Webster, the eminent engineer, for his adjudication on their respective merits. A new bridge at Howley has often bee q advocated and this too is a pressing question which demands serious and early attention. We are glad that the Howley scheme is to be included in the Bill and power is also to be sought for the construction of a road or roads leading to the proposed foot-bridge. The widening of Chester-road is also to be taken in hand. In addition to the bridge schemes, numerous and varied undertakings are embodied in the Bill and if many of them could be carried out a transformation of Warrington would be effected. They include the widening and improvement of streets and roads ; the opening out of Victoria Park; extension of the Town Hall, baths and technical school; improvement of the water supply; concessions to gas consumers; the removal of dilapidated buildings and the stipulation of the area of habitable rooms; and various sanitary measures. Authority is to be sought to enable the Corporation to collect all rates upon one basis of assess- ment, to consolidate all the rates levied in the borough, and to provide for the same being collected upon one demaud note. A proposal which will be generally endorsed is that the Corporation shall have power to subscribe towards hospitals, infirmaries, nursing associations, charities and other benevolent objects which too often are hampered in their public work through straitened financial resources. Of course,the passing of the desired Bill would not imply immediate intention on the part of the Cor- poration to put all its clauses into operation, for there must be consideration for the rates, but it would obviously be an advantage to have as comprehensive *powers as possible so as to save the cost of promoting other Bills as the various schemes come forward.

Some of the Protec- THE INGENIOUS tionist countries which FOREIGNER. find their tariffs pro- duce nothing like enough revenue for their purposes show that they have no small resourcefulness, to say no more, in what (as against tariff imposing) is generally referred to as "Free Trade finance." When Mr. Lloyd-George announced his special Income-Tax exemption on account of children the British nation tittered. Not that anybody denied the excellence of the innovation, but . . . it was so funny . . . it was so novel. If our good fellow-citizens could go abroad they would soon get used to novelties. The German Finance Bill as intro- duced contained proposals for taxes on advertisements, on matches, on railway fares, on electric light, on electric power. And any of these (they are mostly, we admit, bad) would have sustained not merely denunciation but overpowering ridicule had it been suggested in this country. And now the Austrian Finance Minister has struck out new lines—the things most British Chan- cellors never think of—with the utmost sang- froid. He puts forward what really are the necessary corollaries of Mr. Lloyd-George's admission that large families ought not to pay as much direct taxation as small ones with an equal income. The Austrian Parliament is being asked to sanction a special Income- Tax on bachelors, and another, a little less severe, on married people who have no children. Finally, he is producing a sugges- tion what at least one Member (who objected to people turning themselves in dirigible human balloons) advocated during our own Budget debates; a tax on mineral waters. We are not hinting for a moment that all these taxes are good ones. But what they remind us of is the comparative conserva- tism of the British mind. Here we prefer to increase old taxes; new taxes are rare things, and when we do get them, it is not until we have thrashed them out for years and had them debated by Royal Com- missions. But the adventurous and ingenious alien brings in new taxes in bunches—often taxes which nobody in the countryi has talked about or expected. This is certainly more picturesque and interesting than our method; but perhaps it is not sounder.

div.head: Examiner Saturday, November 20, 1909
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, November 20, 1909
NOTES AND NOTIONS.

One would think that Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., was the prospective candidate for Warrington by his careerings up and down the town. Last week but one a yellow motor car containing the Baronet was seen spinning along Liverpool-road. It pulled up near St. Luke's Church, but the church was closed—and the Albions were away. Sir Gilbert must have mislaid his fixture card, or forgotten the date. *** _ _ _

If the action of Lord Lansdowne and his co-peers is surprising, the intention attributed to the Opposition in the House of Commons is still more astounding. We are seriously told that when the Lords take the fatal step they will be supported by Mr. Balfour and his followers. * * *

In other words, the Opposition, from this time forward, intend to turn themselves into a sort of Parliamentary "Suicide Club," having for their object the destruction of the House of Commons and the elevation of the House of Lords. And it would seem that they are actually going to plan a General Election in which they shall go up and down country placing that programme before the electors of the United Kingdom. *

The obvious conclusion would be that they would refuse to stand as candidates for the House of Commons. If the House of Com- mons is to be reduced to this contemptible position, then as men of dignity might they be expected to stand aside. But it is credibly reported that, on the contrary-, the Unionists propose to make a vigorous effort to capture seats on this programme, and they even hope to obtain a majority in the House of Commons. * * *

In such a hope they are reckoning with- out their hosts. The English people, let them be quite certain, are not possessed of suicidal tendencies. They are fond of their institutions, and would not even interfere with the House. of Lords if it kept in its place. But they are, above all, fond of the House of Commons, and will not stand by and see it massacred to make a landlords' holiday.

* * * There is a new fact which may. come out amid the turmoil of the next few weeks. The House of Lords claims to be acting impartially, and desires only to give the people the chance of deciding their own affairs. But the House of Lords is also a House of Landlords. They own a fourth of England. Are they, therefore the right authority to. have the final decision of the Budget which sets up land taxes? • * * It will be interesting to see how many of the six hundred peers—the bulk of whom rarely vote at all unless their personal interests are touched—turn up next week to defend their pockets from the proper contri- bution towards Naval Defence and Old-Age Pensions. We presume that they will throw out the Budget when encouraged by their own numbers. If they do, then the only possible answer from the public is "never again." Otherwise, when the Liberals have won the election, this sort of thing may happen again every year. Every year the business of the country may be thrown out of gear. The Treasury tell us this year that the deficit will be £50,000,000. , This is as great as any aunual deficit in the Boer War. Can that go on for ever? Do the Lords imagine that their coronets are worth £50,000,000 a year to the British people'? In short, we are faced with all the losses and troubles of a war. And it will indeed be a war—a civil war—which can only.eod :when the power of the Lords has been curtailed, and the supreme right of the people to govern them- selves been demonstrated beyond challenge or question. * * * _ _ _

Mr. Norbury Williams and the "Man- chester City News" have been joint defendants in an action for libel this week brought by Mr. C. A. Wood, a Manchester City Councillor. The municipal trading question has been at the root of the matter. M. Wood is largely interested in a limited company which supplies carriages to the Corporation and his position has been publicly assailed by the defendants who plead justifi- cation. The hearing of the case has developed some interesting arguments on the trading question as we understand it here, but unfortunately no decision has been come to whether the defendants did libel Councillor Wood, or were justified in their criticisms from the point of view of the public interest. Yesterday, the case for both plaintiff and defendants was concluded, but the jury disagreed and were discharged. A verdict either one way or other could not have been other than very interesting.

* * * Mr. A. J. King, M.P., had a rousing recep- tion at Stockton Heath on Monday evening and his striking!y lucid and convincing exposition of the Budget was listened to with great interest and approval. The mem- ber's democratic sympathies and his con- sistent support of progressive legislation have maintained the confidence and respect of his constituents, and we believe they will be with him in his whole-hearted backing of the Government's equitable and epoch- making financial proposals. Mr. King has announced his willingness to be the Liberal standard-bearer in the Division in the coming momentous struggle, and we have every confidence that he will again carry it to victory. Cheshire does not " love a lord" so devotedly as in the good old days when Egertons and Warburtons rode roughshod over a subservient agricultural community. * * *
On a mug in a farmhouse in Buckingham- shire, presented by a landlord to his tenants, is the following rhyme: Success to the plough, The fleece, and the fail ; May the landlord ever flourish, _

Ana the tenant never fail. The difference between the suggested assured condition of the landlord that of ever flourish- ing, and the pious hope that his tenant may succeed in not failing, is indicated with delightful naïveté (says the " Westminster Gazette.") Just now the "ever flourishing" are grumbling at the Budget, and talking loudly about te duty they owe to themselves in keeping up the flourish, whilst the other members of the community have to think of the duty they owe to themselves by keeping their expenditure down so as not to fail.

Lecture on the Smoke Nuisance. An interesting and instructive lecture on the smoke nuisance was delivered by Professor Graham, of Manchester, in the Academy-street Adult School on Thursday evening. Mr. Henry Roberts presided over a fair attendance. He said the smoke nuisance was not merely a matter of local interest but of national interest.lt was because of the magnitude and importance of that that one hoped that science and humanity would before long compel some ameliorative Influence to be brought into existence to )aaake life better worth living than ' under the conditions that obtained at present in our industrial towns. —Aldermen Bennett and Smethurst and Messrs. J. Morton, Geo. Walker and, W. Nightingale. spoke briefly in favour of the smoke abatement, and the• usual votes of thanks concluded an instructive evening.
