div.head: BABY'S BODY IN A SEWER.
div.p: BABY'S BODY IN A SEWER.

William Groves, of 17, Church-street, Widnes, an employee of the Widnes Corporation, made a gruesome discovery while emptying street gullies on Monday morning. At 11.30 he was in the passage at the buck of Parsonage-row, emptying one of the gullies, when he unearthed the body of a newly-born male child. From Police-constable Hillser's inspection, the body had been wrapped up in a newspaper and tied up with cord, which probably had fallen away, and the cord was found round the neck and acioss the abdomen, but not sufficiently tight to cause strangulation. It had probably been in the sewer for three weeks.—The body was conveyed to be mortuary.
IMPORTANT ELECTRIC LIGHTING AND POWER
SCHEME.

The Castner Kellner Alkali Company Ltd., Weston Point, Runcorn,will seek powers in the ensuing session of Parliament to carry out an important scheme to supply electrical energy for all purposes within the Urban District of Runcorn and the township and parish of Weston. Full particuiars of the proposed Order appear in our advertising columns. It would authorise the company to generate, store and supply electric energy for liebting, heating, power and all other purposes, public and private, and also to acquire by agreement or to take on lease the necessary lands and property. and to construct and maintain upon them stations and works. A map show- ing the boundaries of the area of supply and the streets in which it is proposed that electric lines shall be laid down will be deposited on or before November 30th, for public inspection with the Clerk of the Peace for the county at his office ar Chester, at the respective offides-of the Clerks to the Runcorn Urban District Council and the Runcorn Rural District Council Runcorn, and at the office of the Board of Trade- Whitehall, Loudon. WIDXES RECTOR'S SELF-SACRIFICE. FATHER BARRY AND HIS CEIEQUE.

On Tuesday evening, at the new schoolroom, Pens ley Cross, during an entertainment given by the school children, Father Melia, the new rector, informed a large audience that they were assembled for the purpose of presenting to their late rector, the Rev. Father Barry, a small token of regard. In the course of his remarks he said that it was a difficult task for him to follow in the footsteps of such a man as Father Barry and keep up the same standard of work. After other eulogiums upon the character of the late rector, he called upon Mr. J, Woods to make the presentation, who paid a fine tribute to Father Barry's work amongst them, and asked his acceptance on behalf of the congregation of a cheque to the value of £7O. Father Barry thanked them for the very evident proof of their love and affection, but be created quite a sensation when he returned the cheque to the Rev. Father Melia for the use of his own mission, where, he 'said. his heart still was. At the same time there was nothing to prevent him from doing the same work at St. Marie's as he had done in Widnes. Father Leeson stated that his new rector was doing as good work with as much success in St. Marie's. and he thanked the collectors and sub- scribers in Father Barry's name, for the testimonial. He marvelled at such a sum collected from so small a congregation. MAYORAL PROCESSION AT WIDNES.

A large throng of Widnesians assembled at the Town Hall, Widnes, on Sunday, to witness the procession of the Mayor and Corporation officials and others con- nected with the borough, to Hartland Wesleyan Chapel, Irwell-street. The Mayor, Councillor T. Smith, J.P. (this being his #econd year of office), looked a picture of healthiin his robes. Departing punctually from the Town Hall square,- large crowds lined the route to the church, the following being the order of the pro- cession :—D Squadron Lancashire Hussars (under the crimmand of Sergeant-Major Stevenson),3rd West Lanca- shire Artillery(under the co mmand of Lieutenant Bibby), West Lancashire Division Engineers (Li eutenan t- Colonel Sayce and Lieutenant-Colonel Oppenheim), sth Battalion South-West Lancashire Volunteers (Captain Caldwell and Lieutenant Calland) ; police under Superintendent Strickland, Mace Bearer, his Worship the Mayor, Magistrates, County Council, Councillors. Edhcation and Library Committees, Board of Guardian, Corporation officials and Fire Brigade. Amongst others who joined the procession were the representatives of the local Buffalo Order. The Rev. L. G. Charlesworth, discoursing from the text "Give unto Cantu the things that are Csar's," dwelt strongly upon citizenship duties. The offertory was in aid of the Queen's Nurses Fund. IN THE MORNING EARLY.—Harold Jones and Bert Lawless, of Main-street, Frodsham, were summoned for riding their bicycles without having lighted lamps attached thereto dnring prohibited hours on the 29th inst.—They pleaded guilty.—Sergsant Broome said he met the young men riding in Halton main street at a quarter past one on the morning of the 29th October, they had no lights on their machines. He understood that they had been to a ball which was being held at Halton that night.—A floe of ss. was iMposed in each case. _

A CARTER'S NEGLECT.—Isaac Elwood, Bold-street, was summoned for allowing a horse and lorry to stand in South-road, Weston Point, without having a light attached during the prohibited hours. P. C. Brown nroved the case.—Defendant said that be went into the Dock Hotel, on business, leaving a boy on the lorry holding a lighted lamp, but the boy got off the lorry in his absence. He admitted that there was no lamp bracket attached to the lurry.—Superintendarit Ennion said that it was an offence if a boy was left with a lamp on a vehicle. The law was that the lamp had to be attached to the vehicle.—Fined 103. including costs.

div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Comicality heads the bill at the above place of, amusement this week and Jack Lane, the Yorkshire Rustic, proves a champicn entertainer clad in the usual garments of a rustic, with long smock and short leggings and a slouch hat ; he makes a great hit. All the time be occupies the boards roars of laughter resound through the building and Lane makes his debut with the well-known song "Has anybody seen Kelly," which he puts in different settings, including how it was sung by a village parson and then by the Salvation Army. At the elose of his allotted time on the stage, Lane introduces " Kelly." Orpheus, an intrumeutalist, proves himself to be a master of melody. He produces splendid music from the latest and weirdest instruments which can be mentioned. The scene is laid at a band rehearsal and when he (the conductor). arrives, he finds the bandsmen have not turncd up and so goes through the different parts himself. He introduces a new instrument stand- ing about five feet high, called the Hegophone, upon which he plays, "Asleep in the deep." Another good turn is provided by Woodhouse and Wells with their cross-talk and patter, during which they employ some original and witty jokes. They close their performance with a clever exhibition of simultaneous dancing. The Weimar& are speciality artists. The male Wiemar was a trumpeter who served under, Lord Roberts in the. Afghan War .and was present in the famous march to Kandahar. They present a mixed tern, of tight rope walking and bugle playing. . The audience is in a merry mood when Nancy St. John is on the stage. 'She gives some capital original songs entitled "When your ship

comes home," and. " Dulcie .and her dulcimore." James Curry, comedian, has a style of his own and presents some excellent patter. The sisters Carlton, are out of the ordinary as singers and dancers. , Rose D'Aulby. is a chorus vocalist and sings "No moon shines bright for pretty Redwin." The Palace Perfection Pictures play an important part in the programme this week and illustrate a tour in the "Emerald Isle," "From Dublin to Killarney." The series of pictures are the best yet seen in the Hippodrome and should not be missed.

div.head: REV. A. M. MITCHELL'S DIATRIBE.
div.p: REV. A. M. MITCHELL'S DIATRIBE.
Strong Repudiation by Magistrates.

The remarkable attack on Warrington made by the Rev. A. M. , Mitchell, Vicar of Burtonwood, in his parish magazine, was repudiated from the Bench at the Borough Police Court on Monday. The article which aroused so much comment was headed "Warrington for Christ," aril the following is an extract from it :

"In all England there is not, perhaps, a town . of similar proportions to Warrington and equal population so completely given over to social unrighteousness. For abominable smells, for abundance of drink, Warrington can easily win a first prize. Its record is not good, nay, it has an evil record. Possessed of eight town churches, with some missions in addition and a variety of chapels, Warrington has gained, notwithstanding, a word-wide notoriety for intemperance, brutality, infant mortality, and civic rottenness. The town is so beer-sodden as to lie offensive, so shimmy as to be disgusting, so dirty, nauseous, and unhealthy as never to be free from epidemic, so depraved and well vaccinated as to have a death-rate of 51.3 per thousand, in a portion of its area, so socially, morally degraded that the drink traffic looms large on at least one of its councils and board of guardians. Warrington for Christ! 'Tis some will think a big order; too big an order for a town so brewery-ridden, so beer begripped, a town so befouled, begrimed and vitiated, whose slums, more slummy than the slums of our great cities, are death-traps and moral cesspools, where crimes and brutalities are daily committed which provide good and constant copy for the daily and weekly Press." Before the business of the Court, presided over by the Mayor, commenced on Monday, Mr. W. Roberts said: Mr. Mayor, I should like, with your permission As a magistrate of this borough, to refer to a matter which ba3 engaged the attention of a large sectiou of the community this week end. I refer to some criticisms made by a certain clergyman not very far from Warrington about the condition of our town. I entirely repudiate the statements contained in those remarks by that clergyman. I deny emphatically that our good old town of Warrington is in anything like the condition which this clergyman has thought fit to state. Our town is not reeking with drunkenness. Certainly we have more than we would like and we hope by the measures which we are all taking to bring about a better state of things that the town will considerably improve in that respect. But I venture to say, Mr. Mayor, that our town will compare very favour- ably with any other town in Lancashire —(hear, hear) and, so far as the slums are concerned, (I think we have sufficient confidence in our Town . Council tq believe that remedial measures are being taken by the authorit es and that we are all hoping that the condi- tion of some parts of our town will very soon be greatly improved, And so far as the corruption of our Town Council is concerned, I entirely repudiate that. It was my honour and privilege to have a seat in the Town Council for three years, and I watched the pro- ceedings there with great interest and with the desire to do what I could for the benefit of my fellow towns- men, and I say here, without the slightest hesitation, that during the three yeats I was in the Council I never saw a single transaction which I could con- scientiously object to. I believe that our Town Council to-day, as it has always been, is composed of men who honestly and sincerely desire to do the best they can for their native town, and I throw back these insinuations and suggestions with the profoundest contempt and with the strongest possible indignation. We are all proud of our native town and we keenly resent these abomin- able insinuations, which are absolutely untrue, and if everybody knew this Vicar as we know him—(laughter) —they would not attach much importance to any thing which he says on these subjects. Unfortunately, coming from a Clergyman of the Church of England, the words are apt to lead strangers to attribute some importance to them. But we know him and appre- ciate him at his true worth. I say, without the slightest hesitation, these baseless, groundless state- ments are a discreditable act on his (Mr. Mitchell's) part, and I hope before he rushes into print on another occasion he will be more sure of his facts and will be more careful not to reflect upon a town of which we are natives and with which we are proud to he associated.

The Mayor, replying to the congratulations of the Bench on his re-election as Chief Magistrate, said : Allusion has been made to the gross libel and the violent attack that has been made upon our good old town of Warrington. My first thonght was to take no notice of it, because I knew that it came from an irresponsible quarter, but feeling that it might get afield in other towns and that those people who read that libel might think that the Vicar of Burtonwood was a responsible authority, I think it only right that I, as chief magistrate of this town, should give it emphatic denial, (Hear, hear). I say that Warrington is remarkably free from serious crime, and my experience on the Bench has been that we have disposed of our cases on an average in about half an hour, so that there could be no serious crime to be dealt with. I should like to ask Mr. Mitchell where be gets his data from with regard to the death-rate, and if, instead of making a general attack upon the Council, he will tell us who he is hitting at, then we will del with him in another way. I can only say, I emphatically deny the gross mis-statements that that man has been guilty of.

div.head: ROLLER SKATING.
div.p: ROLLER SKATING.
THE EMPIRE RINK

Lovers of skating have lately been conjuring up prospects of enjoying a few hours on real ice, but their hopes have so far not been realized. However, they are able to enjoy the pastime to the full at the Empire Rink, Winmarleigh-street, where ,rinking is becoming increasinglz popular. ,Thursday night was a special night when there were over 300 skaters, and almost that number of spectators. Two races, a gentlemen's balloon race and ladies' hoop race were contested with interest. The balloon race was very exciting and laughable as the balloon, when launched into the air, had only to be struck with the left hand until it was knocked, over the barrier at the end of the rink. The winner of this race was Mr. W. Wadsworth. In the hoop race Miss Cissie Green was first. The prizes were :—Balloon race, a handsome wallet; and hoop race, a scent satchel.

On Wednesday a league match between the Empire Rink hockey team and a team from Farnworth Hall near Bowden, was played. The visitors, who are a first-class team, beat the local team by four goals to nil. The Empire team was as follow':—Bowcock (goal), Reardon (back), Walton (right wing), J. H. Hulme (centre), and Wadsworth (left wing) ; Gleeson was reserve. , On Thursday evening next there will f)e a grand " moonligh`t " carnival, and there is again an attrac- tive prize list. The engagement of a local comedy band is announced. THE PALATINE RINK.

The first ladies' hockey match which has been played at the Palatine rink attracted a capital attend- ance on Tuesday evening. Both teams were associated with the Palatine club, and were as follows :—No. 1: Miss E. Hackney, goal; Miss B. Cotterill, back; t Miss Bessie Hewitt, left wing; Miss Kaltenback, centre; and Miss Singleton, right wing. No. 2: Miss E. Hill, goal; Miss Hall, back; Miss Dora Singleton, left wing; Miss Ethel Hewitt, centre; and Miss Arbour, right wing. The game was well contested through- out, and the result was a goalless draw. Mr. Leslie had charge of the whistle. This (Saturday) even;ng there will be ,a hockey match Palatine v. Wigan. Comb:l,g events include : Thursday next, lady and gent's two step competition; Monday; November 29th, special engagement of the Territorial Band; Thursday, December 2nd, masked carnival.
MOSELEYS FOOD.—An ideal food for Tnfauts. Soothing, comforting, easily digested and full of nourishment.—Advt.

div.head: REV. F. B. MEYER. The Bishop of—tii—Free Churches.
div.p: REV. F. B. MEYER. The Bishop of—tii—Free Churches.

FREDERICK BROTHERTON MEYER was born on April Bth, 1847,- at Lavender Terrace, Wands- worth-road, when that now thickly populated district was still a pleasant semi-rural suburb. Ile was the second child and only son of his parents, and in •the truest sense of the phrase he was "well-born," for he came into a cultured Christian home, and inherited from both father and mother high traditions and honourable 'ancestry. Throughout his youth, according to Miss Jennie Street, in her interesting book entitled " F. B. Meyer, his life and work," he had a great desire to become a, preacher; and one Sunday evening after his mother had retired, he found courage to seek his father, vile had stayed in the dining-room reading, and confess his secret hope. He spoke, his father wrote afterwards, "with great modesty and deep feeling, and the most touching expressions of conscious unfitness." As long as he could remember, he said, he had wished to be a minister; and though he was unable to speak accept- ably, he was sure God would prepare him and use him in His own way. Mr. Meyer heard his son with surprise, for in all the family conclaves about the lad's future the ministry had never been mentioned. But he listened with the fatherly sympathy that had. never failed his children, and talked with him wisely, pointing out that he was still young and inexperi- enced ; his views might change as he grew older; it as right for him to go on praying for direction.

Frederick Meyer was too humble and too much in earnest to dispute the decision, but his resolution was 'not shaken. On his seventeenth birthday he talked the matter over with his mother, who made a private record of what he told •her. "My desire still continues" he said, "and I feel it would not continue if it was not God Himself who lied given it to me. I know I shall gain nothing by it in a worldly point of view, but it is for the glory of God, and I feel there is nothing else worth living for. And if I am not able to speak many words,. I would still be a hard- working minister for the good of souls." However, he went as a clerk in a tea-merchant's office. While in this capacity one experience especially impressed him. It is best told in his own words : "When I was a clerk in a tea-house conrected with Mincing-lane, I mislaid one of the valuable weight- notes entrusted to my care. I hunted everywhere for it in vain. On any day that note might be required: to enable our firm to obtain the chests of tea which it represented. And every day I lived by faith that it would not be called for, or that if it were, it would somehow be forthcoming. "Three or four nionths passed and it was not required, and I persevered in prayer. One morning, however, when the letters were opened, there was an order for those very chests. My heart failed me, but I fell back on the promise that those who wait on the Lord shall not be ashamed. I went back to look once more in my desk, and there, between two sheets of blotting-paper, was the missing 'note.; and with an over-flowing heart, I hid my face dgainst my open desk and gave thanks." The clerk who lived by faith and prayer in Billiter Square and Mincing-lane did not forget his call to the ministry. He gave his evenings to lectures and classes, or quiet hours of study at home. Later it was agreed that he should seek admission to Regent's Park College.

During the earlier part of his residence at the College, he attended the ministry of the Rev. Thomas Jones, but later on he preached once or twice every Sunday, and in 1868 he was given a small , charge at Richmond. Here he won his first success. He gathered a congregation and established a Church, which was afterwards housed in a permanenebuilding. It is now known as Duke-street Chapel, Richmond. Thirty years after- wards, one of the Christ Church Bank-holiday excursions to Richmond was welcomed at Duke-street Chapel, and of all the addresses given on that occasion none was more enjoyed than that of a venerable deacon who had, Mr. Meyer said, "taught him how to preach." In 1869 he accepted a call to Pembroke Chapel, Liverpool, as assistant to Rev. C. M. Birrell and in 1872 he became pastor of Priory-street Baptist Chapel, York. One morning the pastor of the York Baptist Chapel received a letter which told him of the death of Dr. Nathaniel Haycroft, of the Victoria-road Baptist Church, Leicester. Instantly the thought flashed into his mind," You will be the minister of that church." The invitation came, and was accepted; and be preached his first sermon at Victoria-road Church in September 1874. . _ _ _

In the spring of 1879 it became evident that the growing Church needed a permanent home of its own, and Mr. Meyer and a few of his friends began to pray for guidance. On Macch Bth prayer was offered that "if it were the will of God that a building shkuld be erected, some donation might be given unsolicited, for that purpose." On the 28th Mr. Meyer called on an invalid lady who was connected with some of his people, and as he was leaving she gave him an envelope, and told him that it was a donation towards the erection of a building for his ministry. It con- tained a 10 note, of which Mr. Meyer says, "it spoke to me as the land-birds to Columbus, after his weary voyage, when they perched upon the rigging of his ship and told him he was nearing land. Dearly do I wish I had kept that note or photographed it, because it was almost the first direct gift of money received in answer to prayer, and was, so to speal, the lure that led me to step out on the way of faith." •

The entire Cost of Melbourne Hall and its site was about X,lo,ooo—twice as much as the amount originally intended for this purpose, and the value of the place was eventually increased by several addi- tions, such as the Walker Memorial Schools, erected by three sons in the memory of their father. A busy place all the week, Melbourne Hall was at its busiest on Sunday, which began, the workers said, on Satur- day night, with four prayer-meetings. Saturday night was market-night, but the rrayer-meetings were always well attended. In 1888 it become increasingly evident that Mrs. Meyer could only reside at Leicester at the cost of much suffering to herself and consequent anxiety to Mr. Meyer. It seemed, therefore, the way out of a difficulty when he received a call to the pastorate of Rbgent's Park Chapel, London, which was then at a very low ebb. In 1892, Mr. Meyer, acting in accordance with the traditions of Regent's Park Chapel, rather than from personal preference, accepted the presidency of the London Baptist Association, which added a good deal to his work, and he continued, also, to attend a large number of conventions and conferences in all parts of the kingdom, which meant, of course, a great deal of travelling. often accomplished by night, in order that the days might be free for more important engagements. In 1892 he received a unanimous invitation from Christ Church, Westminster Bridge-road, to succeed his old friend, Dr. Newman Hall. . .

Some months ago, however, he came to the decision that a wider sphere was possible for him and relinquishing the pastorate of Christ Church he became the ", travelling " bishop of the Free Churches. He travelled up and down the country, encouraging, advising and stimulating Christian, workers. At the beginning of 1909, he went on a tour for the purpose of investigating and aiding missionary effort in Europe and Asia. On his return he was called again to the pastorate of Regent's Park Chapel, and doubtless he will con- tinue the blessed work there which he began in 188 S.
THE REV. F. B. MEYER, Who will give three addresses in Parr Hall on Monday next.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday, before the Mayor and other magistrates, Harry Hope, a young man, who gave his address as Grove Park-road, Port Sunlight, was charged with begging in Knutsford-road, on Saturday, November 6th, and with obtaining by means of a certain false pretence from Francis Williams, Baxter-street, goods to the value of 2s. on November sth, and further, with obtaining in the same manner food to the value of 6d. from Jane Standish of Beatrice-street,

The Chief Constable said that the prisoner was before the Court the previous Monday, charged with begging and he was remanded. Inquiries had been made with the result that it had been ascertained that prisoner had obtained food in two cases by false pretences. On November sth, prisoner came to War- zington and went to the house of Mrs* Williams, a widow residing in Bixter-street. He made a statement to her that he was employed by Lever Brothers of Port Sunlight, and was canvassing the town. By this pretence he obtained from her, food and lodgings to the value of 9s. Later in the day he went to the house of Mrs. Standish and told her the same tale, and obtained sixpennyworth of food. Later the police apprehended him begglng for in Knutsford-road. It was a very low down trick, especially as the food was stolen from widows who in nine cases out of ten could ill afford it. The police had communicated with prisoner's mother in Bolton who refused to have anything to do with him as he was of previous bad character. He was not deserving of any sympathy from the bench as he had sponged on those widows and got what he could out of them. His mother had not heard of him for nine months.—Prisoner was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour.

div.head: ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSE.
div.p: ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSE.

CASE DISMISSED ON PAYMENT OF COSTS. At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, James Edward Newton, a muffin dealer, 102 Syril-street, was charged with cruelty to a horse on the 3rd of November. —Francis Lane, an inspector of the R.S.P.C.A. said 'that at three o'clock on the 3rd November, his attention was called to the defendant who was in charge of a grey gelding attached to a two-wheeled cart in the Bridge Inn yard. He told him to take it out of harness and on examining it he found it in a fearful condition. There was a wound about three inches long at the root of the tail, from which there was a dischaige which was wade worse by the crupper pressing into it. Witness pointed it out to defendant who said "Yes, I noticed it a day or two ago." Underneath the tail also there were a number of wounds. Defendant said a lad named Newton had been hitting the horse. Witness made enquiries in Hardy-street, and was unable to ascertain if boys had been hitting the horse. Witness asked a lad named Hyham who had injured the horse and be said" Him," 'pointing to defendant. The wound bad apparently been done by a blunt instrument.—ln reply to Mr. Browne, who represented defendant and pleaded "Not guilty," witness said the wound could have been caused by a blow from a stick. —Mr.Browne said that on the day in question defendant Was on his way to Runcorn with a small load on his cart. On getting over the Wilderspool Crossing and into Chester-road he found that the pony was bleeding from a wound under its tail. He at once turned back, and on getting by the Warrington Bridge he saw an officer and said "Look at my pony." The officer advised him to to take it into the Bridge Inn yard. The officer then went and informed Inspector Lane. The pony had not been worked for some days prior as defendant had ient his cart for the recent elections. Mr. Browne empha- sised the fact that on defendant's own information to the constable be was before them that morning. After having stabled the horse at the Bridge Inn be waited for Inspector Lane, and then they went to Hardy-street, where a woman told them that she had seen a number of boys thrashing the boys withia stick. In conclusion he claimed that there was no cruelty whatever.—Mrs. 31aalutry, 102, Hardy-street, said she saw a number of boys ill-treating the pony on the Friday evening pre- vious to the elections.—The Chairman (Mr. H. Roberts) said that defendant was guilty of negligence in not examining the pony after being informed of it being ill-nsed.—He was ordered to pay the costs of the case, ,6s. 6d.

div.head: Warrington Borough Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Court.
TUESDAY.—Before7Councillor H. Roberts (cbairman), Messrs. J. Rymer Young and C. Jackson Holmes.

MAINTENANCE ORDERS.—James Waterworth, 175, Hope-street, Leigh, was summoned for being £2 in arrears towards the maintenance of bis father in the Warrington Union, on an order made in 1907. Mr. Shearer said tbe man had made a promise to pay 2s. per week and the Bench made an order for that amount. George Waterworth, 2, Reeve-street, Leigh, was simi- larly summoned for a like amount. Mr. Shearer stated that this man was not so well off as the other, as he had a wife and four children to keep. He had paid some- thing towards the arrears and something towards the order. The case was withdrawn.—Asher Waterworth, Holt-street, Leigh, was likewise charged, and the Bench ordered him to contribute is. 6d. per week.—Napthali Waterworth, 76, Oxford-street, Leigh, was also on a similar order, ordered to pay is. 6d. per week.— William Mac Mullen, 99, Fox-street, was summoned for being .£2 Bs. in arrears towards the maintenance of his father in the Warrington Union. Mr. Shearer said an order was made for defendant to pay 2s. per week in December, 1908. He had been previously committed for arrears.—The case was adjourned for four weeks.— William Ellis, Heald-street, Earlestown, was ordered to pay 23. per week towards the maintenance of his daughter in the Workhouse and James Hensbaw, 76, Park-street, Haydock,was ordered to pay 7s. per week towards the maintenance of his wife.—Francis Molyneux, 97, Hindley-road,Daisy Hill,West Houghton; James Molyneux, Klondyke Cottages, West Houghton; and Charles Molyneux, Tideswell-street, Leigh, were all summoned for arrears of maintenance in respect of their father, who is chargeable to the Warring- ton Union. As only James Molyneux appeared, the Bench made an order on him for the payment of 2s. per week.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Charles White (in the chair)
and other magistrates.

THEFT OF HORSE HAlR.—Edward Burke, lodging- house, Barbanld-street, was charged with stealing a quantity of horsehair, valued 6s. 6d., frdm the yard of Messrs. G. and J. Weaver, upholsterers, Bridge-street. Edward and James Bolton, father and son, residing at 38, Hardy-street, were charged with receiving the same, knowing it to have been stolen.—The Chief Constable explained that on Monday morning a sack in the yard of the pr6secntors containing 501bs. of horse hair had been cut open and a quantity stolen. From enquiries made by the police it was found that a broker named Joseph Matthews had purchased ISlbs. of hair on Monday from the younger prisoner Bolton. The
'LINSEED COMPOUND' for Coughs, Colds and Bronchial troubles. sp., 1/I.—Advt. .

prisoner Burke • was subsequently arrested and he admitted having stolen the hair from the premises of Messrs. Weaver. He said he met Edward Bolton in the street and sold it to him. The police had recovered three sacks full of horse hair from Mr. Matthews,which had been sold to him by the prisoners Bolton.—A remand of seven days was ordered, bail being refused. THIMSDAY.—Before Messrs. C. White (chairman), W. Roberts, J. Rymer Young, W. T. Williams, J. Upson, and Dr. aden. _ _

_ To REDEEM HIS CHARACTER.—Thomas Bennett, of no settled abode, was again brought before the magis- trates on the charge of stealing a bicycle, value £2 10s., the property of James Nairns.—The Chief Constable said that on the sth of July, 1908, the prosecutor, Mr. Nairns. a joiner, residing in Aitkin-street, was walking along Museum-street with the bicycle when the prisoner came along. Nelms asked him to take the bicycle home, mistaking him for another man. He gave him threepence to do so, but prisoner absconded with it to Ashton. He then went to Pendlebury, and pledged the bicycle for 7s. 6d. The case was adjourned from last week in order that they could recover the bicycle, as the pawnbroker at Pendlebury had re-sold the machine. Since prisoner had stolen the bicycle, he had been in the Army, and had been discharged with a bad character.—Prisoner said it was all through drink, and if they would give him another chance he would turn over a new leaf and start again.—The Chairman said they would give him another chance, and advised him to leave drink alone.—Prisoner was sentenced to fourteen days. A PERFECT PEST.—WiMaIII Norbury of DO settled address was charged with obstructing a free passage in Winwiek-street, after being sake() to desist. Prisoner was summoned to appear before the Court on Tuesday,but he failed to do 'so and a warrant was issued for his arrest. The Chief Constable said prisoner was a perfect pest about the Central Station. fie was always there and practically lived there. Prisoner was fined ten shillings and costs or fourteen days. FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the: chair) and other

magistrates. ALLEGED 'MEAN THEFT.—Thomas Henry Huskisson, a stranger, was remanded for a week on the charge of stealing, between Wednesday and Thursday from the British Workman's Cocoa Rooms, liorsemarket-street, a suit of clothes and other articles valued at £1 17s. the property of Alfred Waring. The Chief Constable stated that prosecutor was employed as a salesman in the Market Place and lodged at the cocoa rooms. On Thursday morning about 6.40 prisoner went to prosecutor's bedroom and asked him to get up, as he wanted to go to bed. Prosecutor got up and prisoner afterwards slept in his bed. After his departure the clothes were missed. The police were informed and inquiries made by detectives Reddington and Clough, and prisoner was arrested. The police had also discovered that prisoner had been to the Rev. Thomas Miller's house and obtained a ticket for lodgings at the Cocoa Rooms when he had money in his possession. During the week it had also been ascertained that prisoner had been attempting to pledge a silver lever watch whic he said had been given to him by a man on the road. 1.1
Bold-street Wesleyan Band of Hope.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Wednesday evening when there was a good attendance. Several new members were enrolled owing to the earnest plea given by the Rev. F. Vaughan on Sunday afternoon when he addressed the scholars. Miss Marrow pre- sided and begged the children whenever they saw a drunken man or woman, not to jeer and mock them but to be kind and pitiful towards them. —Mr. Hamblett (secretary) reminded the boys and girls that the Band of Hope was to help forward the Kingdom of God, and they must take their part in this great work by becoming little missionaries and getting others to join. A dialogue "The Temperance Meet- ing" was very cleverly given by Misses Olive Meyer and Emily Ball. Miss Alice Nuvbe sang very sweetly "The Precious Bible," and Master Charlie Hamblett sang in his usual good style "How can He leave them." Miss Holt was the accompanist.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

As Sunday las-t was Temperance Sunda-y, a temperance service was held by this society. Mr. Himsworth pre- sided, and spoke of the advantages of being total abstainers in the various duties of life, and the confidence placed in men of character and men who were total abstainers. Mr. James Shaw gave an address upon " The best and safest side." He dealt with total abstinence from the practical and medical side of the question. We had in trying to convert the people, to contend with the prejudice and ignorance on the question, but when seriously considered from medical and practical sides, total abstinence stood to the front. The premiums on Insurance policies also proved the advantages of being on the side of temperance. Mr. C. Cotton read the lesson, and the Secretary led the prayer. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., presided at the organ. One member signed the temperance pledge, one new mernlier also received a hearty welcome into the brotherhood.

div.head: Rev. F. Vaughan and Socfal Regeneration.
div.p: The Rev. F. Vaughan and Socfal Regeneration.

The Rev. Frank Vaughan addressed the Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday school scholars on Sunday afternoon. He said alcohol was doing the most deadly harm, and it was a strange thing that animals who possessed no intelligence, but were guided by instinct, passed dangerous things over, In very many cases in this town and nation of ours, men and women who from their very nature and composition were the most majestic things God had made—or ever would make—lacked the power of selection. It seemed to him that since the use of alcohol was producing suck sorrow and misery, the work of the temperance cause was, perhaps, the first work of the Christian Church. He believed the problem would never be solved unless the Christian Church as a Church set itself to solve it. Continuing, he said that if boys and girls had no other object in life than the fact that they were proud of their nation they should be total abstainers as every mighty nation that the world had ever seen that had wielded universal power bad been destroyed by the ravages of luxury and strong drink. England had grown and was now in the front rank of the_pations for Christian enterprise and for commercial enterprise. Wm; she going to be destroyed by alcohol? If not they had no right to have anything to do with it because it had ruined the nations that preceded us. He could not as a Christian man get away from the fact that if it were true that God forbade His priests the use of strong drink it was only right that his people should not indulge in it unless they said that God made a mistake in the beginning, if only they could shut the public houses and hold in subjection tbe brewing and the distillery interests for five years they would have gone nine-tenths of the way to solving the social problem and they would have prepared for the millenium period. Concluding he maintained that it would be done by no political party, but it would be done by people having a personal Christ and in no other way. If only the Christian Church would be true to her profession and her creed and would love their neighbours as themselves, and make God their first love and their neighbours second the whole of the social problems would be solved. They wanted national regeneration,but they would never get it until they had individual consecration.

div.p: Bevisey-rOad Wesleyan Church.

Visit of Rev. J. Klngsiote Greenland. The anniversary in connection with Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church was celebrated last week end, when the Rev. J. Kingscote Greenland popularly known as "W. Scott King "the novelist preached on Sunday morningrand evening. He also lectured on Tuesday. In the morning he preached on" Home Life" to a good congregation. He said that the future of the Church depended absolutely on its children, just as the future of England did. From the Church to the Sun- day School we had looked upon our children as toys and until within the last 10 years we had only begun to take notice of them. At the present we had one of the worst educational systems in the world and the Church looked upon the care of the children as a side show. He was not a scare monger—he would have all scare mongers shot—be believed the makers of panics did it from ulterior motives—and yet if he here to be panic stricken it would be over the state of home life. We were witnessing not the disestablishment of the Church but the disestablishment of the English home. Never did parents have so little control over their children and every year the school was more. and more taking the place of the household. We had been told that the law of progress lay not as much in going forward but in going backward. The economist told us to go back to the land ; the pllysician told us to lead a simple life as we were suffering from the disease of civilisation. If they were going back the chief thing to go back to was to the home life. He did not know what their. views were with regard to the Church, but he would turn it into a home for the people. It seemed to him that when they had killed the last rag of ritual; when they had stripped the Church of Eastern ecclesiasticism ; when they had turned it from a place of worship into a place of work and love; an when they have turned from conventional services,they would have Christianised the Church. If they had got a majority; of fathers who were only business men and mothers who considered children were a nuisance, then it was practically unimportant what educational system we had got: there was no future for England nor did there deserve to be. He maintained that the people should revert to the old Punt snical home life and then the future of England would be assured. _

On the Tuesday evening Mr. Greenland lectured on "The reign of the young people." Dr. Ferguson presided over a good audience. The Chairman said Mr. Greenland as they were all aware, wrote those gowerful paragraphs to young children in the 'Methodist Recorder." He was the editor of a paper of his own called the "Young man" and wrote to a great number of other periodicals, and so was very well-known. (Applause.) During • his lecture,

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 20, 1909
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 20, 1909

Mr. Greenland said that in this country, a man's views on politics were called his manifesto, but in America they would be called his platform. It was a very good word because their political views were something we stood on and so was a platform. Now, platforms were made up of planks,-and his platform that he was going to speak on that night was composed of five planks, piety, study, friendship, recreation and service. With regard to the first plank, piety or goodness, the lecturer said tbat religion and bnsiness could not be put together. A man could not be an architect,a freetrader and a Christian. He could only hea Christian architect and a Christian free- trader.A man could not be a schoolmaster,tari IT reformer and a Christian. He could not be those three things, he could only be two, a Christian schoolmaster and a Chris- tian tariff reformer if there were such a thing.(Laughter), Referring to study, he said that there was no excuse nowadays for a youth or man to be condemned as an ill-read man, for the very best hook on history, auto- biography, religion and science, could now be secured for a guinea. The lecturer then gave an illustration of the predominance of cheap literature. He was in a train the other day going to Clardiff. In his compart- ment were two business men: he knew that because they were talking business. On reaching a cartain station the two men called for the newsboy in order to buy some light literature to while away the journey. The train jogged on and he began to wonder what they had bought. He happened to catch sight of one of the papers at last. One was recruiting his muddled mind on 4` Pick-me-up " and the other on "Ally Sloper." (Loud laughter.) Mr. Greenland emphasised the fact that good sound wholesome literature was wanted for the young men and women. With reference to recreation, the speaker said we had not enough athletes. Men were not athletics who watched twenty-two other men kick a ball about. It was like him employing an artist to paint a picture and then calling himself an artist. (Laughter). The lecturer, who is of rather slight build, next drew attention to the great importance of having a sound healthy body and said that he once wanted to insure himself but none of the companies would take him on. He went to one office and was examined by a doctor who was a Scotchman. On seeing his body the doctor gave vent to an exclamation something like "0 Lor'." (Laughter). The lecturer asked him what was the matter And he replied "why you have no body." Continuing he said the state of a man's body had a con- siderable lot to do with the state of his religion. Referring to friendliness he said that fellowship was sometimes only gained at the cost of drunkenness, and the drink traffic would never be stopped until a non- intoxicant substitute was obtained. (Applause.) In conclusion be addressed the young portion of the audience and said there was a great work for them to do, as in his opinion all the great battles which had been fought and won would have to be refought. On the proposition of the Rev. E. B. Keeling a vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer.

for you at once. Since Pamela is wiring to help, I'll gladly let you go. Still, dear, let me warn you. 'A girl without fortune,' is said to be 'a cart without wheels.' So don't be too ambitious • or too hopeful. A pretty face is not everything." Marion laughed. She was too radiantly happy to be annoyed. All she required, she told herself, was opportunity. The oppor- tunity would soon be hers now. So, in spite of her lack of fortune, her hopes ran very high. "They think more of beauty in London than in the country, mother:" she said, de- murely. "But I won't be too hopeful, I promise you." And she ran lightly from the room.

The roses were all in full bloom, and as every window of the little cottage was open morning, noon, and night every part of it was filled with •their delicious perfume. Marion had been gone a month, and as yet breathed not one word about coming home. Mrs. Lyle and Pamela rejoiced to know that she was enjoying herself, and were not in- clined to hasten her return. They were busy from early morn till dewy eve, and perfectly happy in each other's society. My little Pam is a winsome creature. But to be appreciated, must be seen at home. Her sweet nature, her brightness, and brave unselfishness would hardly be noticed in worldly society," Mrs. Lyle thought one day as she watched her youngest daughter flitting in and out amongst the flowers. But here— anywhere, indeed, with those she loves—she is—charming and—" Down the path from the cottage the little znaiZservant came, in breathless haste. "Please, ma'am," she stammered, red and hot with excitement, "there's a splendid motor at our gate, and a lady in a beautiful long coat, and a handsome young gentle- man, laughing and pleasant, have got out, and insisted on my shewing them into the drawing-room. They must, and will, see you and Miss Pamela. So—ah ! why, here they are. Well, now, this beats all,' she gasped. "Coming out by the window! They're the boldest visitors I ever saw."

"Certainly a cool pair." Mrs. Lyle looked annoyed, then advanced, in a frigid and stately manner„ towards the unknown, and wholly unexnected. intrudera. e al mud atp timop paitog 'schwa Jag apply ttAtoitp Sawn; - ‘otvin oto paw „‘unip -yaw .Aidtup—laams gt 9util `mou 'Ham marvellous confection of muslin and lace. "A charming and refreshing sight after the heat and turmoil of London. Via I guess, now, you haven't the most remote idea who I am?" "I confess there must be some mistake.

"See that ' now," the lady laughed. "I told Norman how it would be. This is my son" —waving her hand towards a tall, manly-look- ing young fellow, with grey eyes and a mass •short, thick, curly brown hair. "He and I are the befit of friends, and so I brought him along. Katherine, you haven't forgotten your old chum, Lenore Kesterton ? " "Lenore Kesterton ? " Mrs. Lyle caught her hand. "My dear, I am glad to see you. And you married and went to America?"
"Why, certainly I did—a dear, good generous man, Lucas Reid, who made me very happy. He is dead, alas! Just ten. years. And this "—proudly—" is my only son."

"I am glad, very glad to meet you again,. Lenore, and to know your son," Mrs. Lyle said, with emotion. "I thought you had for- gotten me." "Well, in the hurry of life over there school friends are apt to get left behind. But as soon as I came to Europe I ,said to Nor- man, 'l'll find Katherine Lyle.' I heard you had been married, you see, five years after I was."

"Yes, exactly. But how did you find me out, Lenore? I lead a hidden life here with my children." Till chance threw your eldest daughter, Marion, in our •way, at a ball last night, I hadn't an idea where you were. Norman danced with her, and told me who she was. She gave me your address, and we came off at once, to pay you a surprFse visit." "How very kind. As in the old days, Lenore "—smiling—" you don't let the grass grow under your feet." "Why, no. And a spin 'in a motor-car is just fine, after hot rooms and late supper. We do our hundred miles most days, Norman and I."

"How delightful! And now "—beckoning to Pamela, who came hurrying towards them, a basket of roses upon her arm—" I must in- troduce you to my second girl. Pamela this is Mrs. Reid, my old schoolfellow, Lenore, of whom I have spoken to you so often, and her son."

Pamela welcomed the visitors frankly and sweetly. "You have given mother the greatest pleasure," She said, looking from one to the other. "And now, of course, you will stay for lunch? We'll have it in the gar- den at the shady side of the house." " Delightful ! ' cried Mrs. Reid. "And Norman will help 'you to carry out the things. He's Al at that kind of busine&l."

Norman laughed, and Pamela blushed a little; but looking at him with her straight, frank glance, said, quietly:. "If it would not bore you, I'd be glad of your help. Our one small maid will be busy cooking." It would give .me immense pleasure to help you; if you will not find me in the way." Oh! not at all," she answered, smiling. "And see, we'll put these roses on the table, in honour of your mother's surprise visit." And she led the way into the cottage. , "What a dear, simple girl!" Mrs. Reid exclaimed, as the young people disappeared. "Such unconsciousness and freshness are un- usual nowadays." "Pamela is a dear," Mrs. Lyle replied, de- lighted. "But she is not as handsome as Marion."
"A different style; but very 'winsome and attractive. You should send her to London, Katherine. She _ should have her chance as well as Marion."

"She is young, and can wait a little. And then "—smiling—" the darling is happy here, and as'she is not pretty, declares she has no expectations." Mrs. Reid turned and looked at her old friend with surprised and inquiring eyes. "Oh, you're fishing for compliments, I see. Well "—gaily—" you shall have them. Pamela is pretty—fascinating. I say. Her bright complexion and unaffected manners are .very attractive, and from the way Nor- man looked at her I feel sure he thinks so too. He's hard to please, my boy. But I know he admires your Pamela. Not pretty indeed! I guess she's— But come along. I'd like to run round your estate." "That's easily done, Lenore," laughed Mrs. Lyle. "A cottage with an acre of gar- den—"
"My dear • soul!" Mrs. Reid gasped. "Well, the flowers are charming. Let's sit down here and wait till the lunch is ready. I guess I'm too tired to walk round in the sun. Here it is most refreshing."

morning. "• Alas! all too quickly: They will go back to America, and I'll never see Nor- man "—her colour rose and fell, tears filled her eyes—" or dear Mrs. Reid again. Oh! if only— But there's no use thinking of the impossible, but just enjoy things as they come. Ah! there's the toot-toot of the motor. Now for a glorious day, and not one thought of the coming by-and-bye." Things went on delightfully till towards the end of July. Marion came back from town— Marion in trailing, fashionable gowns, her hair exquisitely dressed, her complexion soft and fair, her manners fascinating and charm- ing. She had enjoyed her season immensely, and although disappointed that it had not had the happy ending she expected, was greatly cheered by, the constant visits of handsome Norman and his lively mother. Life at the Cottage had, indeed, changed, and the change raised her spirits, and put her into the best of good humour. As she moved round the house, or walked in the garden, there was an air of distinction and savoir faire about her that, whilst it filled Pamela with admira- tion, struck her with sudden dismay. Beside her elegant sister she felt countrified and dowdy, and her heart sank low, as she watched Norman chatting pleasantly with beautiful Marion, discussing amusing inci- dents of the season, and talking over people of whom she knew nothing. "I Might have guessed how things would be," she thought sadly. And I must not be jealous. He was kind, that was all. And" —het' eyes filling up with tears—" I will be glad, and 60 will mother, to see Marion happy. So I'll keep out of the way—be busier than ever "—a sob choked her— and then I shan't see—or—feel—it all so much."

Thus, soon after Marion's return, the Reids saw very little of Pamela. She was always at Herne Bay or Canterbury with her flowers and eggs, or down in the village order- ing things that had been forgotten in some unaccountable way. "She's avoiding me," Norman told him- self impatiently one afternoon, greatly an- noyed by her absence, "that's quite plain. Does she dislike me, and mean to shew me what she feels? And yet, after all our happy walks and talks she cannot surely do that. Have I unwittingly offended her, I wonder? Oh! Pamela. somehow—somewhere—l must ana will speak to you to-uay. Of that I am determined.

He lit a cigar and sat 'down in a basket- chair, so placed that he could see both the front and side gates. No one could go in or out of the garden without his being aware of the fact. His mother's fine motor-car stood at the hall door, and presently the three ladies emerged from the cottage fully equipped for a long drive. "That's right, Norman, I'm glad to see you ready," Mrs. Reid exclaimed. "You'll drive, of course? So Green (her smart chauffeur) need not come. Four is a pleasant number for the car. Jump in and take the front seat, Marion; the old ladies must go behind."

Norman rose up and, taking the cigar from between his lips, said, quietly: - "I'm not on for driving 10-day, mother. "I've got a bit of a head." • "Poor boy! Well, I guess that's not agree- able," she answered, a soft twinkle in her eyes. "And the sun is hot. Would you like one—or two—of us to keep you company in the shade?"

"No, no, don't think of such a thing," he said, hurriedly. "I'll be all right alone. And, then, you'll get back to tea? "Why, certainly. Pity "—with a mis- chievous glance-,--" Pamela has so much busi- ness of late. However, ta-ta ; a restful time will do you good. Now, Marion, come along." And, smiling, Mrs. Reid stepped into the car, making the beautiful, but wrathful-loolting Miss Lyle now take the back seat beside her. "Your mother will enjoy driving in front, my dear, and I," she remarked, quietly, "will be glad of a little talk with you." Marion murmured something quite unintel- ligible, and there was a shadow on her fair face as the car glided away down the road. Half-an-hour later the side-gate opened, and Pamela, pale and weary-looking, went slowly across the lawn to the Cottage. In a moment Norman was beside her. "At last! " he cried, trying to meet her eyes. "Pamela, why are you so unkind?" The girl started and crimsoned to her hair. " Unkind? " She laughed nervously. "Oh ! I'm not unkind, only busy. 'You see '—keep- ing her head turned well away—" I have lost a great deal of time lately. And now that Marion is back to entertain you and Mrs. Reid, I—l—must look after things—a little." "Quite right. But you might allow me to help you as I used to do." Pamela's lips trembled. " Ma:Zan said I Tel. No. 123.

"You must cultivate contentment, Marion, and make yourself happy at home.o, . Marion pouted, and her dark brows met to- ether in a frown. "When you were young, mother, you, had -fun and amusement. You went out, and danced and enjoyed yourself. Why, only for that time in London with the Drews, you'd never have met father—might have died an old maid. Think of it! And' —moving restlessly towards the fireplace, and gazing at her own handsome face in the look- ing-glass—" that will assuredly be my fate, if I go on wasting my sweetness on the desert air of Wendover Cottage. Besides, love and marriac-e apart, I'm bored—really bored to death!?

Mrs. Lyle glanced at her tall, slim young daughter, and thought how lovely was her colouring, how beautiful her features. "She'd look well in a ballroom, if properly dressed," she told herself, "and this invita- tion is tempting, very. But, alas! the -dress is the difficulty. At present-" "When will you come again my faithfu' Johnnie?" " Whea the corn is gathered, And the leaves are wi,thered, I will come again, my Sweet and bonnie." sang a blythe, fresh voice in the hall. Mrs. Lyle smiled, and her eyes grew bright. . _

Marion- frowned, and shrugged her shoul- ders, saying- sharply: "I wish Pamela wouldn't sing such silly songs. In this place —so dull and lonely—her Johnnie will never come, and, therefore, cannot come back." The door opened, a merry face, round and rosy, peeped in, and Pamela Lyle, aged seventeen, wearing a short Serge skirt, straw hat, and a pair of strong, low4meled shoes, cried, gaily: "What solemnity, Marion! Mother, what can be the matter?"
"Marion has had an invitation—in fact, you have both been invited to London for the season by Mrs. Jameson."

Pamela drew a deep breath, and her eyes danced. ." How perfectly lovely!" she gasped. "I'd see the National Gallery, and the Tower, and-" "Yes, dear. But you must know, understand, darling, that at present I could not afford to get all the things you would require for such a visit."

"For two—no,., of course not." Pamela's ,heart sank, and she looked away. But in a moment she was smiling again, her arm round her mother's shoulder. "Let us send Marion. I have a few pounds saved. My hens have laid well this spring, and I've sold quite a lot of flowers."

"But, darling, you are the one who should go. Marion never makes or saves one penny." "She hasn't the way, poor dear, and " with a sly little glance at her handsome sister —" is a wee bit too anxious about her com- plexion and her hands." "I certainly wear gloves and carry a sun- shade,— Marion said, snappishly, "honing to be fit to be seen, in case anyone worth while did turn up. You are an object, Pam, sun- burnt, and—" _ _

" To' be sure I am, and quite unfit for civi- lised society. Mrs. David says I am a real country mouse, born to blush unseen, on ac- count "—laughing--" of my all too rosy coun- tenance. She also declares that you ought to have a London season, that--"
"But you would enjoy it too, Pam," Mrs, Lyle cried, kissing the girl's soft cheek. "And 6ince you have money-" ,

"Which shall be Marion's. So pray lel that be settled, mother mine. I have no ex- pectations.; she has many. I am happy at home with my chickens and my flowers. She is not. So we'll Work hard, make her a nice little trousseau, say Blpss you, my child,' and send her off. And, who knows, she may marry—a duke."

Marion flushed, and her eves sparkled. "Don't talk nonsense. Pam," she cried. "I am not quite as ambitious as that. But you're an angel, all the same. If I do have a good time with —blushing to her hair—" a happy ending, I shan't forget my small sister." "The country bumpkin," laughed Pam. "How sweet of you. But I've made up my mind to be an old maid. Mother won't mind, and the country is, far in a way, the best place for me. So, whilst thanking you " with a low curtsey—" for your amiable and sisterly intentions, I pray you not to trouble about _me and my future."
"I'll never forget your generosity, Pam, you may be sure," Marion said, in a low voice. "And you cannot imagine what this visit to London means to me."

"Oh yes I can, well," Pam answered, quickly. "But now I'm off. I've a lot of things to do." And she hurried away, singing the last verse of what Marion was pleased to call her silly song: "And shall we part again, my faithfu' Johnnie?" "So lang's my e'e can see, Jean, That face so dear to me, Jean, We shall not part again, my sweet and bonnie." Mrs. Lyle's eyes grew soft and. tender. "Dear unselfish little Pam! What a sweet nature she has."
"She has. But it would be waste of money, to take her to town."
- - "There are many things she would enjoy, Marion."
"Oh, of course. But, Mill, it's a good thing she's happy at home. Pam is not beau- tiful, mother."

"Strictly Apeaking, no. But there's some- thing very winning and charming about her." "She always was your favourite." Marion's head went up. "It's a good thing she's not likely to leaye you. And she's--=-" "When do you think of going to Mrs. Jameson, Marion?" _
"Her ball is on the 10th. I'd .like to get there the day before." "Very we)). Wart...i4srib.-..- sit. w ttAw dr,p wee

Having once made their wtly to Wendover Cottage, Mrs. Reid and her son were not slow in returning. Indeed, as the season pro- gressed, they found the country roads, with 'their green bodges run over with wild roses, the little house and shady garden, more at- tractive than the dusty streets, crowded parks, and drawing-rooms in London, and scarcely a week passed withput their motor- ing down, sometimes once, sometimes twice or three times, to enjoy a cup of tea, or an al fresco lunch with kind Mrs. Lyle and her charming young daughter. At first Mrs. Reid had pressed Pamela to pay her a visit in London, promising to give her a real good time, and shew her round everywhere. But the invitation had been gently but firmly declined. Till Marion re- turned she would not leave her mother. When that happened the season would be at an.end. Admiring the girl's unselfish affection Mrs. Reid ceased •to Surge her, told her she was right, and set to work to make life at Wend- over Cottage as lively and happy as possible.

For Pamela, this summer was a time of un- alloyed bliss. Long runs in the motor; pic- nics in shady lanes; merry tea-parties in hayfields; or, later, amongst the stacks of newly-cut corn, appeared to her the most de- lightful entertainments in the world, and she told herself over and over again that never in her life had she been so happy. that is— But, oh! 1 know—M. 'it was wrong to keep you running round carrying food for the chickens and things-60-----" "You went off by yourself, and left me to kick my heels about doing nothing? It wasn't kind, Pamela." _

She flushed, but made no reply. She did not dare to look up or speak. She dreaded meeting his glance, lest he should read her heart through her eyes. ." However," he smiled, "I forgive you, on one condition. and that is that you will come to-morrow with mother and me to inspect a house an 4 place that we have bought close by." "Take Marion," Pamela stammered. "She knows more." "But I don't care what Marion knows or thinks," he cried, vehemently. "And I shall not ask her opinion of my house. I want to know whether you like it or not, because if you don't VII have nothing to do with it. The deeds aren't signed; we can get out of it."
Pamela forgot her desire to conceal her feelings, and raising her head gazed at him in .open-eyed astonishment. _

"Norman, it can't matter much what / think of your house?" "But it does—that is, if "—catching her hand and pressing it tightly within his own— "it was to be my home and yours some day. If— Oh! Pamela, we have known each other for two months. We have talked for hours, told each other everything. You know me inside and out. I know you "—his voica dropped to a low whisper, his eyes shone—. " and love you with all my soul.' " Norman ! " she gasped: "Oh, Norman!" 1" Sweetheart—darling—you— But tell. me, could you love me—be my wife? "

"Poor plain little me?" A wave of crial- son swept over her sweet face, and she turned away with a deep sob, though her heart was quivering with joy and happiness: "Norman, I am not fit, not—" He drew her towards him and looked down at her with adoring eyes. "My darling, to me you are lovely! The sweetest, truest, best—for I love you. Pamela tell me, can you love me—be mine for ever?"
"Yes," she whispered, raising her happy, radiant face to 'his, "I .do love you, Norman, and will gladly—oh! so gladly—be your wife."

RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT FRODSHANT. RUNCORN MAN GETS A FOOT CUT OFF.

A Runcorn man was the victim of a sad accident at Frodsham Railway station on Saturday evening at six o'clock. William Davies, a labourer, of 34, Egerton- street, Runcorn, was found on the permanent way near the level crossing with one of his feet cut off. First aid was promptly rendered and the unfortunate failosr was conveyed to the Chester Infirmary by the next train. He could give no explanatinn at the time of the way the accident happened.

The Germans, it appears, have lcst no time in appropriating Mr. Louis Brennan's wonderful invention of a self- balancing single-rail tar fitted with gyroscopes. A working model of Mr. Brennan's invention was shown two years ago in London, and the idea seems to have been promptly adopted in Germany, for on the same day as 14r. Brennan's tests in ent last week a German mono-rail was tested in Berlin. The Germans claim that their .train, of which we give a photograph, is an improvement on the Brennan invention, which, by the way, it is claimed will carry passengers with greater safety and more comfort than now at the rate of from 150 to 200 miles an hour. - -
