div.head: WARRINGTON CHAPTERS. ) GLIMPSES OF BY-GONE STOCKTON
div.p: WARRINGTON CHAPTERS. ) GLIMPSES OF BY-GONE STOCKTON
HEATH.
Village Amusements.

It is a pity that Southey did not chance to land at Stockton Quay upon the occasion of the. annual 'Wakes, for had he done so he would have found a fine subject for his descriptive powers. Remembering the monotony of village life we will judge with tender judgment the methods by which our ancestors stirred themselves to an annual excitement. And if bear lAiting does depress us as a demoralis- ing and cruel thing we will not forget that it amused no less enlightened an audience than the Court of Queen Elizabeth. Time and tempers have changed; let us not judge harshly. The outstanding event of the Stockton Heath Wakes was the horse racing. We do not suggest that the event was of the nature of a Derby or an Ascot bu Citlwas the local Derby day, and the villagers arose that morning with every symptom of an excitement which afterwards rose to a great altitude while they surrounded the race course, and became a frenzy under the flow of Mulberry Tree ale and' the shouts of the bull ring.

div.head: BEAR BAIT.
div.p: THE BEAR BAIT.
After the classic entertainment of the horse race the real fun began. The evening before several unusual visitors had sought accom- modation at the Inn. Bears with unuSually

ragged skins in the care of men no less attractive, and a bull with curiously embellished horns had been quartered in the stable. They wait patiently until the racing is over and then the fun comes fast and furious.

The bear is chained to a strong post in front of the Mulbury Tree. A big leather muzzle adorns his head which keeps him from biting, and as a secondary object saves his own head from the teeth of the dogs. As an additional protection his hind quarters are wrapped in strong sacking, and thus armed he waits the attack.

The natives are proud of their dogs and bring them forward to bait the bear. One at a time they come forward,their owners pay- ing a fee of two pence to allow them to try their teeth on bruin. Sometimes the dog is larger and stronger than the bear and may score the great triumph of overthrowing him. If so there are shrieks of delight from the crowd and the owner demands the return his twopence. But that is a rare occurence. Bruin is a born wrestler and stands poised on his hind legs awaiting attack. Encumbered by his chain and sacking he is often torn by the lithesome dogs but now and again the attacker is trapped between his forelegs and a sound of cracking ribs brings a groan from the onlookers. A _FAMOUS BRUIN.

The bears seldom suffered anything worse than a rough fall and the loss of a mouthful of fur, and they appear to have taken their calling very philosophically. One well- known bear -called ** Old Nell" regularly made the round of the Wakes in Cheshire and Lancashire and came to Stockton Heath no fewer than fifteen years in succession. When she had finished her days work and was released from the stake she would quietly trot off, oblivious of the snarls of her late tormentors, and curl herself up in the stable of the Inn. Her business in life was to be tormented and having done the days work went for a well-earned rest. Outside business hours nothing would draw Nell into a quarrel.

div.head: CHESTER CIVIC BEAR BAIT.
div.p: THE CHESTER CIVIC BEAR BAIT.

Such was bear baiting, and nowhere did it hold the people more firmly than in Cheshire. In the county town of Chester the annual bear and bull bait was attended by the Mayor and Corporation who wore their civic robes while assembled round the City Cross. It was on this occasion that the City Crier gave the solemn warning" Oyez! Oyez! If any man stand within twenty yards of the bull ring let him take—what comes." The Liverpool Corporation, too, had its official bull bait which was held on the occa- sion of the 'election of Mayor. The Chief Magistrate attended in his civic regalia and was accompanied by the members of the Council, whilst his sturdy halbert men kept the ring. How long this continued does not appear from the records but it was certainly a recognised institution as late as 1782.
The baiting was abolished in the City of Chester in 1803; but it continued in Stockton Heath for quite thirty year.s longer.
THE BULL BAIT.

In the bull bait the bull was chained to the stake and the dogs were set to the attack. To prevent the too-speedy 'extinction of the dogs the horns of the bulls were covered with lead. These, while they prevented goring, did not prevent him from tossing the dogs high into the air, or from killing them at a stroke. Again twopence was paid for the privilege of entering a dog, and when the animal had been tossed high into the air, the owner,at the risk of his own skin,would often run in to catch his falling darling. Bull baiting was also,it may be mentioned, a customary part of the harvest-home cele- bration as observed by the estate owner or squire. His best bull took its stand against the tenant's dogs and made merriment which lasted by the hour. The following little

picture is from the diary of Nicholas Blundell a local squire of nearly two centuries ago, "I baited a large bull in ye bottom of my new marl pit, he was never baited before as I know of, yet played to admiration, there was 8 or 9 doggs played ye Ist bait and onely two ye 3rd bait, I think there was not above 2 doggs but was very ill hurt, I gave a colkr to be played for but no dogg could get it fairly, so I gave it to R, Spencer being his dogg best deserved it." It is difficult to picture a Mayor and Corporation gathering round a bull ring to take their official amusement, but when we blush for them we must remember that future readers will also blush when some gossiping antiquarian tells them how in the Twentieth Ceatury the educated and govern- ing aristocracy kept hounds all the year round that they might bait foxes in the winter and watch nimble Reynard torn to pieces. . _

And when they have read with a tingle of shame of :the brutalities of badger hunting —the .fine sport of Cheshire gentlemen—they may make instructive companions between the tastes of the common people and of their cultured betters.

div.head: TRAVELLING CURIOSITIES.
div.p: THE TRAVELLING CURIOSITIES.

The Annual Wakes brought also its annual crop of travelling freaks and curiosities. A manuscript of 1712 describes the attendants at a Fair on the other side of the river and we imagine that the descrip- tion would apply to most other such occasions of the period seeing that the objects were taken from place to place. There were of course the big man and the Tom Thumb, but in this case the miniature creature was a woman, "little Catherin a Hanoverian, she was near one yard and inch high as Could be." Another professional curiosity was Mathew Buckinger who was born without hands or feet. Says

the Chronicler "I saw him write very well with his stumps, and tipe very dexterously some nine pins down, and play tricks of Leger-de-Mene." And again "a child which, was born in Garston without legs or arms.'

The -list includes a tiger and a civet cat, and, most rare of all at that period, an elephant. The love of the marvellous was catered for by "a man who eat fier and had a piece of mill stone greet about four inches thick broke upon his breast with a hammer." The blue horse and performing ape made attractive side shows and though the departure of the shows left a sad and unwelcome blank the Wakes at least gave material for village conversation that lasted many a day. A.M.

div.head: fIscELI4r4NY.
div.p: fIscELI4r4NY.

A few weeks ago we gave a reprcoduction of Millet's striking but little-known picture "The Man with the Hoe." This painting travelled to San Francisco, and at the period of the grpat fire was reported to have been destroyed. It would be interesting if some reader could tell us whether this report was correct, and as our paper travels to that far latitude we insert this enquiry in the hope that it may bring imformation as to the fate of he canvas.

To commend early rising in keen November weather may seem a sure method of losing popularity and we only venture to suggest it with diffidence. Those however with courage to leave their bed at the chilly hour of 3 a.m, may enjoy the rare privilege of see- ing in one day all the five planets known to the ancients, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Mercury: and Saturn. Jupiter is the earliest riser and at about 3.30 may be found without difficulty in the 'southern sky. At about 6 o'clock on the lower south-eastern sky Mercury rises, a twinkling yellow light, the rarest seen among the planets.

The remaining three are easily found after sunset. As the sun goes down Venus shines brilliant in the south eastern sky. Mars rises in the south west and travels south to south east, and though not so brilliant as a few weeks ago still shines glarightly with her red light. Saturn follows later in the wake of Mars, and may be easily identified in the southern sky. . . . .

Our references on this page to Stockton Heath have brought us many expressions of interest and have stirred up memories of the days of water travel in the minds of the older inhabitants. We have materials at hand for several other sketches based upon the dis- trict and its inhabitants,—for Stockton Heath and Hill Cliffe have been peculiarly rich in history and character—which will appear in due course, and the making of the famous Bridgwater Canal must yet engage our attention. It is a source of peculiar pleasure to know that our glimpses of the past are being so widely read and appreciated.

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, M.P.
THE LABOUR CAMPAIGN.

In view of the probability of an. early General Election it may be interesting to give one's impression of the outlook for the Labour candidates. Before a General Election became imminent the Executive of the Labour Party had arranged for a series of meetings to cover the constituences which are to be contested by Labour candidates at the election. The Labour M.P.'s were made up into pairs, and each pair were given a week's meetings to address. This campaign has been almost concluded, and it has been successful beyond all expectations. The meetings have been crowded and enthusiastic, and a spirit of hopefulness per- vades the movement. On the tour which was allotted to my colleague and myself we visited Bradford, Clithero, Glasgow, Dundee, and Newcastle. In each of these places, there is a sitting Labour member, and if the character of the meetings is any indication of the opinion in the constitutency the pre- sent Labour M.P. -will certainly be returned. I was pleased to find that the state of the organisation in the constituencies has been very much improved, and this will have its effect on the poll.

div.head: THREE CORNERED CONTESTS.
div.p: THREE CORNERED CONTESTS.

In some of the constituencies now held by Labour members, the Liberals are moving to obtain candidates to oppose them. This, of course, is a matter about which the Labour Party cannot complain. The Labour Party have never considered the convenience of the Liberals when they thought fit to put forward a candidate for a seat held by the Liberals. If the Liberals are dissatisfied with a sitting Labour member they ought to oppose him; but they ought to be prepared to give their reasons for such an action, and to • reconcile it with their professions of sym- pathy with Labour representation,

div.head: ADVANCE GUARD.
div.p: THE ADVANCE GUARD.

There is a justification for the Labour Party attacking the seat of a sitting member which the Liberals cannot put for- ward for opposing a Labour member. The Labour Party stand for much more than the Liberals profess, and if they are ever to get the Parliamentary representation they think they are entitled to, they will have to dis- place either Liberals or Tories. But on the other hand, the Liberals profess to regard the Labour Party as just the advance guard of the Progressive forces; and the Liberals cannot therefore complain that they are misrepresented by a Labour member. When a Liberal Government is in office, the Labour Party gives a general support to the measures brought forward; and when the Labour Party opposes or criticises it is to make the measures more advanced. THE WHIG SECTION.

I can quite understand that the Whig section of the Liberal Party do not approve of the Labour members. They are far too revolutionary for them. And the Liberal opposition to the sitting Labour members is coming from that section of the Liberal Party. The possibilies of letting in the Tory has no terrors to these men. But the Liberals who are genuine reformers, who are enthusi- astic for the Budget, who want the House of Lords dealt with, who would be prepared to go farther than anything this Government has yet proposed, incur a serious responsi- bility when they join the reactionary Whigs in opposition to a Labour member.

div.head: ELECTION ISSUES.
div.p: THE ELECTION ISSUES.

I am interested in these matters from the point of view of the Labour Party, but also from that of the issues upon which the next election is going to be fought. The Liberals will need every vote they can get if they are to return with a working majority. If the election is going to be fought on the House of Lords question it is absolutely vital to the future of reform that a decisive majority against that institution must be returned. Any increase in the Tory strength will be taken as a confirmation of the position of the Peers, and that House will be more arrogant than ever in consequence. The Liberals are unwise, in their own interests, in seeking to divide the forces which are in agreement on the great issue of the fight. If the reason for the Liberal attack on Labour seats is retaliation for Labour attacks on Liberal seats,it may be said in-reply that the Liberals are in a position quite different. from that of the Labour Party. The Liberals are great and powerful, and they can spare a mag- nanimity the Labour Party cannot afford.

div.head: AN UNCERTAIN OUTCOME.
div.p: AN UNCERTAIN OUTCOME.

But it by no means follows that the inter- vention of a Liberal candidate in a con- stituency now held by a Labour member will be to the disadvantage of the Labour member. On the contrary, in more than one constituency where that is threatened the Labour Party welcomes the action of the Liberals, because it makes the Labour candidate's 2,hances more certain. In some of these constituencies the relations between th two parties are so strained that many Liberals would not in any case sup port a Labour candidate. Their dislike of the Labour Party is stronger than their desire to abolish the veto of the House of Lords. It is unfortunate that political controversy should develop these antipathies, but it is the regrettable fact.

div.head: REGRETTABLE POSSIBILITY.
div.p: A REGRETTABLE POSSIBILITY.

I see that a leading Unionist journal is assuming that their party will gain thirty seats at the election as the result of three- cornered contests. This cannot possibly be the case, for there will not be so many con- tests of that description unless more than are at present fixed should be undertaken. In view of the supreme importance of the _issues of this election, it will be a calamity for the House of Lords and Tariff Reform to obtain votes in the House of Commons on a minor- ity vote in the constituencies. But this is a situation which has been foreseen for years, and something ought to have been done ere now to make such a thing impossible. The Labour Party has come to stay, and it will ,grow in numbers and in influence, and at every succeeding General Election it will put forward more candidates than at the preceding one.

div.head: FOREIGNER'S WAY.
div.p: THE FOREIGNER'S WAY.

The multiplication of political parties is a a feature following the conferring of a democratic franchise in every country, and unless minorities are to gain an undue pro- portion of representation some system must be devised to prevent it. In Germany, they the Second Ballot; in Belgium, Pro- portional Representation ; and France is agitated just now about adopting the latter system of voting. The Government has had no opportunity of dealing with electoral reform in a comprehensive way, so that if an election comes now the best will have to be made of the absurd system we have.

The recent elections in Saxony and Baden, in which the Socialists have won such phenomenal successes, show the advantage of having some system by which a voter can dispose of his vote freely without fear of the seat going to a candidate representing a minority of the electorate. These German elections have been fought mainly on one issue: that of taxation; and the overwhelm- ing victories of the Socialists are rather victories for Free trade and direct taxation than for a theoretic Socialism. Electors who are not Socialists have in these elections supported the Socialists because they are a party who are sound on the taxation question.

div.head: IN THIS COUNTRY.
div.p: IN THIS COUNTRY.

-Tho same thing would happen in this country if there was anything like the Second Ballet in force. , A vast number of British electors do not now vote for a Labour candi- date, though they are in sympathy with his views without sharing them altogether, because they are afraid their votes will be wasted, or they may help to "let in the other man." This fear operates largely where the Labour candidate is for the first time attack- ing a seat, or where a former vote seems to indicate that he has not much chance of success. Where the Labour Party hold the seat it is different, and it is the Liberal who will suffer from being the "outsider."

div.head: VOTING ON PRINCIPLE.
div.p: VOTING ON PRINCIPLE.

If the General Election, about which every- body is now talking, comes on the Budget and the House of Lords it will be an election in which, more than at any election of this gegeration votes should be given on the issue before the country, apart from per- sonal prejudices or dislikes. If that be the idea which will influence the voters, then the Labour party has nothing to fear. The Party will retain its present members, and it will add to their number ; and there is no social reformer, whatever he may call him- self, who can regard the increase of Labour representation with feelings other than of satisfaction.

div.head: REV. H. DUNNICO'S SERMON TO THE " TRADE!'
div.p: REV. H. DUNNICO'S SERMON TO THE " TRADE!'
The Public-house a Social Necessity.

The Ittsv. Herbert Minnie.), of Kensington Baptist Chapel, Liverpool, and formerly of Warrington, held a apecial service for liccnsecs and barmen on Sunday afternoon. There was a large congregation, which included many of the class who were specially invited there.

Mr. Minnie() toek for his text I, Corinthians x., 31. : " Whether, therefore, ye rat or drink, or whatso- ever ye do, do all to the glory of God:* The preacher wished, at the very outset, on behalf of himself and the ollicen, to extend to them a cordial welcome to a church which was wide in its outlook and broad in its sympathies. It was cne of the few churches in that city in which men were selected to hold office who differed in their theological views. That church bad invited his hearers there not in the interest of any sect or political party, but in the name of their common humanity. With regard to the trade in which they were engaged, thousands had been spent by the brewers in defend;ng it, and by the teetotalers in attacking it. He thoudit the truth- lay ntidway between the two extremes. Ile was one of those who believed that, after all was said and done, whatever might take place in the future, so far as the present is concerned_ the public-house was a social necessity. That there are many evils attached to the drink trade they were all aware. The mistake was in assuming thatsother people were not as anxious as they were to see some reform in it. I the public-house efts a social necessity, and it was abolished, what were they going to put in its place? The Church could not meet that social necessity. The public-house was the most democratic institution in the country, and how were they to reform it without the aid of those conducting it? Let their trade be what it may, they were in the trade, and were meeting a social need. The Church had no right to treat them as social outcasts. In all their efforts to better their conditions of life the Church was on their side, and if necessary, would come to their assistance.

div.head: NAPOLEON'S GREAT FEAT.
div.p: NAPOLEON'S GREAT FEAT.
A Romantic Discovery in the Alps.

When Napoleon found the mountainous Alps barring his way into Italy, he summoned all his courage and skill and made his engineers carve a road practically out of the rock for his troops to march along. It was a splendid engineering feat, and proof of the general's resourcefulness, ability, and tenacity of purpose. Within reach of Napoleon at that time there lay another secret which, solved since by science, has meant untold benefit to millions of people, and saved the lives of an even greater army than Napoleon sacrificed on his historic march. The pine-clad slopes of the Alps have for centuries been noted for their peculiar health-giving and balmy air. The unfailing robustness of the Swiss shepherds in those regions proved beyond all doubt that the atmosphere of the pine forest is permeated with healing and soothing aromatic vapours, which have a marvellous curative action in all diseases of the chest and lungs. The problem presented to scientists was how to collect those life-giving essences and use them for the benefit of our throat, chest, and lung troubles. With Napoleonic determination, scientists started on this new conquest of the Alps. The campaign was long and costly. For years the Alps baffled all attempts to penetrate the health giving mysteries of their pine-clad slopes. At last, however, advance was made along new lines of investigation which led up to the discovery of a novel method by which the lung-healing vapours of the pine forests could be con- cettrated in handy tablet form, now known by the name of Peps, the great breathe-able remedy. Here we now have the triumph of a new principle in medicine—a principle that is safe, rational, and common-sense, and one that leaves behind the old-: fashioned cough mixtures, lozengers,and oily emulsions, many of the former laden with: dangerous opium and morphia in one form or another. As a Peps tablet dissolves in the mouth, certain medicinal fumes are given off, and these fumes are carried with every indrdwn breath into the. throat, chest, and lungs. Thus sufferers from bronchial trouble enjoy almost the identical benefits the famed pine woods confer. It is impcssible to over-estimate the importance of such a discovery, for the effect of these wonderful tablets is two-fold. First, Peps completely allay the irritation and tickling, i.e., the sub-acute inflammation of the delicate memblane which lines the air-pipes and lungs; and secondly, they destroy the germs lodging in tissues out of the reach of liquid medicine. By this system of applying a medicine straight to the seat of the lung trouble, a real cure is obtained; that tickling phlegm is loosened and easily coughed up; the breathing tubes are cleared and healed, disease germs are destroyed' ; bronchitis, however old or neglected, is quietly but surely got rid of ; and the lungs and chest are afforded valuable protection against pleurisy, pneumonia, and inflammation in these damp and changeable days. Peps bring "A Pine Forest in Every Home" when one cannot think of going off to the famous Alps directly that old winter cough returns, or that half-forgotten chest weakness once again asserts its grim reality,
CHESEIIRE EDUC#TION SCHOLARSHIPS SCHEME.

At a meeting of the Cheshire County Education Com- mittee, at Crewe, on Monday, the Higher Education Committee submitted a scholarship scheme for the county. The Examining Soard submitted the offer of forty junior scholarships, tenable at a secondary school for boys and girls, but this was referred back for further consideration. The committee, however, agree to offer intermediate scholarships, not exceeding twenty-five, to boys and girls between fifteen and six- teen years of age, and who are or have been in attend- ance at a secondary school for at least three years, to enable them to continue at a secondary school for a further period of one or two years; bursaries for intending teachers; four technological scholarships. and nine University scholarships; also a special Agri- cultural Usiversity scholarship,to be held at Manchester University and the Agricultural College,Holmes Chapel, for a University degree ; an so t scholarship, tenable at the Royal School of Art, South Kensington; a scholar- ship in music; special scholarship in domestic science for women, six scholarships in agriculture and horti- culture, and three sets of dairy scholarships for females, tenable at the Cheshire Dairy Institute, Worleston. It was also decided to offer twenty scholarships to evening students, tenable at Liverpool, Manchester, or other centres, to enable students to take up advanced instruc- tion in technological or science subjectc,

div.head: OUR SERIAL STORY.
div.p: OUR SERIAL STORY.
['ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.I

ping every now and then to listen, as though for the sound of that pursuit he had heard through the long night. And alvt aye the woman watched him, with curious, fascinated eyes fixed upon his face. Presently he made sian to the other men to leave them to. ;ether, and Voles and his fellow slunk away. Then she turned to the man and spoke quite calmly and quite ruthlessly. . .

_ "Silo's deadr- she said. He looked up at her with a frightened ex- pression in his eyes; looked all round about him; shivered once, and then nodded.. She drew a deep breath, and began to pace up and clown the room, stopping every now and then as though on the point of making some remark, and then resuming her restless walk. Finally, she stopped before him again, watch- ing in that fascinated way his hand that was playing with a knife upon the table. How did it happen?" He looked up at her, almost whimpering. "Don't look at me like that'!" he exclaimed, like a petulant child. "I. know what it means, and I know what I've done; you needn't ma.ke it out worse than it is. She was in the way. She meant to give the whole show away and ruin us all. There was no other way to stop her tongue." "I suppose you understand that they'll look for you first of all?" said the woman. "Unfortunately, you've a long record—and a bad one; unfortunately, too, you've been seen with the girl, and she has talked about you. You've put. your neck in a noose this taxi:.

unless - " "Unless what?" he demanded, as elle stopped "Never -mind; it was only a thought that occurred to me," she replied. "Tell nle, when it happened, and where you left her. Tell me everything." Slowly, and with much hesitation, he told her what had happened—excusing himself now and accusing the dead; sometimes break- ing down, and pleading with her to help him —to stand betwoen him and 0.1 law be had outraged. She listeeed in a grim silence. Only onee or twice she beat her hands to- gether softly, without looking at him, and with the air of one beating out some problem in her mind. When ,at last. she spoke it was apparent which way her ideas tended. "It is necessary, first of all, to know what has happened since you left her there," she said. Have you the courage to go back— to see for yourself?" "And fall into some trap?" he demanded, quickly. "Not likely. The further I can keep away from that place, the better for me." " Then 'someone else must go," she debated to herself. "We're fighting in the dark, un- less we know exactly whether you are sus- pected, or whether, • in fact, the body has yet been found. I suppose you haven't thought of the other possibility, have you?" "What other possibility?" lie asked. "Jahn Baxendale," she whispered— Baxendale, in whose very grounds almost tilt,- dead girl is -lying; John Baxendale, whom 'MN helped to escape; John Baxendale, w.5,‘ knows her. Have you thought of that?" He shook his head gloomily.." They won't suspect him," he said. "She was known as knowing me." "Even that difficulty may be got over;" she retorted. "At any rate, the first thing to be done is for us to know what has hap- pened. I can't trust. Volcs-or the other man; I must go myself, I suppose. Will you wait here until I come back?"

"No—l'm safer moving," he replied. "They may find me here; they may drop clown on me in a mdment.. I'll come with you.,, So they set off together, with the man for guide, attracting no notice in that quiet part of the country--two wayfarers tramping along in the dust of the -highway. Coming to the place where, on the previous night, the man had come flying out. of the woods as though bewitched, Ile hesitated now, and drew back. "1 can't—l won't!" he whispered. -" I should scream aloud if I came upon her now. You, must go alone." "You had the courage to kill her," she sneered. "Point as nearly as -you can, then, where you thin& you left her." He pointed, with a shaking forefinger, an,) she plunged at once into the wood and appeared. She was gone a long time, as iL seemed. And' once the wretched man heard footsteps coming along the road, and saw ft countryman going home from his work in the fields, and trembled lest the man should look at him too closely, or should inquire why he waited there. To his horror, the man stopped and asked for a light for his pipe; seemed disposed, indeed, to linger, and to talk about the weather, and to ask awkward questions as to whether the man he had met was a stran- ger—and what his track was. Receiving but curt replies, however, he nodded at last and tramped away; and a moment or two after- wards Johanna Cridge emerged from the wood.

Her face was white, and she seemed to look at the man with a new gravity. "The luck of the Baxendales has changed," she said, solemnly—" and it's come to you. You must come and look for yourself; you wouldn't be- lieve me." "Is she dead?--..and is she there?" he whis- pered, almost with a sob in his voice. "‘ She is dead—and she is there," replied the woman. "Come and see for yourself— come and see the miracle!" She laid a strong hand upon his arm, and plunged with him into the gloom or the woods. Curiosity alone prompted him to the ad- venture—a curiosity that overcame his dread of what he should find. So that when at last. still with that strong hold upon him, she had drawn him to the foot of the tree against which the dead woman lay, and had shewn him what was 80 dreadfully written there, Ile could not at first understand what it recant to himself. He spelt the words over blunder- ingly, watching where the dead finger of the woman had trailed down the wood; where, with a last effort, she had written the final word— " John Baxendale killed me." "I don't understand," he faltered. "Why should she write that?"

"To eave you, of course," she retorted. "Can't you see for yourself that the way is clear for you? There can be no stronger wit- ness than this.' The man' must, hang, as surely as ever a judge and a jury Come face to face with him. I'm a little afraid myself," she added, slowly—" a little afraid when I think how everything is playing into my hands. I did not mean quite that he should die—and for such a crime as this; but in that you have served' me better than you thought, Rufus. In that, too, everyone seems to have served me—even this dead thing here." She touched the foot of the dead girl callously enough with her own as she spoke. "But what am I to do?—and what will you do?" he whispered. "You will get away, and remain in hiding until this John Baxendale is accounted for to the law," she said, sternly. "I have my own plan of what is best to be done; you can leave yourself in my hands. You know where to hide. There are half-a-dozen places where you can take up ,another life for a time and shift for .yourself and save your neck. Go!" He needed no second bidding. He set off then and there into the wide world that should hide him until another man had paid the penalty for his crime. At the last—et the very edge of the wood—he looked back to where that .dead thing lay; but all that he saw was the old. woman seated ncuir to it, as if on guard over .the secret it held. And so, with that dreadful remembrance of her, he left the place behind him. In -a sense, there was a feeling of freedom for him, because he knew that for her own purposes she would .guard the truth, and would bring the other man to the gallows. Rufus Cridge was safe. The woman did not remain beside the dead girl long, however. There was work still .for her to do before that close puzzle she was fitting together and arranging was absolutely complete and perfect. Certain strings of Abe net she had prepared .must be drawn More tightly; there must be no loose ends any- where. Knowing that it was unlikely that anyone would come to the wood that evening, she set off at a great rate for the inn at w hie% she had left Amos Voles and the man Tuttle for they would have parts to play in the busi- ness,_ and must be instructed.
Behold her, therefore, ,preeently, in an inner room of that vinfunnus inn. with the
heads of the two men bent over a table close to her own, and, with her sharp, incisive whispers sinking into their minds, to he well remembered afterwards.

"The girl's dead—don't: forget that," she said, noting with some scorn that Saul Tuttle turned his head sharply to look Over his shoulder into the shadows of the , room. "Don't forget, -ftlso, that Rufus killed her. Now, cast your minds back over what has happened during the past few days, and see to what it brings you." "There's the other man to be considered," said Mr. Voles. • There you've hit the right nail on the head," said the woman, laying a hand upon his arm, and looking from one startled face to the other. "Even in death this girl was true to the man she had loved, poor fool! Even in death she wrote a lie that should in• criminate not Rufus Cridge, but John .Baxen- dale. But the difficulty arises that we have still to connect her with Baxendale and tt sweep Rufus aside altogether." "You'll find that difficult, Mother Cridge," said Saul Tuttle. "Too well . known Rufus 'as bin."

"But you don't grasp .my meaning," ex- claimed the woman, impatiently. "You. have seen for yourselves the ,extraordinary likeness between these two men; you know the story of their birth. What if we declare that there never were two men at all? That John Bax- endale and Rufus Cridge WeDe one? Such things have happened before—when a man has led a double life: one half virtuously and as a fine citizen; the other half as something unclean and in the depths. What if we say that Join Baxendale came out Of this great house, and lived among Us, and dabbled in those things in which we have dabbled— under the name of Rufus Cridge? Wht: then?"
a great scheme," rep!ied Amos Voles "And it puts Rufus out of it altopther."

"It saves Rufus entirely," said Johanna Cridge. " John Baxendale has lived this double life. John Baxendale, tiring of re- spectability, has again and again come amongst us, and under the 'name of Rufus Cridge has sinned against society, has tasted prison-" " Ah, there's the danger!" exclaimed Tuttle, holding up a warning finger. "'Ow are you goin' to account for the time Rufus was in.quod?" . .

"This other man has travelled abc,ut; has been abroad. The dates might happen to fit together," said the woman. "It's the. broad question we have to look at—that the two men are one. That accounts for the highly respectable John Baxendale knowing such a woman as Bella; accounts for her following him here; supplies the motive why this man, fearful that his secret may be discovlred, should kill her. The thing is as plain as day- light." And what becomes of Rufus? And where do we come in?" asked Mr. Voles, pulling at his grey beard thoughatilly. "There are a hundred things that may happen, a hundred chances for us," she re- plied. "But that is not the point so far o‘' I am concerned. All that concerns me is that the house of Baxendale will be in the dust, that John Baxendale must stand trial of his life for such a crime as this, and .that the real man—the creature I have trained—gees free and unharmed. Is there nothing in that?"

"And there may be pickings," said Amos Voles, rubbing liis hands, atid smiling at the other man. "Trusty to me. swear blind there was only one man, and 'e was John Baxendale at 'ome, an' Cridge somewhere else. Come to that, 'aven't I seen 'im as Criclget " he added.

"Then do your work," exclaimed the woman, rising from the table and facing them. "Spread the lie abroad; inquire here Bella Ogden has, got to; drop a whisper here, and a whisper there, about John Baxendale and the double life be has led. You should know how to do it by this time. As for me, I shall get back, to 6ee what happens when they find the girl, and find what is written above her."

So they separated. And once more the woman went out into the darknesg, with that fell determination in her, mind to see the thing brought to en issue, and to see John Baxendale with the clutch of the law upon him.

Meanwhile, there had been happenings at Baxendale Hall. Those who, in a sensP guarded the place from further intrusion may be said to have felt that at any moment some cunning trick might be played upon them again, and the enemy might be found at their gates. Mr. Felix Goode, the lawyer, was so certain in his own mind that that enemy had not been entirely routed, that he determined to remain where he was for the present, the better to face the new situation • that might develop itself; and Mr. Dick Munby, rather enjoying, if the truth be told, the sport of the thing, determined that he, too, would watch. Perhaps the most careless person of all, now that the real danger was past. was John Baxendale himself, for, in reality, he felt that the happenings of the past two clays had been little more than a dream, happily ended. They had done with Rufus Cridge. If by chance the man ever crept back to that place, it would be only to sue for some help that would be readily given him to start a new life in another part of the world. The chief difficulty in John Baxendale's mind was the " covering up of that secret con- cerning himself and the other man. He re- membered that Evelyn had met that other man' thought, with a flush of shame, of how that other man must have held her in his arms under the guise of John Baxendale. That could never be explained without sham- ing her unnecessarily, and without giving away that secret that had been 60 jealous 4 guarded. The maddening thought was that Baxendale himself knew nothing of what the other man might have said to the girl. For him there was nothing to do but to take up the tale where the other man had dropped it, and so save the girl from understanding this truth..

Asa matter of fact, she had referred to what had seemed to be John Baxendale's ex- traordinary- conduct to her on that occasion, when, completely deceived, she had for a moment come face to face with Rufus Cridge. It was on_a day in her aunt's house that, hesitatingly enough, she spoke of the matter. John Baxendale had had so many things to discuss with his friends, and so much to con- sider, that he had not found time to go to Evelyn, so that, as a matter of fact, the last person she had seen in his shape was Rufus Cridge. She seemed to look at him with some mis- trust and doubt, but finally crept into his arms, and looked up at him, albeit with hesi- tation.
"Where have you been all this time?" she asked, in a whisper. "Too busy, my darling, even to come to see you," he answered, as lightly as he could. "I have been worried and troubled."

"So I nought, Jack dear," she replied, with a quick glance at him. "The last time I saw you you were not like yourself in th; least, you were almost rough with me." Shame at the thought of the other man who had held her in his arms made John Baxen- dale bow his head. He lifted her hands in his and put his lips to them, and •so brought another strange remark from her.

"I couldn't understand in the least; you were not like the same man," she whispered. "Why, your hands were different, they seemed rough and scarred. But they're all right now, she added, looking at them critically. "Yes, I know. I've been doctoring them a little," he said, quickly. "If at times, my dearest, I have seemed different, don't judge me harshly. A man has troubles to bear that he must bear alone. And if ever you should hear anything against me," he added, earnestly, 'promise me that you will not be- lieve it; promise me that you will tell me be. fore you judge me. I can explain, and I will explain to you, if necessary." _ They were wild words, wrung from the man's heart in the torture of the thought that that other man walked the 'world in his image, and that John Baxendale might be held responsible for what that other man did. She seemed frightened, and begged again and again that he would explain his meaning more clearly. But he put the matter aside lightly enough. That was the first of several meetings, alit It seemed, in that day or two, that doubts and fears had been set aside, and that there was nothing more to dread. They kner nothing, these happy lovers, of the man who lay bidden in the darkn. n, nd wittehPd

div.head: HIS FATHER'S SON.
div.p: HIS FATHER'S SON.
By TOM GALLON
'Author of Tatterley," "Dicky Monteith,' "Kiddy," "A Rogue in Love," "Fate's Beg- gar Maid," The Charity Ghost," &c.
CIIAPTER VII.

That strange creature, Johanna Cridge, had not remained dormant for a quarter of a century for nothing. She may, in a sense, be compared to some slow spider, that had spun a web, and then had been content to wait un- til that for which the web was spun had flut- tered int) it. Deep in the thwarted, twistee• soul of her she had nursed and nourished that scheme of vengeance; had seen the boy grow up with the stamp upon 'him of the man ,who had wronged her, and in the knowledge that he was evil; every indiscretion—every sin that met with its punishment at the hands of ''lstice was so much of a score in her account with the dead man. Rufus Cridge was a pup- pet in her hands; the fact that he lived in his father's image -was enough; she could play upon him and with him as she liked. But now, as by an accident, the mine had been sprung, and the matter taken out of her hands. Rufus Cridge had penetrated the secret; and, so far from leaving Johanna Cridge to carry out things in her own fashion, had actively taken matters into his own hands. That was what she would have wished; her sole fear was that the man might blunder, and so might ruin all that she had prepared in that long process of waiting that had occupied five-and-twenty years. With the coming of John Baxendale to Middleton's Rents the woman had seen the actual realisation of her dream. A new John Baxendale would take the place of the old one; would reign there in vice, as the old one had reigned in purity; would drag the name of Baxendale in the dust, and make it a thing to be scorned among men. The very dead should turn in their graves at the thought of what John Baxendale was doing; while, ,on the other hand, a double vengeance was given to her by reason of the fact that the man who had enjoyed prosperity all these years was suddenly reduced to the gutter, and must perforce bear the sins of his brother. So much the woman had thought when the game was at last in her hands. But, as we know, another woman had out- matched her and had snatched from her part at least of the spoils of victory. Bella Ogden, greatly daring for the sake of hex t love for a /worthless man, ha , •blundered intc the story at a most inop tune moment— which is only another way o -2 „ying that most men, good or bad, provide i e for their owr backs of their own making. 'Rufus Criclge, as we know, had, found a short • and swift way to break that rod at least; and poor Bella had paid for her temerity with her life. But that Johanna Cridge did not know ;. at pres- ent she was merely possessed of an indefinite fear that something might go AN rong with her cherished plans, and that the man she had trained might kick over the traces and go headlong to perdition on a new road of hie own finding. She determined that the moment had ar- rived when she must take some clear action in the matter for herself; when the strings must be gathered together in her strong, capable hands; and when she must shew the way. Consequently, when it was decided that the two men, Amos Voles and Saul Tuttle, were to follow Cridge (lest by some chance he should want help in his devilries), the woman . made up her mind to go with them. After all these years there was a secret feel- ing of delight at the prospect of herself in- vading the house of Baxendale, and setting her own hand to the coming work of destruc- tion there.

For five-and-twenty years the woman had, for her own purposes, lived in the depths and known intimately those who dwell there. Their ways are not as the ways of more civilised people; they are a world apart. So now she had means of communicating with Cridge if by any chance he was anywhere in the neighbour- hood of Deepington. Arrangements had indeed been made by which he was to be found at a certain place in the event of disaster or fail- ure coming upon him. With her satellites. she had gone to that place, her mind filled with the thought of Bella, and of how that woman might in some fashion have spoilt the scheme that had taken so long to mature. The place in question was a villainous little public-house in a village on the outskirts of thin town of Deepington. It was frequented by every shady poaching character in the neighbourhood, and had long been a blot upon the fair, smiling country in which it was situated. The landlord had been suspected not alone of harbouring poachers but occa- sionally cheating justice by larger methods; but he had never yet been laid by the heels. To this place came Johanna Cridge on the day following the murder of Bella; and here she took up her quarters, certain in her own mind that in tine course news would come of Rufus. She knew that in the long run nis cunning must outmatch that of the man he was set to destroy; she could afford to wait with some show of patience. Meanwhile, the wretched man who had left that thing lying stark in the woods had fled from it as from something at which he dared not look again. Now he was certain in his own mind that the woman was dead; now, on the other hand, he felt that he had not struck deeply enough, and that she was at this moment rising up before some horrified stranger to declare who had killed her, and why. Now in his vision she seemed to be lying there, undiscovered, among the trees; now there was a crowd about her, and a hue- and-cry across the country for a man answer- ing to his description, who had been seen lurking about that place. He had hated the girl, and, still more, had hated what she had done in the way of betraying him; but he would have given years of his life now to have that thing undone, and the blow unstruck. Above all, it shut him out from any pros- pect of gaining that position that had been mapped out for him by the woman who had had him in hand for training. Until this matter was settled, one way or the other, he was a fugitive and in hiding. The game was clearly with John Baxendale. Also, he dreaded, as other men did, the "stern, relent- less eyes of Johanna Cridge. He wondered what he must say to her. _ . - - . .

But in time lie also made for that haven to which Johanna had gone. He had spent a night in the woods and fields—a haunted, hunted man—now seeing shadows stealing to- wards him across the landscape, now hearing his name cried by the very winds, now seeing, horribly enough, the dead woman start up, with blood upon her, and gibbering mouth ac- cusing him. He had not rested, having made a wide circuit of the country. It was late in the day following that he staggered to the place where he knew news would reach him of Mother Cridge and the. others. He wits scarcely surprised to be told that they were Already there, and were waiting for him. Sullenly enough, lie went into the room vhere the ,woman and the two men were wait- ing. He faced them with defianoe, and with animmediate request for food. "I've walked the night through—and what there was of to-day," he said; flinging himself into a chair, and pressing his palms over his aching eyes. "Oct ..me something to eat and to drink—and don't stare at me. like that," he added savagely to Amos Voles. Mr. Voles, being one of those persons born to plunge into awkward plaees, asked a ,ques Lion now that brought the hunted man to his feet with a cry: "And what's become of the girl?" he asked. Rufus Cridge turned upon him savagely enough.- "What do you mean? What should I know about her?" he demanded.
Saul Tuttle took up the tale. "But you know, Rufus, you was gain' after 'er," he re- minded the wretched man. "You said yer- self-

"Let him alone," exclaimed Johanna Cridge. "Let him eat and drink; then per- haps he'll tell us what has happened and what he s been doing." They eet food and drink before Le began to eat like one famished. only ttop-
The Examiner, Saturday, November 20

mem walking in the garden. More than all else, they knew nothing of that which was hidden in the wood, with the dreadful writ• ing above it. But that could nbt remain hidden long. It was to be • discovered in the most casual way; the quiet town of Deepington was to be set ablaze in a moment,- as it were, with the news. But before that happened Mr. Felix Goode and Dick Munby were to have the dreadful tidings sprung upon hcm, and once again to feel that a blow had fallen upon the -house of Baxendale from which it would be hard for it to recover. John Baxendale had walked across the grounds in the direction of Miss Dorcas Stubbs's cottage, leaving the two men in the house alone. Felix Goode was writing letters, in his precise, neat handwriting, and Dick Munby was reclining on his back on a couch smoking, when there floated to their ears the sound of .running feet outside—hurried, scrambling footsteps, as of a man badly fi ightened and with a tale to tell. Felix Goode laid down his pen, and Dick Munby got to a sitting posture. They looked at each other, seeming in that moment to hold their breaths with suspense. "What has. happened now?" whispered the lawyer.

The door was burst open, and a man, a young servant, rushed in. His face was pale, and he was shaking from head to foot. It was with difficulty that they got his tale from him. He caught his breath in great, dry sobs as he talked; he clung to a table and got out his words with difficulty. He had been walking with his sweetheart in the woods, and he had come upon the dreadful thing lying beneath a tree. He had seen the words the dead woman had scrawled upon the blazed trunk of the tree. He begged that someone would go with him now and see the sight for thenlselves. His sweetheart had gone running back to the town to her mother; the news must be everywhere by this time. If only the gentlemen would come and see for themselves, if only they would warn the young master of his danger. The three went out together in a little bunch, the man still whispering earnestly and the others urging him to shew them the way. A lantern was got from the Stables, and they went rapidly through the grounds, almost running, and so came at last to the place. Seeing the shadowy thing lying on the grass the man cried out that he could go no further, and handed the lantern to Felix Goode, who went forward with it. There lay the dead girl, with one arm still outstretched, and pointing, as it were, to that deadly accu- sation she had written. Felix Goode, after a glance at her, swung the lantern aloft • and stepped forward to the tree itself. He started back with a cry. For someone was sitting there on the great roots of the tree—an old woman, with black eyes earnestly watching him, and with her chin propped on her hands that were folded on the head of a- stick. She did net move, and as he fell back from her she spoke his name quietly. "Felix Goode—you remember me?" __ _ _

"Johanna Cricige ! " he exclaimed, at- mo6t in a whisper. "What are you doing here?" "Guarding the dead, and the secret of the dead," nhe replied, sternly. "Send that cry. ing fool away '--ehe pointed to the shaking servant—." I want to talk to you.".
(To be continued.)

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

lhe Memorial to Sir John Moore.—The unveiling of a memorial to Sir John Moore at Sandgate this week by Miss Mary C. Moore, a grand-niece of the hero, is naturally an event of some interest to our Royal visitor, the King of Portugal. In the Peninsular war, which continued from 1808 to 1814, Britain was fighting by the side of Spain and Portugal against France. In December, 1808, Sis Johh Moore was forced to retreat to the north-west coast of Portugal, but, turning on the evening, he fought and defeated the French at Corunna on January 16th, 1809. It was there that Sir John Moore met his death, falling like Wolfe and Nelson' in the moment of victory. The memorial unveiled by his grand niece tokes the form of a bronze bust, and stands on the Esplanade at Sandgate, close to Shorncliffe. The Steinheil Trial.— L'Affaire Steinheil" which has been the one absorbing topic in France for the past two or three weeks, has ended as was expected in making a popular heroine of Mme. Steinheil. On May 31st last year her husband and mother were found strangled in their beds, but it was not until November 28th that Mme. Steinheil %A as arrested on the charge of being the author of the crime. Thus nearly a year has elapsed before the concluding scene which presented all the emotional and hysterical features peculiar to the French system of conducting a " famous trial." Mme. Steinheil is acquitted, but it will be some time before Parisians cease to talk about her extraordinary adventures, and the wonderful cleverness with which she took advan- tage of French legal forms to gain the pity, and even the active sympathy of those who were asked to condemn her. In France, the judge is not cnly judge, but prose- cuting counsel as well. The accused is denounced as guilty with every breath, tortured and persecuted with questions until a wave of pity sweeps over the Court, and justice becomes more a matter of emotion than evidence. Of that, the usual order of things, Mme. Steinheil made the utmost, and did it with an ability that has seldom, if ever, been surpassed in • French criminal procedure. American Women.—The members of the Society of American Women in London, had the gratification of hearing from Miss Marie Corelli, a somewhat effusive encomium of themselves and their countrywomen ; but one cannot help thinking that the best of all the qualities which she ascribed are to be found just as readily among the women of Britain as among those of the United States. If any are lacking they are those that we do not want, not because we deprecate them, or because we think that the American woman would be better without them, but because we havit our own standard of taste and ideas, just as the people of other countries have theirs. We have beautiful women in these islands, and what is more important good loyal, affec- tionate womanly women. It is no doubt an advantage to President Taft—if Miss Marie Corelli rightly described the position—to have a wife who is able to set him right on all occasions, but common-sense is not the monopoly of any people, and there is as much sound judgment among British women as there is among members of their sex in any part of the world, not- withstanding the freaks and follies of the Suffragists. The Mayflower Pilgrims.—Miss Marie Corelli is said to have remarked to her audience of American ladies, that "there was only one woman on board the May- flower "—but in this she was doubtless incorrectly reported The party known as the Pilgrim Fathers, who sailed in the Mayflower on September 6th, 1620, consisted of 41 men, 28 women, and 33 children. One of the women, the wife of one of the voyagers, was drowned. Another, Mary Chilton, was the first ;of the party to land in America; to whom possibly Miss Marie Corelli intended to refer.

The Poor Childrens' Boot Fund.—Every parent has occasion to know that the boot, bill enters largely into the household expenditure, and that the amount has not tended to diminish in recent years as the quality of boots has in the aggregate deteriorated. And if the cost of childrens boots is rather a severe tax upon the better provided, how much more must it be so in the case of the poor, especially where the breadwinner, through no fault of his own, is unable to obtain employment. In order to assist the poor in these circumstances, Lady St. Helier and Sir' John Kirk, have issued an sppeal for £3,000 on behalf of the London Poor Children's Boot Fund. Of course we know that the question is quite as important in the provinces as it is in the metropolis, but happily there are in many places local efforts to supply the need, promoted by the Mayor or some other influential personage. In any event, the question is one which merits attention wherever it arises, and certainly not least in the metropolis where a large proportion of the children attending elementary schools are found by their teachers to be most insufficiently shod. The Poor Children's Boot Fund proceeds on the lines of requiring the parent to pay half the cost of the boots, and it requires a guarantee from the vendor with regard to the quality. Cleaning Furs.—To clean sable, a quantity of bran is required. This should be placed in a dry tin box, near the fire until so hot that it can only just be handled. The fur should then be stretched upon the table and with a warm hand, the bran shout,' be well-rubbed into every part of it. Finally the fur should be thoroughly brushed and shaken. Ermine is best cleaned by dipping a flannel first in warm water, next in dry bran, and rubbing gently until all dinginess has vanished, and the flannel is perfectly dry. A piece of soft muslin should then be dipped in dry powdered magnesia, and rubbed over the surface of the fur, when it should look as fresh and dainty as when new. An Innovation.—Knitted skirts to match the knitted coats, promise to be well patronised by out-of-door girls and women, that is if they keep their shape, and neither" sag" or drop. These skirts are very short and in pale colours, and white especially, look par- ticularly well. Knitted hats to correspond, have also , appeared, and in some very becoming shapes. The Coiffure.—The " csp "of hair has decidedly "caught on," indeed so violently that it promises to be speedily " off "so far as exclusive dressers are con- cerned, Certainly never has afashionable coiffure been so easily and quickly arranged, that is, when "acquired "looks are employed. The " cap " of hair surrounded by a plait, or twisted strand of the same, needs only that the wearer's front hair be drawn upwards, or parted as may prove most becoming, and the ends gathered and tucked beneath the" cap," when the arrangement is complete. Many Rings and No Gloves.—Very fashionsble women are .appearing at the theatre in the evening
If you are careless about yourself don't ruin the future of your boys and girls

Children are full of action from morn till night. They use up a lot of vitality—you couldn't take as many steps as they do. They are growing, and so require more nutrition or they will be small and puny men and women. Quaker Oats is the best food for them— to play on—study on—grow on.

These gloveless ones, how- ever, invariably carry muffs of the most airy-fairy description, usually matching the wrap. When flowers appear upon these dalnty creations they are Nature's own handiwork, artificial flowers and foliage being " barred " just now.

The Topaz.—Coloured stones are in high repute at the moment, and among "lesser lights" the topaz—the gem cf November—is greatly to the fore. There is hardly a precious stone that varies more widely in tint than the topaz, but whatever this may be, from the expert's point of view it is always either true or false, the true specimen coming from the Far East and South. while the false is found in the Western world. Strange powers are claimed for the gleaming November gem, one old sage, having made the study of the topaz a labour of love, and experimented assiduously with it, offering the statement that it " calms the anacreontic ten3perament," while another acknowledged authority on charms declares that" it has great healing powers, curing mcntal disease and sleep-walking." __ s

div.head: TEMPERANCE SUNDAY.
div.p: TEMPERANCE SUNDAY.
MEETING AT PARR HALL.

Last Sunday was Temperance Sunday and to celebrate the occasion a meeting was held in the Parr Hall under the auspices of the Warrington Band of Hope Union. rs. James Dodds presided, and amongst others on the platform were :—Revs. C. Harvey Cooke, T.-Miller and 11. Wall, Messrs. Arthur Black (Secretary, Sunday School Union), James Dodds, F. Gandy, R. Pierce- Williams and J. Jarman. There was a good audience. Mrs. Doians said she was very proud to preside over such a meeting as that, and she was glad to see them there as it showed the signs of the times. She woad do anything to forward the cause of Temperance in Warrington. Perhaps the cause which lay closest to her heart was the Band of Hope. (Applause.) They wanted to get for themselves a good name and they were beginning with the children, knowing that the children of to-day would. be the men and women of to-morrow. They wanted them to be good, righteous and sober men and women. (Applause.) That was the object of the Band of Hope. It was the Master's own work and they were there in His name and they might rightly expect that His blessing would be upon them. (Applause.)

Mr. ARTHUR BLACK said he supposed the chief reason wby he had been asked to come was because he was an old Band of Hope boy. In the Band (V Hope he was first a reciter, then a Secretary and then a very poor and faltering speaker, and therefore he owed a good deal to the Band of Hope in addition to the splendid influences of his home life. The Band of Hope opened to him a field of training for all forms of social and public service. He prayed that out of it in this town there might rise up a whole army of meh and women for the Church and for the public good. Continuing he said he had a grudge against Warrington as a temperance man. Warrington ales were very largely indulged in in Liverpool. ("Shame.") It was regarded by many people in Liverpool that beer was the chief article produced in Warrington. He was quite aware that liquor was the least important thing in Wa rrington, whether it was the chief article pro- duced or not. Every trade must be judged not merely by what went in but by what came out. There were gigantic evils resulting from ourpresent licenced traffic. Of course it provided employment and it also provided unemployment. The Lord Chief Justice had said that 90 per cent. of the crime in this country was caused through drink. Through drink the lunatic asylums were full and more had to be built. The Poor Law Commission had reported that the use of strong drink was one of the chief causes in the production of pauperism. There was to be said for the brewers that they provided unemployment and gave revenue to the country. But what was the fruit of the traffic? He thought they could see that the balance went against the public house. If they could only sweep away the excessive strong drink they would be on the royal road to reform in the country. (Applause). Drink deteriorated the health of the people; it degraded the morals of the people; and it destroyed the soul of the people. Drink de-humanised man and destroyed the Divine faculties. They must judge the trade by what it produced. The speaker instanced that in a district of little more than a square mile in Liverpool there were 99 public-houses now, and 24 had been demolished in recent years. In that district be found the death-rate among children was twice as high as in some of the upper working- class districts. He found that the great amount of crime came from that particular quarter; the chief poveity of the city was all concentrated in that district awl along with an almost similar district on the other side of the city, they bad concentrated all the evils and vices that were almost the despair of Christian workers and civic reformers in the city. Drink hindered them in the making of the Empire. Continuing, he said that since their last meeting the Children's Act had been passed. (Applause.) That meant very much, but even now in this matter we were very far behind many of our colonies and many parts of the United States. Our present Act forbade the sale of intoxicants to children under fourteen and prevented the giving of intoxicants to children under five. That was in the right direction, but it was not very far. In many parts of Canada no one under 20 years of age must be served with liquor. In New South Wales the age was 18. In those places they thought more of men than of vested interests (Loud Applause.) Continuing he said that there was a need to make more provision for boys and girls during the,unguarded years of their lives, say from 13 to 18, so that they could have company, recreation and some form of amusement for the exercise of their own powers of mind and body. If the Bands of Hope and Sunday Schools could satisfy, that need they would preserve many of the young. We were not merely con- cerned as a British people about our own folk in the homes of England and Scotland. We were an Imperial race and upon us depended the future destiny of millions of people, moral and spiritual. During a visit to South Africa not very long ago the contents of a newspaper bill contained nothing but an announcement of drunkenness in Liverpool and that quite convinced him that the people of that country. looked to England f)r their morals. God had given to us as a nation tke Gospel, the Bible,' the Church and all the blessings of the Christian civilization. He had also given us the chance of teach- ing people the Gospel of Christ, out the Church often failed in the task. We have to confess that we gave 'about 1 per cent, to the cause of foreign missions, and to the building up of the Christian empire abroad, of the amount we spent in this country on drink. If we only gave 10 per cent of the money that was squandered in strong drink to foreign missions, we could bring the Gospel to the reach of every human soul. If only there were the spirit of self-denying sacrifice, and if they could have Paul's ardour,- many evils would be righted. Everywhere in the world, drink was the direct enemy and hinderer of the Gospel of Jesus Christ for which our Churches stood. Drink was the work of the devil, and Christ °me into the world to destroy the work of the devil. In conclusion, he appealed to his bearers to enlist themselves in the work of the Band of Hope. (Applause). The Rev. HARVEY CooK proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Dodds for presiding and to Mr. Black for his address. He said the now Messiah for the 20th century

div.p: was the care of the child. They were glad to take up the message of a now Messiah. It struck him with poignant pain to know the alarming increase in children who were born feeble-minded and he could not, but ask what was the cause of it? If we did not look after the children we should become a second rate power. When he was in Canada and the United States he was surprised at the tremendous influence of Liverpool, Manchester and London upon the morals of the people with whom he came in contact. and it was for England to rise as she had ever done to take a front place in the path of truth and goodness and against evil. Our feeble-minded children were the expression of the righteous wrath of the Divine on account of our careless attitude to the children. Thera was no great final day of judgment; judgment proceeded with us now and we were reaping it now and the world was reaping the result of what it, was sowing. We were reaping in the increased feeble- mindedness God's judgment. It was all very well for them to speak as though they were the happenings of Providence. It was a blasphemy to the very name of Providence to charge God with the increased feeble- minded of our children. In the United States a great steel trust was realising the harm that drink was doing and they were determined to buy up all the public- houses round about. They, were going to buy them at a capital cost of two million pounds so that they could diminish the drinking. They had found out that the day after pay-day they got such terrible bad work and ' so few men turned up that it would pay them to do it. (Applause). Mr. GANDY seconded and the vote of thanks was accorded.

div.head: WHOLE FAMILY WITH ECZEMA.

Fierce Running Sores on Father, Mother, & 3 Children.
Zam-Buk's Wonderful Achievement.

His usual ointments and lotions proving useless we had another doctor, and afterwards a third, but all failed to give us relieftfrom the smarting pain and to check the spread of the sores, "All the doctors told us that my husband had most likely caught the infection while at his work, as many of the men from his place had been treated by the doctors for eczema. COMMERCIAL FA ILU RES.—A °cording to "Keen Mercantile Gazette," the total number of Commercial Failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, November 12th, was 141, viz. New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the "London Gazette, 84; Deeds of Arrangement registered, 60. The respective numbers in .the corresponding week of last year were: Bankruptcies, 83; Deeds of Arrange- ment, 87—total 171; betng a decrease of 27. The total number of Commercial Failures recorded during the-46. weeks of the present year is 6,833; the total number recorded in the corresponding 46 weeks of last year wasa 7,328, showing a decrease of 495.
