div.head: Newchurch.
div.p: Newchurch.

NEWeIirRCH SCHOOL SOCIAL.—A social and dance was held in this place on Friday the 12th inst. Refresh- ments were provided the tables being beautifully decorated with flowers. Mr. E. Overton acted as M.C. and Mr. Hindburst of Leigh was the pianist. The social which was organized by. the Culcheth recreative
society was a huge s-uccess anil the proceeds were given to the Rector in aid of new lamps for the school.
Moore.

WESLEY G UILD.—On Wednesday evening last a very profitable and enjoyable literary evening was spent in the schoolroom. Mr. Arthur Ward, of Padgate, gave a lecture on " Thackeray." He gave a very interesting sketch of the great writer's life and dealt with him as poet, artist, and novelist. Like several other great men Thackeray never excelled at school and some excellent stories were told of his school life as well as of other times in his life. Mr. Ward also very briefly reviewed some of the author's best known works in such a way as to inspire those present who have not done so, to make their acquaintance at the first possible oppor- tunity. A very hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Ward was proposed by Mr. J. Jackson, seconded by Mr. Tanner, and carried.

div.head: Stockton Heath.
div.p: Stockton Heath.

ST. Thomas's BAND OF HOPE.—An entertainment in connection with the above was held in the Parish Room on Tuesday evening. There was a good attend- ance of parents and children. Recitations were very nicely given by N. Clegg A. and A. Rutter, B. Howard, P. Clegg, L. Whiteman, A. Rustage, J. Judd and F. Ogden, as was also a dialogue by L. Rathbone and F. Clare on" Playing and working," a duet by L. Rathbone and M. Hallows was very well given; also an action song by several girls, a violin solo by Sam Smith was well received. An address was given by the Rev. C. F. Cross, vicar of Stratton on " Life's Purpose." The subject was brought well within the reach even of the youngest by a verity of illustrations and so won their attention all through. A humorous dialogue "Peter Squills downfall" given by the members under the care of Mr. Whiteman was a treat and well deserved the hearty applause it !received. Votes of thanks by Mr. Hallows to all who taken had part brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: Padgate.
div.p: Padgate.

PADGATE WESLEY GUILD.—A very interesting meet- ing of the Wesley Guild was held in the schoolroom on Monday last, the subject for the evening being a debate on "Are theatres beneficial ?" The delence was in the hands of Mr. England and the opposing forces were well represented by Mr. Plinston. After a very well thought argument between the two leaders, speeches for and against were made by several of the members, and at the close a vote was taken the result being 13 for the 'motion and 14 against, several of the members abstaining from voting. The Rev. T. Cladding occupied the chair and the debate was thoroughly enjoyed by 'all prpsent. • WEDDING: FOSTER—BATE.—The marriage was solemnized at the Padgate Wesleyan Church on Satur- day last of Miss Ellen Bate, second daughter of Mr. H. Bate of Padgate, and Mr. William Foster of Warrington, the officiating minister being the Rev. T. Gladding. The bride who was given away by her father was attired in a biscuit coloured crepoline dress trimmed with pink ribbon and wore a beautiful picture hat to match. Her sister, who acted as bridesmaid, wore a lake green crepoline dress with hat to match. She was also attended by her two young sisters, Misses Annie and Edith Bate, and Miss Gertie Hughes and Miss Eva Latham as maid s-in-waiting, who all wore cream dresses trimmed with deep lace. Mr. Foster, brother of the bridegroom very ably performed the duties of best man. Mr. A. Domville officiated at the organ playing Mendelssobn's wedding march as the happy couple left the sanctuary. A reception was afterwards held at the home of the bride. A number of beautiful presents have been received.

div.head: Penketh.
div.p: Penketh.

LIBERAL CLI:I3.—On Tuesday evening another interesting debate took place at the above club. Mr. Dendy prfsided over a good number of the members and friends. The question of debate was "Should bachelors be taxed." Mr. J. H. Mainley opened in favour of a tax being imposed on bachelors, the trend of his remarki being that they did not pay their fare share of taxes. He would impose a tax of 7 per cent. on income over and above £lO4 per year. Mr. D. Ridyard of Warring- ton opposed the tax in a convincing way. There was a majority of bachelors present, who spoke in strong condemnation of such a tax. Several questions were answered by Mr. Mainley. The evening was a most enjoyable one and was brought to a close by Mr. Midwood who proposed and Mr. Mark Ray seconded a vote of thanks to the speakers and chairman. SOClAL.—ThelPenketh Wesleyan Men's Bible Class held their annual social on Saturday in the Sunday school. Mr. C. E. Parker, the president of the Bible class presided. The audience numbering about 80 were favoured with a first-class musical progrrmme which consisted of the following :—Pianoforte solo, Miss Rosemond Parker; solos were also rendered in first- class style by Miss Jennie Hewitt, Mr. W. Hughes, and Mr.McArthur. By request Mr.W, Hughes sang a solo in Welsh. The President on behalf of the class made a presentation of a framed photograph of the Bible class to Mr. A. Seed and Mr. J. Walters who have left the district. Mr. Parker spoke in bigh terms of these two gentlemen and said they had been most active members. Mr. Walters responded in suitable terms. Refreshments were then handed round and a variety of games indulged in until 10.30 p.m. On the proposition of Mr. Miawood seconded by Mr. W. H. Shaw a vote of thanks to the singers, and the singing of "Mild Lang Syne " brought a most pleasant evening to a close. CO-OPERATIVE CONCERT.—A grand concert promoted by the Education Committee of the Co-operative Society took place on Thursday evening in the Wes- leyan schoolroom. Mr. A. T. Clay presided in the unavoidable absence of Mr. W. Hough. There wore also on the platform Messrs. J. T. Rushton and N. Cook. At the outset Mr. J. T. Rushton moved a vote of sympathy with the family of the late Mr. A. H. Rathbone whose deattt was so much regretted. The motion was passed in silence, the audience standing. An excellent pro- gramme was submitted, which was as follows : Chorus, "Crusaders," the Co-operative choir; concertiea solo, Mr. Aukland ; solo. " Roses," Miss Silcock ; solo, "Asleep in the deep," Mr. Hodgson; trombone solo, "Dream of Paradise," Mr. Hacking; duet, " Maying," Miss Silcock and Mr. Fairhurst : humorous song, Mr. Aukland ; part song, "In absence," the Choir; solo, "Come hack to me," Miss Silcock ; solo, "Roll on," Mr. Hodson; trombone solo, Ora pro-nobis " Mr. Hacking; quartette, "Softened splendour," Messrs. Fairhurst,4o:aylor, Phair, Hodgson: humorous song, Mr. Aukland ; chorus, "Soldiers chorus," the Choir.
On the proposition of Mr. W. Moores seconded by the Chairman a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the artistes.
The Examiner, Saturday, November 20, 1909.

div.head: Lymm.
div.p: Lymm.

ACCIDENT.—WhiIst returning home on Saturday evening last, Mr. Ralph Wheeler of Cherry-lane, was knocked down by a cyclist near, the Crown Inn in Booths Hill. He was very much bruised and hurt and has been unable to follow his employment this week so far. But he is now progressing favourably.

LYMM LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—The members of this association met on Thursday evening for t smoking concert, the programme for which had kindly been arranged by Mr. J. H. Brazendale. Vocal and instru- mental music was rendered by the following gentlemen: Messrs. J. Isaacs, E. A. Jones, J. H. Brazendale, E. Moss. Mr. Tom Blakeley gave a humorous sketch and a ventriloquial performance. Mr. Leonard Orson rendered a whistling solo and Mr. Leslie Crouch a couple of recitals. A most enjoyable evening was spent which was brought to a close by a hearty vote of thanks being accorded to the gentlemen mentioned and to Mr. T. M. Eastham who kindly acted as accompanist.

CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH GUIL D.—ln connection with this society a lecture was given on Thursday even- ing by the Rev. J. Johnson, of Ashton-on-Mersey on "The pictures of G. F. Watts. R.A.," illustrated with lantern views. The lecturer dealt with the following well-known pictures of the artist :—"Dawn," " Into the light," "Faith," " Love," "Hope," "Time, Death and Judgment " and "Love and Death," explaining in a very lucid and interesting manner the symbolical significance of these masterpieces. The rlecture was listened to with rapt attention and at the close the words of thanks tendered to the lecturer by the Rev.A. Barrett were very cordially endorsed by the audience.

OUGHTRINGTON MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— The third meeting of this Society took place on Mon- day last, when a paper was read by Mr. J. D. B. Smith on " Ancient civilizations," in which he introduced the question of the present day progress being altogether satisfactory, advocating the wider acceptance of socialistic teaching as a means of mitigating the evils which beset society at the present time. This question was warmly debated by several \of the audience, the general feeling being against the views expressed by the reader of the paper. The next meeting should have been held on the 29th inst., but owing to the school- room being required for a missionary meeting it has been postponed to Monday, December 6th, when a paper on "Ancient Rome," illustrated by lantern views, will be given by Mr. F. J. Wright.

div.head: LYAIM PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: LYAIM PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. A. Watkin (chairman) and Major Groves. DEFRAUDING THE RAILWAY COMPANY.—Arthur Samuel Newton, Statham Avenue, Lymm, was charged with two offences, first, that on the 30th September he travelled from Manchester (Oxford-road) to Dunham Massey without previously paying his fare, and with intent to avoid payment, and secondly that he travelled between Dunham Massey and Manchester (Knot Mill) without paying his fare and with intention to avoid payment.—Mr. Mason, solicitor, Euston, prosecuted on behalf of the L. & N.W. Railway Company and said defendant was charged with travelling without paying and with intent to defraud which was the most impart- ant part of the offence. On September 30th defendant presented himself at the ticket office at Heatley Station and asked for a return ticket to Dunham Massey. The station master having suspicious caused a telephone message to be sent to Dunham Massey. This was the place where defendant ought to have got out but he did not do so and travelled on to Man- chester. He also returned from Manchester and proffered the return ticket from Dunham Massey to Heatley. When questioned by the Heatley station master he confessed that he had travelled from Manchester.— Walter Timperley, stationmaster at Heatley Station, said on September 30th he was on duty at Heatley, when defendant obtained a ticket for Dunham Massey, and went on the 10.24 train from Heatley. Later in the day witness received a communication from Dunham Massey Station and in consequence of this he spoke to defendant on his leaving the train and asked him where he got on the train. Defendant said "at Broadbeath." Witness said "Are you sure of that ? " Defendant replied"l will tell you the truth Mr.Ti mperley, I got in at Manchester." Witness then spoke to him with regard to his morning journey and defendant finally admitted that he got off at Knott Mill. Witness asked him for his outward ticket and he replied that he had thrown it away. He then asked witness to accept the excess fare but witness replied that he could not do that. Defend- ant said witness's statement was perfectly correct.— John Gilbert, stationmaster at Dunham Massey Station said he received a telephonic communication from the last witness and watched the train that defendant was travelling on. He did not get out at Dunham Massey nor did he join the train there at night.—William Bmdburn, a porter at Heatley Station, said he received a return ticket to Dunham Massey from defendant who came by the 3.40 train from Oxford-road.—Detective Ernest Clarke, of the London and Nortb-Westein Railway, said he interviewed defendant, and he said he was very sorry; he had no intention to defraud. He hoped he would do what he could for ixlm to ask the Company not to prosecute.— Defendant now said be had no intention to defraud. On arriving at Manchester (Knott Mill) no one was collecting tickets, and he walked straight through the barrier. The reason why g went on to Manchester was because he met a frieud.—The Chairman, after dis- cuising the matter in private with his colleague, said they could not for a moment believe defendant's story. He was guilty of a very mean fraud upon the raiNay company. lie would be fined .£l, with .£1 16s. 6d. costs, and also £1 is. advocate's fee (£3 17s. Gd).

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.

NVarrington A.C. had a nice muster on Saturday last when the first round of the points competition was decided with the following rehlt :—J. Parsonage 10 points, J. Twiss 9, A. Siddell 8, F. Antrobus 7, H. K. Jepson 6, W. Antrobus 5, R. Bennett 4, %V. Siddall 3, G. I\icholson2, W. Drury 1. In this competition the first ten men home in each round, count points—the winner 10 end the others in proportion. At the end of the season these are totalled up and the member with the largest number is declared the winner. - -
The team race between sides selected by the captain and one of the sub-captains resulted in a win for the former as follows:
JEPSON'S TEAM (1), J. PARSONAGE'S TEAM (2). J. Twiss A. Siddall 3 F. Antrobus H. K, Jepson It. Bennett G. Nicholson

The points in a team race being reckoned inversely to a points competition, the captain's team with the smallest aggregate won by the narrow margin of three points. The course covered was about eight miles of mixed going with the plougki nicely spread out. The pace was good. Parsonage won fairly comfortably. The race for second place was exceptionally good, Twiss, A. Siddall,and F. Antrobus being close together throughout. To-day's fixture is an ordinary run from Bridge Inn at 3.15 p.m.
CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING AND CHARITY. NEXT SATURDAY'S MEET.

The local clubs are looking forward with interest and Ryland's Recreation Ground will probably have a new gate record. There is great diversity of opinion as to the probable winners in both the team and scratch races as the fact of the course being fiat, and almost devoid of the obstacles generally encountered by cross country runners, enhances the chances of some and materially lessens the chances of others. About 100 runners are expected to take part in the team race and before the last of the ten laps (I mile inside the ground) is covered, many changes will ha apparent owing to the series of struggles for position; of course in an affair of this kind nearly all the runners complete the course and the winning team may have to wait anxiously for their last counter. Many are fancied for the individual honour of first man home. _ _ _ _ _ _ _

The scratch race will really decide who is local champion at six miles and although there will be fewer competitors than in the team *race yet the winner is certain to be severely tested,as on their best form there are quite a dozen within easy 'reach of each other at this distance, but "condition' will decide the issue in both races. _ _ _

The Territorials (Volunteers) must now be added to the honours list as the meet secretary has received a letter from Sergeant-Major G. H. Ingram, 4th South Lancashire Regiment, of which the following is an extract :—" I beg to inform you that they (the Band) are quite willing to give their services on the occasion of the Harriers meet on the 27th inst„ and that Colonel Fairclough has no objection to their attending,

div.head: Death From Anthrax: County Court Sequel,
div.p: Death From Anthrax: County Court Sequel,

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday before His Honour Judge Shiress Will K.C., Mr. A. Browne made an application on behalf of Harriet Parker, 283, Thelwall-lane, under the Workmen's Compensation Act, with regard to the death of her husband Charles Parker, a tanner who died recently from anthrax.lle said that deceased's employers,Messrs, Pierpoint and Bryant paid into the Court the sum of £205 Bs. This the applicant had accepted. There were two children as well as the widow dependent. His Honour made an order for the eum of 120 to be paid to the applicant and ;C:2 10s. a month for maintenance.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. A. H. RATHBONE.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. A. H. RATHBONE.
WARRINGTON.
Success at the Crystal Palace Show,

At the exhibition of-poultry, pigeons, &c., opened at the Crystal Palace, London, on Tuesday, Mr. 0. W. Reynolds, of Massey Hall, Thelwall, with his White Orpingtons, secured a first and special for cockerels, a second for hens, and a first for pullets. Mr. T. Welsh, of Warrington, was awarded a first for his exhibit in the novice class.

I.L.P. Debating Class. On Monday evening Mr. H. Wardman presided o% er a good attendance at the above class. Mr. C. E. Parker read a paper on "Land and Caßkal," which was followed by a discussion in which Messrs, W. Lowe, A. Spencer, W. Whitely, and R. P. Williams took part. A vote of thanks to the motion of Mr. E. Horrocks, seconded by Mr. E. Highley, was passed to Mr. Parker.

Wycliffe Young People's Society. This society held a successful open meeting on Monday evening in the Memorial Buildings, the Rev. John Yonge presiding. The Rev. Harry Wall gave an ikteresting lecture on "Lakeland," interspersed with lantein slides. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the essayist, on the motion of Mr. Fred Womersley, seconded by Mr. C. Eccles. The lantern was manipulated byllllr..Ashton. MOSELEYS FOOD.—A most vgreeable and acceptable food, stimulant and restorative for invalids and convalescents.—Advt.

Warrington Philomathic Society. A meeting of the above Society was held in the Old Academy on Wednesday evening, the chair being taken by the president (Mr. Hedley H. Taylor.) The evening was devoted to short papers on James Watt, George Stevenson and Lewis Paul. The lives and inventions of these men were eulogized by Messrs. E. G. Burgess, C. H. Robertson, and N. Cook, junr., respectively, who delivered papers which were much appreciated by the members, and which calsed an interesting discussion.—A vote of thanks wasilassed to the openers, on the proposition of Mr. Sydney Burgess, seconded by Mr. J. Bamford', jun.

div.head: Will- of the Late Mr. W. C. Jones.
div.p: Will- of the Late Mr. W. C. Jones.

The will has been proved of the late Mr. W. C Jones, M.A., St. Asaph, J.P. for Cheshire and Denbigh- shire, at £404,434. Mr. W. C. Jones left to his wife during widowhood an annuity of £5,000 or interest; on her remarriage a life annuity of £5OO. He left £lO,OOO to the Skin Hospital of Manchester and Salford, but only in the event of his son failing to attain his interest and his daughter failing to have issue. The duties of the late Mr. Jones's. property will amount under the new scale to about ;02,000, whereas the duties under the scale hitherto in fare would have amounted to about £31,000. "HERALD" KITCHEN RANGES save 50 per cent of fuel.—Agent J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, 51 to 55 Bridge et., Warrington.—Advt. Penny Popular Concert.

The-re was another large attendance at the concert in Bold-street Wesleyan school on Saturday evening, and an interesting programme included songs,recitals, sketches, &c. Mr. W. Milne, who is a favoinite at these concerts, scorecta success with his songs "The waiter," "Nr. John Smith," " Undertaker," and several others. A recital by Mr. Wilson Nicholson, " Tantler's Sister,'.' caused much amusement, and a good song " When his mother-in-law is at home" was contributed by Mr. H. Addison. The humorous sketch, "April Fools," by Messrs. Dumbrowne and ll Addison was also thoroughly enjoyed. The Rev. T. Miller gave an address during the interval. TABLE AND HANGING LAMPS, new now designs showing.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt.

Musical and Dramatic Entertainment. A musical and dramatic entertainment arranged by Mr. and Mrs. Cooke, was given in the I.L.P. Rooms at Friars Green House on Saturday evening, and proved highly successful and enjoyable. Songs were given by Mrs. F. Cooke, and the Misses V. Cooke and L. Coke, and Miss L. Sims ; recitations by Miss Lotty Sims ; and violin solos by Master C. Cooke. Master F. Cooke gave a humorous sketch. A dramatic performance entitled "Miss Belinds's Burglar" was quite amusing and the folloming were the characters who acquitted themselves remarkably well :—Mrs. Belinda Pretty- love, Miss B. Cooke; Mrs. Johnson, Mrs. F. Cooke; Bertha Graham, Miss C. Cooke: Sarah, Mrs. H. Cooke; Policeman 146, Mr. F. Cooke. The proceeds are to be devoted to the Infirmary Million Penny Fund.

MOSELEYS FOOD.—" Made in a minute." Strongly recommended by the Medical Press and Medical men. Ask your doctor.—Advt. Women's Circle. Mrs. Simpson (president of the British Womdn's Temperance Association) took the chair on Sunday, assisted by Mrs. Harvey Cook: The choir opened with a temperance song. Three interesting and well- attended meetings have been addressed by Miss Lucy Broad, White Ribbon Missionary, who was invited es a joint effort of the Britiih Women's Temperance Association and the Circle. On Sunday afternoon she spoke especially to girls on " Walking in white, with some sketches from Korea," and pleaded for the open- ing out of girlish hearts to all that is beautiful and true in the conflict with what is shadowy and evil —the active influence that lives and tells. Many converted Korean girls had, she said, chosea for their new name "Blessing." By a telling illustration from plant life the necessity of taking the grip of the upward way was emphasized. When the tendrils took hold God would create "the white .life." Referring to her travels, Miss Broad said she had travelled 60,000 miles and spoke at 1,000 meetings. She concluded with some account of life in Madagas- car,• and gave a hymn in the native tongue. Miss Long helped with two solos. On Sunday evening the chair was taken by Mr. John Upson, who in a few remarks brought his vigour and hearty touch into the meeting. A duet" Peace," was given by the Misses Hamer. Miss Broad then gave a lecture, in costume and with curios, on Fiji and her graghip descriptions made the island real to her hearers. On Monday the chair was taken by the Rev. C. Harvey-Cook who pie- pared the way for the lecture. He dwelt with the reciprocity so helpful in Christian service,. The fol- lowing musical items were heartily received : Songs, "Beloved, it is morn " and " Because "Mrs. Ken- worthy; humorous recitation, Miss Dorothy Browne: songs," Stir of my heart " and'• The Garonne," Mr. W. Hughes. Miss Broad then gave what, if any dis. tinction may be made, was the best of her talks on "Life and Work in Japan." The first part was illustrated by good slides the lantern having been provided by Mr. Clatwortby, and later a Japenese boy and girl appeared in costume Fith curios and sang native chants, which brightened the descriptions.

the story of those days--Mr. F. Monks, J.P., William Jones, and,Mr. J. H. Knowles. The Society had a great struggle to undergo before any sub- stantial headway could be made. The Board realized the necessity of appointing a conscientious and hard- working secretary and manager and, at their invita- tion, Mr. Rathbone agreed to relinquish his position at /Messrs. Stubs's works and undertake the new duties at a very modest salary. At that time the goods had to be taken out in a handcart to the small number of MEM- bers, and several members of the Board used to assist behind the counter. Under Mr. Rathbone's careful guidance progress soon began, and Mr. Rathbone's first balance sheet showed tctal sales amounting to £7Ol, against £630 of the previous quarter. Ultimately the old shop in Sankey-s*reet became too small for the volume of business and the, society decided to erect the more commodious building which has recently been pulled down to make way for the handsome now premises now nearing comple- tion. After serving the society devotedly for twenty- five years, the members were so satisfied with his work that they presented him with a clock and ornaments, a display cabinet and a tea urn. The urn bears the following inscription :—" Presented to Mr., A. H. Rathbone by the members of the Warrington' Equitable Industrial Co-operative Society, in com- memoration of 25 years of loyal service as its manager and secretary, and also as an expression of their unabated confidence and earnest hope that he may long be spared to continue the services he has in the past so faithfully rendered. September 4, 1889." Mr. Rathbone's fidelity to duty, his keen desire to promote the best interests of the society and to encourage thrift iri the homes of the workers gained for him the respect and confidence of all who knew him. The Board from time to time acknowledged his worth and talents, and his counse I was always received with the respect to which it was entitled, coming from a man with such experience and business ability. In October 1905, on completing forty years service Mr. Rathbone was the recipient of a handsome token of regard. This took the form of a cheque for three hundred guineas and an enlarged photograph of him- self. The presentation was made at a crowded meet- ing, held in the Parr Hall, by Mr. F. Monks, whose friendship Mr. Rathbone had enjoyed for an unbroken ,period of sixty years.As showing the striking advance the society had made, Mr. Monks mentioned that the sales for the year; prior to Mr. Rathbone taking over the management totalled £2,545, whereas the sales for 1904 were £146,590. At the same gathering the President (Ur. T. Critchley) said that the prosper- ous condition of the society was due mainly to their worthy manager, who deserved credit "for the care- ful, and economical tact he had shown in the disposal of the funds he had to deal with, the able manner in which he had managed the business, and for the shrew d qualities he possessed in buying at the right time." In July 1907 Mr. Rathbone resigned his position and retired into private life. It is a monument to his exertions that the Society has now ten 'places of business in different parts of the town, with a membership of nine thousand and annual sales approaching £200,000. The Board of Management placed on record their high appreciation of his long services and the fact that he left the Society in a strong financial position—" one of the soundest in the Cooperative movement." It may be interesting to note that whilst he was associated with the Stores no less than £2,250,000 passed through Mr. Rathbone's hands. It may truly be said that his life-work was given to the advancement of the Society and it was a delight to him to see it grow in numbers and stability. He was thoroughly methodical and punctual in his habits and set a worthy example to all who worked under his direction. In politics he was a staunch Liberal but he shrank from taking any prominent part in public affairs and he could not be induced to offer himself as a candidate for the Town Council, although ha would have made a very useful representative in that assembly. He was for many years a member of the Liberal Club and of the Wartington Cricket and Bowling Club and enjoyed the good-will of all connected with those organiza- tions. He was a life-long abstainer ; in disposition somewhat reserved, but one( in whom the utmost reliance could always be placed. His wife, to whom he was greatly devoted, predeceased him five years ago.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ST. HELENS CHARITY SPORTS.

The Mayor of St. Helens (Alderman A. J. Foote) pre- sided on Tuesday night at the annual dinner of the Committee of the St. Helens Charity Sports and dis- tributed £l3O, the result of this year's effort. Tbe St. Helens hospital, Providence Free Hospital, and Nurses' Home received each, and the Fresh Air Fund £lO. SUNDAY NIGHT SCENE AT ST. HELENS.

Albert Tucker, a one-armed St. Helens hawker, was brought before the magistrates at St. Helens, on Monday, charged with drunkenness' using obscene language and assaulting Constable Matthews. The officer said that on Sunday night, when two other officers were locking up some men from Salisbury-street Tucker began to abuse the constables, and when Matthews interfered he collared him by the neck and began to kick. He kicked him about the ribs, End when they were on the floor aimed a kick at witness's chin, which he only partially evaded. Obtaining assistance he locked the man up.—Tucker was fined 10s. and costs, or fourteen days on each of the first two charges, and sent to gaol for twenty-eight days for assault—two months altogether.

HOME BROKEN UP.—COLLIERY CONTRACTOR AND HIS WIFE. At St. Helens, on Monday, Isaac Hughes a colliery contractor, of Sntton Heath-road, was dealt with on a charge of deserting his wife and child and leaving them destitute.—The Relieving Officer said that fifteen weeks ago the wife and child had to be taken to the Work house. The guardians had tried to get Hughes to make some offer, but he refused. He got as much as ,£l4 per week, but told the guardians that he bad to pay it out to the men who worked for him, and he often had as little as 17s. to take home. Hughes said that was so. Mr. Marsh : The guardians thought it was mare _ . .

likely to be £3 or £4. 'it was true that:when the parties were before the Bench over a year ago, the man proved that his wife had misconducted herself, but he took her back and forgave her. Since that time be had come to the conclusion that the man was as bad as the woman in many ways. The PolicelCourt Missionary said that the man broke up the home by drinking. Hughes was ordered to pay 30s. down or go to gaol for 28 days, and to pay 12s. a week in future.

div.p: Sir,—After having read your last week's editicn and noted the scathing remarks passed upon our town by the reverend gentleman at Burtonwood one might think he has done something clever in exposing the evils of our town. We know it is rather bad but he might at least dr aw a margin and not give it us in the very extreme. . .
There is a passage in Shakespeare that says: "The evil that men do lives after them,
The good is oft interred with their bones."

Perhaps his principles are based upon that passage. Seeing that he is continually looking upon the bad side of things, always extracting the evil and corrupt ,deeds and entirely ignoring the good ones, he might at least, seeing that he is a minister of the Gospel, look upon the good points of the town and not the bad ones. The bad points give us no encouragement, they rather make us feel just a little ashamed. I should be glad to hear his opinion upon the good side of Warrington. It would encourage us far more than his exposition on "The had side of Warrington."— Yours etc,
"A MARTYR."

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Merry Widow."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Merry Widow."

Warrington has waited a lodg time for "The Merry Widow," but the fascinating lady has at last honoured the town with a visit, and light welcome to our midst she is. There is no more attractive stage personality, and no play or musical comedy anything, like as nolnlar. "The Merry Widow" has had an astonishing run both in England and on the Continent, where it was first produced. People have raved over the catchy music, -the voluptuous dancing, and the gaiety of the whole thing, but satiety is not yet. Crowds have besieged the Royal Court Theatre every night, and the number of people who have made second visits is excellent testimony both to the play and the performance. We may say at once that the production here is first-class in every respect. The orchestral work, under the direction of Mr. Harry Burton, is such that no one can cavil at it, and the bewitching airs which have made Franz Lehar a notability and a wealthy man, are rendered with a delicacy and executive skill which compel admiration. The singing of the, various principals are uniformly good, and the mounting and dressing of the piece are superb. Altogether "The Merry Widow" is admitted to be one of the most finished productions ever seen in Warrington. What is Sonia—" The Merry Widow "—like? is one of the first questions an interested person asks 'before seeing the company. There have been many Sonias since the play first captivated the public, and they have all been good ones. Miss Sylvia May is entitled to rank among the best, though we should, of course, give the palm to such artistes as Lily Elsie and Emmy Wehleu. But Miss May is a charm- ing actress, with a splendid conception of the part. She realises to the full the exquisiteness of the comedy of the famous love-quarrel between her- self and Prince Darilo and the passages between the two are full of delight to the audience. In the famous waltz, she and Danilo are magnificent and are recalled as often as they can comply with the demand for more of tbis seductive scene. Miss May's singing, too, is capital and her interpretation of " Vilia " evoked a &tom of applause-, As Mince Danilo, Mr. Fred Leslie, also scores a great success. In our view he tends to slightly over-act the fine comedy of the first act, where the festive prince comes home rather the worse for a night out. Mr. Leslie must avoid appearing really drunk. In every other respect his acting of the part was high-class and indicstive of considerable ability. He is a Danilo -Whom the ladies will like, and that is the chief test. We must award high praise also to Miss Ada Thomas, who acts and sings brilliantly as Natalie, the wife of the Ambassdor. Her duet with Jolidon" For I am a dutiful -wife "was delightfully rendered on both sides. Mr. 'Ripley Evans makes an excellent Jolidon and is the possessor of a tuneful tenor voice. Much of the comedy of the more obvious type and therefore the more readily appreciated, is provided by Baron Popoff, the Marsouvian Ambassador. In this role Mr. Edward D'Arcy has great opportunities and truth to tell, he does not neglect a single one of them. In his mannerisms he was irresistibly suggestive of Eric Thorne, and was as funny as that great comedian himself. Higher rraise we could not bestow of Mr. D'Arcy. Mr. Fled Fowler, as Niscbe, the prince's valet, alp fulfils a comic part in good style, and greatly disEnguishes himself in the two dances with Frou Frou. That young lady is represented in the dainty person of Miss Katie May, who has a future as a danseuse. The "dense d'Apache " creates a furore. In so big a cast, it is difficult to particularise, and we can only add that the whole company is a credit to Mr. George Edwarde's iscrimindation.

div.head: OPENING OF THE NEW LOUNGE.
div.p: OPENING OF THE NEW LOUNGE.

There was a pleasing little ceremony at the theatre on Monday evening, prior to the first performance of A` The Merry Widow," when the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) formally opened the new barge which has been added to the building. The management are doing everything in their power for the comfort and convenience of patrons and the lounge, which occupies a position immediately over the old frontage of the theatre, is constructed and fitted on the most up-to-date lines, reflecting great credit upon Messrs. J. M. Green- halgh and Co., who had the work in band. Amongst those who attended the opening, in addi- tion to the Mayor, were : Councillot s Birtles, Councillor lingers, Mr. T. Longdin, Mr. lZ owson, Mr. Lister, Mr. W. Fletcher, Mr. J. M. Greenhalgh, Mr. M. Nicholls, Mr. Elleringten (St. Helens), and Mr. A. M. Loader (general manager of the theatre). Mr. LOADER expressed regret that Mr. Beecham was unable to be present to personally welcome the visitors, as he was detained in London. On his behalf be (Mr. Loader) offered those present a hearty welcome and be had great pleasure in asking the Mayor to declare the saloon open. The MAvon said he was pleased to accede to Mr. Beecham's request to perform that little function. They all knew how the Royal Court management were catering for the public amusement. They were bring- ing here some of the best pieces and some of the best companies, and they were making the theatre very nice and comfortable. That beautiful lounge had been added so that the patrons could take their refreshments at the intervals with comfort, and he was very pleased to declaie it open. (Applause). Mr. LOADER thanked the Mayor for performing that little duty. He said if any of them had seen that building two or three days ago they would have said it was an absolute impossibility to complete it by that evening. It bad been done, and it was nothing short of a miracle, and he desired to acknowledge the services of Mr. Greenhalgh, for the excellent manner in which he had pushed the work forward to com- pletion. (Applause). The health of Mr. Beecham and Mr. Loader and Success to the Royal Court Theatre" was then drunk, on the proposition of the MAyoR. A new electrical plant has now been installed at the theatre, and the interior of the builifing fitted with new electrical lamps, this work having been carried out by Mr. H. Rogers. div.head: FIRST VISIT OF "THE MARCH HARE."
div.p: FIRST VISIT OF "THE MARCH HARE."

Next week we are to make the acquaintance of the very latest, and what is, according to the unanimous verdict of each and every town visited, the funniest, cleverest and most original farcical comedy within living memory. Nothing like "The March Hare" has ever before been seen. The greatest dramatic critics of the country have stamped it as the most immediately successful play in the category of farcical Comedy. The author is Mr. Harold Smith, a gentleman well-known in the political world. Mr. Smitb is the prospective Unionist candidate for the borough of Huddersfield, and brother of Mr. F. E. Smith, K.O , M.P. The March Hare is presented by a company of artistes absolutely impossible to beat, each one is said to be the finest procurable in his or her line of business and the powerful combination includes charming Miss Aida Jenoure, Miss Babs Stuart, Miss Wanda Meryl, Miss Elizabeth Rosslyn, Miss Madge Severne, Messrs. Alfred Ibberson, Howard L. Tracy, Horace Sinclair, Walter T. Clifford and J. H. Roberts. The "March Hare "is a" scream " from start to finish, three hours of con- tinuous chuckling laughter.

div.head: ELECTION ISSUE,
div.p: THE ELECTION ISSUE,
MR. CROSFIELD'S MANIFESTO TO THE ELECTORS.
NO TRUCKLING TO THE LORDS.

Mr. CROSFELD yesterday sent the following in response to our request for his views on the present political crisis : Sir,—l very willingly reply to your ques- tions as to my opinion about the issues to be decided at the coming election. There are several: 1. First let us consider THE CONSTITUTIONAL ISSUE.

That supremely important question is, shall we or shall we not allow the Lords to usurp the right and power hitherto exclu- sively possessed by the nation to control its own taxation, and to give or withhold that support on which the life of Ministries depends. For my part I have not the least doubt what the final answer of .the people to that vital and fundamental question will be. It is extremely significant that,like the lesser luminaries in his party, Mr. Balfour in his speech at Manchester did not even refer to the Constitutional revolution which is to be attempted by the wild men of the Lords. I should not be surprised if he con- tinues to evade this great issue, just as for six years he has shuffled with the question of the taxation of food. But he will find that just as we have made quite clear what the disastrous consequences of food taxes would be, so we will make equally clear what would be the consequences of surrender to th Lords. And just as the English nation is much too wide awake to have anything to do with the one, so they will absolutely refuse to bow the knee to the other. 2. The choice lies—and it is another clear- cut issue which divides the Party of Progress from the Party of re-action—between the policy which accentuates, and that which tends to modify the existing disparities between extreme wealth and extreme poverty. 3. A decisive issue at the election put very simply comes to this—shall a small band of men (who happen to be the sons of their fathers!) be made to shoulder their fair share of the burden of taxation like men, or are they to be allowed to shift this burden to shoulders so much less able to bear it—the shoulders of their poorer and less fortunate fellow countrymen.

div.head: MENACE OF THE TRADE.
div.p: THE MENACE OF THE TRADE.

4. Years ago Lord Rosebery said the time would come when the country would have to decide whether the State should control the "Trade," or the " Trade " control the State. That time has come now. It is not many years since not indeed the licensed victualler,but the Lords of the Liquor Trade had their hand on Mr. Balfour's throat; can we doubt that the same silent but potent pressure has been brought to bear recently on both Lord Lansdowne and Mr. Balfour, and that the same powerful and menacing influence at the present moment overshadows the political horizon?

5.- If one turns to the constructive political programme which has been before the country one may fairly quote as another issue the contrast between a policy of con- ferring favours and piling up privileges for those who already have, to say the least of it, their full share of this world's goods, and that other policy which seeks the greatest good of the greatest number. In a masterly and comprehensive letter addressed this week to the electorate of Lancashire and Cheshire

that in the end the counsels of more states- manlike and far-sighted Conservatives in the House of Lords would be listened to, and many of them are absolutely opposed to the policy of the wild men," and indignant and alarmed at the reckless and suicidal course they are taking, but it seems that after all the more thoughtful men among the Con- servatives are not to be listened to.

THE WILD MEN OF THE LOIIDS and their allies, the precious gang of " Con- federates " in the House of Commons are to have their way. The unexampled toil Of the Ministry, of the permanent officials and indeed of the whole House of Commons which has passed the People's Budget is to count for nothing ! after a few days' discus- sion by a few score of ignorant and stupid but very selfish men it is to be wantonly destroyed. Regardless of • the fact that trade is improving and unemploy- ment is steadily diminishing (comparing this year's figures with last) these same wild men of the Lords will throw the whole system of taxation into a stato of chaos; they will derange the money market and credit in a way that will seriously hinder the normal and steady improvement of trade ;which is taking place; and they will even encroach seriously on the preroga- tive of the Sovereign. Yes, they are able to do this to-day, but every true friend of Progress, whether in England or Old Ireland, whether North or South of the border, nay, I had almost said every lover of his country must see to it now that ,we effectively curb the power of these pre- judiced and selfish men so that never again shall they be permitted to work such evil in the State.—Yours &c., _ _ A. H. CROSFIELD,
Hoylake. November 19th, 1909.

div.head: MR. CHURCHILL
div.p: MR. CHURCHILL

refers in his customary graphic and power- ful style to new taxes placed by the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer on the unearned increment of land values, and illustrates their immense importance to Lancashire. Both the tax on unearned increment and the other tax on undeveloped land, moderate as as they are----erring, if they err at all, on the side of moderation—are important as Mr. Churchill shows as a source of revenue. But we value the undeveloped land tax no less as a method of bringing land more easily into the market and as a means of diminish- ing the evil and curse of over-crowding in the more congested centres of our population. If one considers such a fact as that, or the system of medical inspection of school child- ren which has been adopted by the present Government; or Labour Exchanges ; or the contributory schemes for insurance against invalidity, and for insurance against the curse and evil of unemployment,—if one considers such remedial measures as these, and the humane provision that is made for the aged among our poor folk, I submit that we are absolutely justified in stating that such measures and such a con- structive policy do in the very best sense of the well-worn phrase, further "the greatest good of the greatest number." And as the Budget finds the money which enables the State to pursue this remedial and humane policy it helps to minister to necessity while refusing to pander to privilege.
.. - , -6. And is- it not A BITTER MOCKERY OF POOR PEOPLE

to say that these remedial measures are all very well, but as money has to be found for them by the State taxes must be put on beef and mutton, and bread and cheese to provide the revenue. The pinch of that taxation would be felt by every person of modest means in the land. It would press upon the clerk and the shop keeper, and upon all that large class of people in the country who depend for their living on small fixed incomes. It would reduce the comfort and lower the vitality of the whole of our artisan class and above all, worst of all, would afflict most severely the very poorest people in the country. And so once again at this election as at the last we are face to face with the gigantic struggle between Free Trade on the one hand and the insidious,reactionary and
PERNICIOUS POLICY OF PROTECTION on the other :

Protection which, both in food and clothing, increases the cost of the prime necessaries of life; Protection, which puts a premium on the indolence of inefficient manu- facturers at the very same time that it places shackles on the energies and enterprise of the more capable cap- tains of industry; . Protection which would bring in its train into the public life of England much of the corruption we see in America—corruption which is so bad there that many an honest man (too many alas) in the United States shuns politics as he would the plague. Protection which in this country would not only increase the cost of living, but would in the long run tend to lower the rate of wages to pay font.
Tli'es-e are some of the chief issues which will have to be fought out during the great and historic struggle on which we are now entering. I for one was inclined to think

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, November 20,1909
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, November 20,1909
EMMANUEL CHURCH SALE OF WORK

The annual sale of work in connection with ,the Emmanuel Church, was commenced on Wednesday and continued until last evening, in the Knutsford-road Institute. The following is a list of the stallholders : No. I, Mrs. Vaughan, Mrs. Lees and friends; No. 2, Mrs.A. Gandy and friends; No. 3 (Refreshment), Mr. T. Allen and friends; No. 4, Miss Straw and Sunday school teachers; No. 5, Mr. T. Lloyd and friends; N 0.6 (Flower and Fruit), Mrs. J. Bibby and friends; No. 7, Miss N. Gandy and friends; Tea-room, Mrs. E. Allen and friends.

On the first day the sale was declared open by Mrs. ZrEca ARMITA GE. The Rev. Frank Vaughan presided over a fair attendance. There were also on the plat: form :—Mrs. Armitage, Rev. John Yonge, and Mr. J. Bibby. The CHAIRMAN said that their Church had established itself among the churches of the town. Their work was needed in Warrington, and they were trying to do it. He was pleased to see Mrs. Armitage with them that day. Both she and her hnsband had been very good friends to them since the foundation of the Church. ' Mr. J. BIBBY, the secretary and treasurer; said that the sale of work was needed every year to keep on the work of the Church. They had no endowments, and no pew rents, and they had nothing to depend upon but the freewill offerings of the people who worshipped with them. It cost £3OO to £350 to carry on the Church every year. They had a very heavy debt on the Institute and they hoped that year by year to clear a certain amount out of the sale of work. They wanted about £lBO from the sale. Mrs. ARMITAGE said that when she was asked to come she was told that there was no necessity to make a speech and therefore she did not intend to make one. (Laughter.) She congratulated them on the way the stalls looked and also upon the beautiful things that were on the stalls. She hoped that there would be a great many bazaars and that all the stalls would be cleared. They wanted to get to work and did not want talk, so she bad much pleasure in declaring the sale open. (Applause.) Mr. W. ATHERTON proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Armitage. _

The REV. JOHN YONGE in seconding said that it was always in Mrs. Armitage's heart to do what she could beyond the limits of her own community and therefore to find her there that afternoon was the result of a natural desire to do what she could for Christian work. The speaker said that be had been at nearly every sale of work in connection with that Church ; be had taken a deep interest in it; and he believed he had been one of the first preachers in the Church. ;He 'wag glad to know that the Church had reached aunt' a point of,suocess as it had. He regretted that Mr. Vaughan was leaving the church and tbe town as he had always found in h;m a friend of the Free Churches. He hoped that the work to which he was going would prosper. (Applause). The motion was heartily carried and the sale was proceeded with.

div.head: SECOND DAY.
div.p: SECOND DAY.

Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS declared the sale open on Thursday in the presence of a good number of people. The Rev. Frank Vaughan presided. Mr. J. BIBBY announced that tbe result of Wednesday's sale amounted to .£5O 10s. 4d. (Applause), Mr. W. ROBERTS, ofter expressing his pleasure at being present, said that they had had their days of success—none greater than now—and they had had their days of anxieties and sorrows and disappointments. He thought that the members of the Church had deserved success, as they were entirely dependent upon their own personal efforts for the carrying on of the work of the Church. If the people were not interested and enthusiastic they were bound to fail, but the very fact that the Church had been so well sustained for many years was a proof that the principles which they advocated and so con- scientiously believed in had endeared themselves to a very considerable section of the community. In Mr. Brigg's sermon last Sunday at the Parish Church he had pleaded for greater unity amongst the various sections of the Christian Church. He (the speaker) was strongly of opinion that they should promnlgate that feeling. They all ought to co-operate with each other for great social reforms. Nothing bad pained him more to see the unwillingness of some to appear on the same platform with others because of their theological differences. The time had come when they must be put on one side. (Applause.) Nothing would have given him greater pleasure if members of the Established Church had shown their broad-mindedness by coming and assisting them that day and helped to make the sale a success. He hoped that they would live to see that spirit manifested. He regretted the departure of Mr. Vaughan and said that his going away would be a dis- distinct loss to the community. Mr. JOHN BIBBY proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Roberts and Mr. W. ATHERTON seconded. The Rev. F. VAUGIIAN in supporting thanked the ministers and lay people of the Free Churches for the help they had given him. He had occupied every Free Church pulpit in Warrington. He also thanked the members of his own church for their help and for their loyalty during the six years that he had been pastor. The resolution was heartily accorded and the sale then commenced.
The proceeds for the second day amounted to £44 7s. 2id
THIRD DAY.
The Rev. F. Vaughan declared the sale open last evening. The total rclult of the sale was £125 10s.

div.head: PROSPECTUS.
div.p: PROSPECTUS.

We would draw the attention of our readers to the prospectus, which appears in our advertising columns, of the Consolidated Bone and Animal Bye-Products Company, Ltd. The capital is £60,000 divided into 60,000 ordinary shares of £1 each, of which 49,000 (subject to the shares subscribed by the directors and other signatories to the Memorandum of Association) are now offered for subscription at par. The company has been formed for the purpose of acquiring the undertaking and business of Mr. Karl Weglau and Mr. Frank Fallholuner, carried on at Neuwied-on- Rhine and at Metternich, Germany, to carry on the various processes for utilizing bone and bone waste both in the German works and at a factory which it is intended to establish and equip in the Liverpool or Manchester district. The various articles now manu- factured by the factories out of bone are of everyday use, and consist of buttons, •studs, curtain rings, S:c. It is stated that the demand for the products of the concern is far in excess of the present capacity and orders are daily refused. The secretary and registered office (pro tern) of the company are Mr. R. W. C. M. Rogers, 1 and 3, Harrington-street, Liverpool.

div.head: MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
div.p: MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT.
" Elijah."

The brilliant success of the concert given in the Parr Hall on Wednesday evening must be a source of deep satisfaction to all well-wishers of the Warrington Musical Society. It is many years since the society entered upon a new season under such wholly encouraging circumstances and there is every promise that the public apathy which has so frequently been , deplored in these columns is at length to give way to enthusiastic interest and that a bright and prosperous era is in store for the society. Whatever the future may bring forth, warm congratulations are due to the: members upon the fact that Wednesday's concert: realized the highest expectations. It was good to see the hall crowded in every part —many people bad to be content to stand—but still more gratifying was the intelligent appreciation with which the in performance of Mendelssohn's great oratorio " Elijah" was followed. The work was happily chrsen. Produced for the first time in Birmingham in 1846, under the composer's own conductrrship, it has stood the test of time so success- fully as to rival in the estimation of the music-lo+ing public Handel's masterpiece "The Messiah." While its most stliking characteristic is an all-compelling dramatic intensity, the contemplative and tenderly .pathetic elements are not entirely lacking, as witness such beautiful and touching themes as " 0 rest in the Lord" and "It is enough." Mendelssohn succeeded in making his characters live - again; "mere musical pictures," as he termed them, did not fulfil his ideal. There is much strenuous choral and orchestral work in the oratorio, and it demands serious and painstaking study if the production is to he at all adequate. The members of tit() Musical Society applied themselves energetically to the task and.the finished performance of Wednesday is entitled to rank high in local musical annals. Allowing for the popularity of the oratorio, unquestionably the chief attraction to the majority of the audience was the appearance of Sir Charles Santley, the eminent baritone, in the titular part. A great reception awaited the distinguished veteran of the cocert platform and no-one is more deserving of honour, for Sir Charles has devoted a long career—he is now seventy-five— to the advancement of his art, uniting a rare charm of personality to his undoubted musical genius, and gaining affectionate regard far beyond the borders of his own country. Time has dealt kindly with Sir Charles. The fact that he is still able to take such an exacting part as that of the stern, zealous, and wrathful Prophet is sufficiently convincing testimony to the remarkable endurance of those vocal powers which have delighted the public for over half a century. The naturalness and earnestness of his singing appeal to everyone ; there is no affectation or resort to sensational methods to secure applause. Sir Charles held the hushed attention of the audience by the sympathy with which he interpreted the whole of the music, and at the Close of the difficult air " Is not His word like a fire," which was characterised by surprising fire and fervour, there was a great outburst of enthusiasm. Sir Charles also appealed to all hearts by the profound pathcs which he infused into "It is enough "—one of the most emotional items in ,the otatorio. The com- mittee had been equally fortunate in their selection of the other principals. Miss Emily Breare makes artistic use of a sweet soprano voice of splendid range and flexibility and her earnest and powerful rendering of "Hear ye, Israel " was meritorious in every respect. Miss Maud Wright acquitted herself with distinction in the contralto part, her excellent enunciation and refinement of expression being especially praiseworthy. She made full use of her great opportunity in " 0 Rest in the Lord " which she sang with a depth of feeling which will not readily be forgotten by any who heard her. Mr. Cynlais Gibbs, tenor, also achieved complete success, the audience being greatly moved by the soulfulness of his singing which, combined with the richness and purity of his voice, enabled him to excel alike in the joycus and stirring .` Then shall the righteous shine " and in the more devotional " If with all your hearts." Cordial acknowledgment must be made. of the valuable assistance rendered by members of the society— Miss Emily Taylor, Miss Jennie Armstrong, Messrs. J. H. Draper, J. W. Bibby, E. Pownall, and Walter Ray--in several choice concerted items. One of the treats of the evening was the bright trio" Lift Thine eyes " which was most tastefully sung by Misses Emily Breare, J. Armstrong and Maud Wright, the voices blending with charming effect. The pleasure of the audience was unmistakable, and a repetition was conceded. Another gem of harmony was the quartet with chorus " Holy, holy, holy." in which Misses Breare, E. Taylor, Wright and Armstrong were pleasingly associated. Of the work of the chorus it is possible to speak in terms of unstinted admiration. There was no suspicion of half-heartedness, the precision of !heir attack and the all-round attention to artistic details of light and shade being a credit alike to the enthusiasm of the members and the tact and skill of the conductor , (Mr. F. H. Crossley), who is especially to be compli- mented upon this happy consummation of devoted and untiring work. The exquisite tone colour of "He, watching over Israel" and the massive and , inspiring harmonies of "Thanks be to God" were , finely realised. The vividly dramatic and picturesque chorus "Behold ! God the Lord passed by "—the wards which are said to have originally suggested the idea of the oratorio to Mendelssohn—was given with thrilling effect, the striking contrasts being well brought out. Of the orchestra, it can justly be said that they too rose to the occasion and played through- out with taste and finish, under Mr. R. H. Pearson's skilful leadership. Mr. W. H. Payton, Moe. Bac. at the organ also contributed not a little to the success of a concert to which all concerned • are entitled to look back with satisfaction.

The great gathering on Wednesday affords eloquent proof that the recent publication of the history of the society, compiled by the hon. treasurer (Mr. J. P. Reynolds) and tbe special efforts put forth by the com- mittee and members to revive interest in the society and secure a largely augmented subscription list have borne fruit. There is no reason why this generous public support should not be continuous, for lovers of music have everything to gain by helping the work of the society as they will make it possible to give the highest class of concerts and to engage the leading musical talent of the day. We are authorised by the hon. treasurer to say that those who have not already subscribed may yet do so on payment cif two-thirds of the total subscription. The concerts to be given are :—" The Messiah" on December 27th (Boxing Day) and German's "Princess of Kensington" and miscellaneous second part on March 10th next year.

div.head: WARRINGTON BAND OF HOPE UNION.
div.p: WARRINGTON BAND OF HOPE UNION.

The annual Council Meeting of the above was held in Wadsworth's Rooms, Sankey-street, on Wednesday evening, when a large attendance of representatives of the various societies assembled. In the unavoidable absence of Mrs. Dodds, (president of the Union), the Rev. J. S. Hughes presided. Rev. C. Harvey Cook opened the proceedings with prayer.—The annual report of the Executive Committee was presented by Mr. F. Gandy (hon. secretary), which showed that a vast amount of practical Ns ork had been done by the Union throughout the year. The financial statement of the Union was presented by Mr. R. Pierce Williams (bon. treasurer), showing that the funds were in a healthy condition. All officers of the past year were thanked for their services, and the following were elected to serve for the ensuing year: President, Mrs. James Dodds; vice-presidents, Revs. John Yonge, H. Wall, C. Harvey Cook, Thomas Miller, J. B. Buglass, E. B. Keeling, R. E. Letheren; Thomas Gladding, F. Welwyn Kernick, M.A., Mrs. Simpson, Miss B. Dutton, Miss Naylor, Mrs. Walker. Mrs. Owen, Mrs. Garnett, Mr. A. Monnfleld. Mr. W. Clatworthy, Mr. J. J. Flab, Mr. Ben Few, Mr. E. J. Guest, Mr. Thornton, Mr, W. T. Moss; hon. treasurer, Mr. R. Pierce Williams: bon. secretary, Mr. I'. Gandy ; hon. assistant secretaries, Mr. H.Wooley and Mr. C. S. Fellows ; Press secretary, Mr. G. Whit- field ; auditors, Messrs, S. Gallop and Howells ; stock. takers, Mrs. Whitmore and Messrs. Gallop and Howell; accompanist, Mr. A. Clatworthy ; conductor. Mr. A. Spruce. It was resolved to hold a grand festival in the coming spring as in previous yea rs.Mr.G.Whitfleld gave a report of the AuturnualConference of theUnitedKingdom Band of Hope Union held at Cambridge as one of the delegates representing the Warrington Union, which was listened to with interest. He was heartily thanked for his services. At the close of the meeting the Rev. J, S. Hughes having intimated that in all probability that would he the last meeting of the Union in which he would take part owing to his removal to Coventry to take charge of a church, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to him for his services to the cause of Temperance during his residence of 16 years in the district, and a hope expressed that his life would be long spared to carry on the work which he had so much at heart, in his new sphere of labour. Mr. Hughes briefly responded and expressed the joy he had experienced in the Band of Hope work throughout the whole of his life.

div.head: TECHNICAL SCHOOLS.
div.p: TECHNICAL SCHOOLS.
PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT THE PARR
HALL.
The Practical Side of Education.

Thera was a large gathering at the Parr Hall on Tuesday evening,the occasion being the annual distribu- tion of prizes and certificates to the students of the School of Art, the Central Technical Institute and the Branch Technical Schools. Mr. Alderman William Oniton, chairman of the Liverpool Education Com- mitte, made the presentations and the proceedings were presided over by Councillor J. Fniton Smith (chairman of the Warrington Education Committee). Amongst others present on the platform were: The Rev. J. Davies, Councillor Birtles, and Messrs. A. J. Jolley, J. Upson and E. Plinston, (members of the Education Committee), Mr. J. Moore Murray (director of Educa- tion), Mr. R. B. Roberts (assistant director), Mr. E. S. A. Robson (principal of the Technical Institutes, and members of the teaching staffs. Before the meeting began an enjoyable organ recital was given by Mr. W H. Payton, Mus. Bac. _ _

The CHAIRMAN apoligised for the unavoidable absence of the Rev. Canon Stevenson and Mr. Henry Robetts. Continuing, he said there had been a marked improvement in the evening schools, which, he was glad to say, from personal observation, was even greater this winter than it had been during previous sessions; he referred to the close attitude of study which every class displayed when one visited it. (Hear, hear). That meant that they were realizing the importance of developing their education after they had p9ssed their school days, and more that impressed itself upon the the young mind the better hope would there he for their success in the future. (Hear, hear). THE PRACTICAL SIDE OF EDUCATION. - -

Alderman OULTON, in course of an interesting address, said he had for many years been impressed with the educational work of Warrington. He came from Liver- pool with no feeling of superiority, but gladly to avail himself of the opportunity of extending his knowledge by acquaintance with the work here. For many years Liverpool had derived light and learning from the War- ington Training College and be was glad to know that his friend Canon Stevenson was maintaining the high reputation of that institution. After reading the reports of the Director, he could congratulate Warring- ton upon a triumph in the work they were doing, a work which would show its wisdom in the future prosperity of the town. He hoped nothing in the way of public opinion would occur to lessen the enthusiastic manner in which the work was being carried on. He hoped they would carry the Council with them, notwithstanding that the work involved a somewhat heavy burden upon the ratepayers. Looking at the report of the Director of Education be was glad to think that the School of Art had regained its old reputation. One of the finest public buildings in Liverpool was adorned by the statuary work of Warrington Wood, and he would view with great regret any lessening of the importance and influence of the school that produced one of the most perfect sculptors of modern times. (Applause.) That section of the work represented by sculptors and painters of the higher order was, of course, a limited one in its appeal to the general body of students, but the work had an intimate connection with handicraft in its relation to design, and on that side the school was doing efficient work. He had no doubt that the students there would develop some very original faculties of design, and it I was in that direction that he looked for greater help, industrially, than to the higher form of work. With regard to the technical schools, he ventured to suggest some rearrangement of the curriculum in the direction of making the course of study in the elemen- tary schools more of an industrial and practical char- acter than it was. It was the idea of connecting the school life with the home life and the future work-a- day life they were now trying to give effect tomn the schools. Hit was to be done efficiently it must begin in the elementary schools, and they must begin now, quietly, not under any sense of excitement or hurry or under any apprehension that something like a cataclysm wonld occur if it were not done to-morrow. They had submitted to the mischief for generations and they were still here, and did not look so bad. (Laughter). The kindergarten system was the first step to bridge over the connection with the brain, the hand and the eye. The next thing that was done was the introduction of elementary science, then manual instruction, cookery, laundr3, and domestic science. By introducing into the schools more directry indt.strial occupations manual work—they were cultivating the brain and they got a more powerful brain to enable the students to efficiently perform their life work. Manual instruction, kindergarten, domestic science and elementary science with demonstration, all tended to brighten and vivify the intellect of the scholars, and they were better able to understand the lessons when they reached the highest phases of tuition than they would be without that instruction. He congratulated the Director of Education upon being able to present such a good report and he hoped the year which had just com- menced would be more successful than the past. (Applause). Alderman OULTON then distributed the prizes, the list of which was a very extensive one.

div.head: DIRECTOR'S REPORT.
div.p: DIRECTOR'S REPORT.

_ The DIRECTOR reported encouragingly on the work of the various institutions. There vas, however, one fact which was most depressing to education com- mittees, that was, the wastage owing to children leaving the elementary schools at an early age to go to temporary employments, which had a bad effect on the children's lives. It was the remarkable experience of the committee that a large number of children who had done well in the day school, commenced their business lives as errand boys, and this occupation prevented their attending the evening schools and continuing their education. Later on these boys began to learn a trade. and then they came to the evening schools to study and found they had lost so much of their element,ry know- ledge that it took them more than a year to get back to their former position. It was only the few determined boys who were not dis- couraged and gave up. The Education Committee had endeavoured to induce these boys and girls to attend the evening schools immediately on leaving the day schools, and in this they had met with some succe s. Boys leaving the day schools in the seventh or top class were now passed straight into the particular trade or business course of the evening school, and there, in the true sense, continued their education, so that by the age of 18 or ]9 years, they had a good general know- ledge of the theoretical side of their daily work. This method had proved so successful that the committee were prepared to meet the special requirements of students who had gone through a recognized course and were consequently qualified, by instituting special advanced lectures. VOTES OF THANKS. - - -

Mr. JOHN UPSON-Jr-1- proposing a vote of thanks to Alderman Oulton, referred to his valuable work as an educational administrator on the Liverpool Education Committee and the Liverpool School Board. In his address he had indicated the line of thought upon which education was now chiefly moving—that was, they were trying to make their methods more and more practical. While they hoped to profit by the Liverpool experiment, they were doing what they could in their own town in various ways in experimenting on the lines he had indicated. But there was a danger that the experiment might be carried to such an extent that they lost sight of the main thing. They held that a boy and girl, the youth and maiden, should have an opportunity of being educated to the very fullest extent of their capacity, but they could not fora moment begin to separate the children and students into the professions and trades that they would follow in after-life. What they aimed at in Warrington was to give an all-round education, to give every boy and girl an opportunity of developing all the powers they could, however limited the financial resources of the parents might be, or however handi- capped by environment. (Applause). As long as that was their ideal there would not be much wrong in the educational system of Warrington. (Applause). Mr. ROBSCN, headmaster of the Technical Institute, seconded and the motion was heartily agreed to, Alder- man Oulton returning thanks. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman said that unfortunately in Warrington public opinion was not always strong enough to see that real educational progress was assured, but if every one in that building was really keen in favour of educa- tion and stirred up his or her friends outside, the work of Councillor Fulton-Smith and others would be greatly lightened and they would see greater progress. (Hear, hear, and applause). A wise man said long ago "In the multitude of counsellors there is safety." He (Mr. Jolley) did not think that referred to Town Conn- cillors—(laughter—)but they bad a few who were keen in support or education and their chairman was one of them.
Mr. E. PLINSTON seconded, and the motion was heartily carried, the Chairman responding.

The Prospectus states among other things:— The Company has been formed for the purpose of acquiring the undertaking and business of Mr. Karl Weglau and Mr. Franz Fallbohmer, carried on at Netrvied-on-Rhine and at Metternich,Germany, to carry on the various processes for utilizing bone and bone waste both in the German works and at a factory which it is intended to establish and equip in the Liverpool or Manchester district. The demand for the products of the factories is far in excess of their present capacity, and orders are daily refused. The various articles now manufactured by the factories out of bone are of everyday use, and consist of buttons, studs, curtain rings, Scc. The bonedust forms a high-class and valuable fertiliser, for which there is a large demand. The vendors have recently entered into contracts for the sale during next year of 200 tons of perforated at a price of about £7 10s, per ton, which, with 60 tons still to be delivered under previous contracts, s htr realize about £1,900. so S. J. Cahen reports as follows : accordance with your instructions, I have liexamined the books of the Neuwieder Beinnopf Fabrik for the twouPll3hldalf-years from July 15th. 1908, to July 15th, 1909. Whereas the profits for the half-year ending 15-1-09 are equal to B,i per cent, those for the whole year ending 15-7-09 show a profit of a little over 18 per cent. yearly upon the capital employed. The profits are arrived at after charging all working and business expenses, including ample depreciation and after charging all interests. (Signed) S. ;r. CAHEN. Without taking into account the increased profits which should be derived from the purchase of raw material and sale of bye-products in this county, the Directors estimate that the profits of the three factories when fully equipped and working should, after providing for Directors'pfees, management expenses, and reserve fund, be snore than sufficient to pay a dividend of 20 per cent, on the capital of the Company. VALUERS' CERTIFICATE. We, the undersigned, have visited, inspected, and valued the freehold land and buildings, &c., belonging to, and comprising the works premises known as " Neuwieder Beinknopffabrik Franz-Wagner," situate at Neuwied am Rheim, in the Rhein Province of Prussia, and, in our opinion, the fair value thereof as for a current going concern (exclusive of goodwill) is the sum of .L 7,709. ROCKED BY EARTHQUAKES. The large island of Hayti, which also embraces the Republic cf Santi Domingo, one of the most beautiful countries in the world, has been rocked by seismic shocks during the past week, and many of the northern towns, inhabited chiefly by negroes, are in ruins. A terrible upheaval seemed to take place at the bottom of the sea, sending a wave of destruction running across the land to a height •of six feet. The loss of life is believel to be heavy, and both in Hayti and Jamaica the floods have caused unprecedented destruction to property. A Veteran Co-operator. Warrington has lcst another worthy son by the death of Mr. Arthur Hornby Rathbone, for forty-two years managing secretary of the Warrington Co-operative Society, who passed away at his residence Beechwood, Bewsey-road, on Satnrday morning at the age of 75 years. Despite his advanced age,Mr.llathbone until quite recently enjoyed fairly.robust health ,and was a familiar and respected figure in the town. Last week he was seized with pneumonia and died after only three days' illness. He leaves four sons and three daughters with whom much sympathy is felt in their bereavement. Mr. Rathbone's career was devoted to important and useful work, particularly on behalf cf the working classes, and he will long be remembered as one of the pioneers of the Co-operative movement. The son of Thomas Rathbone' a filecutter in the employ of Mr. Peter Stubs, Mr. Rathbcne was born on November 21st, 1833, and in his early years he was associated with the same trade as his father. His environment was calculated to assist in developing that sterling character which in later years stood him in such good stead, for with Mr. F. Marks and other young men he lived for some time with thp late Philip Carpenter,.the distinguished minister at Cairo-street Unitarian Chapel. Mr. Rath- bone was one of a small band of men who felt the time had come when an effort should be made to folio w the lead Of Rochdale in establishing a Coopera- tive Society. Only three of the pioneers remain to tell
